#### The Organizing Society: 

###### GDMB Society for Mining, Metallurgy, Resource and Environmental Technology 

The GDMB is a non-profit organization. Its activities focus on combining science with practical experience in the fields of mining, engineering, tunnelling, mineral processing, extraction, recycling and refining of metals, as well as on the manufacturing of semi and finished products. There is an increasing emphasis on associated environmental issues. The GDMB is internationally active with a European basis and covers a wide variety of topics from applied geology via processing to recycling. These include many important areas of chemistry, especially the complex metallurgical chemistry and, last not least, also analytical chemistry. As a consequence of their increasing importance, aspects of industrial minerals are addressed in addition to the traditional fields of metals and alloys. In order to remain a vibrant and attractive professional society, the GDMB draws on the experience and interests of its worldwide members.

#### Preface 

###### Copper – Indicator of the progress of civilization 

This is the motto for the 7<sup>th</sup> international copper conference, the most important copper seminar in the world, which has been organized by the GDMB, the German based Society for Mining, Metallurgy, Resource and Environmental Technology, together with IIMCh from Chile, MetSoc from Canada, TMS, SME from USA and MMIJ from Japan. 

The copper conferences bring together the highest level of science and technology: universities, metal producers, manufacturing companies, suppliers and finally the people who work with copper: scientists, technicians, engineers, traders and many more. 

An extensive programme has been arranged for this conference and an abundance of contributions from all over the world dealing with the different aspects of copper making and its use are registered already, for which we gratefully thank the authors. Apart from plenary addresses, separate sessions will be held for economics, mineral processing, pyrometallurgy, hydrometallurgy, electrowinning and -refining, downstream fabrication and application, process control and automation, recycling and sustainable development, environmental control, health and safety. Copper, one of the oldest metals used by mankind, is still today one of the most important industrial metals and indispensable for modern life. It is the indicator of industrialization and progress in every country. It is used everywhere, where electricity flows and thus is still valued so highly today. The increased economic potential of newly industrialized countries, above all East Asia and China, has increased the significance of the red metal once again. More recent technologies in production, processing and application often provide new answers to old questions. From the middle of the last century there was another innovation surge resulting in totally new technologies, a trend still going on. This has made each copper conference into an exciting adventure. It is positive and reassuring that particularly the high industrialized countries have become the vanguard, not just in technical innovation, but also protection of environment and nature and preserving resources. They repeatedly prove that ecology and economy may go hand in hand. 

Many sponsors have contributed to the conference’s success, for which I would like to express my sincere thanks! 

Hamburg is expecting its guests! Hamburg, the old Hanseatic city with a 1200 year long tradition, one of the biggest and most beautiful cities in Germany, combines a wonderful mixture of industry, commerce, nature and culture. Not only the “Copper 2010” in the Congress Centre awaits you, but rich offerings

of sightseeing and shopping in a cosmopolitan city, one of the largest harbours in Europe, the Alster lake in the city centre, green parks and plenty of cultural events, some of which we hope to show you in the companions programme. 

We are delighted that you will join us and look forward to a highly interesting conference! 

_Michael Kopke_ Chairman Copper 2010

###### Is the Copper Industry Fit for the Future? 

Dr.-Ing. Bernd Drouven, CEO, Aurubis AG, Hamburg, Germany 

The copper world has already changed a great deal during recent years. But what still lies ahead of us? What are the changes in conditions that we have to cope with and how will our solutions look? 

The rise in the demand for raw materials is unrelenting. At the same time, both the primary and secondary feed materials have a specific complexity, the customers’ needs are becoming increasingly differentiated and their orders are placed at increasingly short notice. Production times for metals have to be faster and inventories minimised. 

The volatility of the metal prices has increased significantly in recent years and we will probably have to live with that in the future as well. The LME functioned well in the crisis, but the copper price is being influenced more and more by funds. 

How can the value added chain change to adapt to this? Which consequences will that have for process technology, production planning and logistics? How will the consolidation of our industry continue? 

This keynote will go into the various effects and challenges – in particular from the perspective of a European custom smelter and fabricator – and present possible approaches for solutions. 

###### Sustainable Growth Strategy for Japanese Copper Business 

Toshinori Kato, Managing Director, Mitsubishi Materials Corporation, Tokyo, Japan 

Business environment, for any industry, has changed dramatically over the last decade. Copper industry is no exception and those involved are experiencing an unprecedented period of upheaval. The landscape of the market has completely altered, with large-scale M&As taking place among miners - creating an oligopoly situation - and a rapid expansion of smelting capacity within devel

oping countries, driven by strong economic growth. Traditional copper smelters and fabricators have been facing challenges, but a long-term sustainability of Japanese copper business is achievable. 

Firstly, an immense amount of effort has been made over the years to develop the clean and one of the most environmentally-friendly processes in the industry. Mitsubishi Materials (MMC) particularly plays a great role in establishing Japanese smelters’ reputation as the most energy-efficient operations in the world. It is our strong commitment to be a leader in this expertise by sharing our technologies with the industry. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

IX 



Secondly, infrastructures for copper smelting have been utilized in developing the recycling business. Exemplified by the operations at Onahama smelter, which has the world’s largest furnace for treatment of shredder residue, the industry has worked closely with other sectors and municipalities. Building an effective structure to make the best use of our facilities is a key for success in this field. It is fair to say that Japanese copper smelters, including MMC, are now regarded as an indispensable part of national environmental policy. 

Finally, progression of integration in the copper fabrication sector has strengthened the industry’s capability of providing a variety of high-value-added products to end-users. Tight relationships with the consumers have been beneficial in developing new use of copper. Evidence of a promising future can be seen in increasing use of copper in the growing sectors such as hybrid automobiles and renewable energy. 

###### Copper Sulphide Smelting: Past Achievements and Current Challenges 

Dr. Carlos M. Dнaz, Adjunct Professor, University of Toronto, Private Consultant, Toronto, Canada 

In the last three decades, increased oxygen consumption in copper sulphide smelting and converting and the implementation of computerized process control, among other factors, have led to higher process intensity and smelter concentrate processing capacity, decreased smelting energy consumption and improved SO2 capture from process gas streams. An annual primary smelting furnace throughput of one million tonnes of concentrate is the new industry standard. Top submerged lance smelting has become an important processing route in recent years. Two new continuous converting routes were commercialized in the 1990s. However, due to substantially improved converting practice and larger converters, Peirce-Smith converting still maintains its position as the dominant technology. 

A major realignment of world copper smelting has taken place in the last 30 years. Spurred by rapid economic expansion and the resulting huge increase in demand for basic materials, a number of modern, large capacity copper smelters have been built in China, India and other Asian countries. Only moderate growth in smelting and electrorefining capacity has taken place elsewhere. Moreover, ER cathode output in t

he USA has substantially decreased. 

In this paper, the author examines recent technological advances and industry changes and highlights issues, such as energy consumption and the corresponding greenhouse gas emissions that will become the focus of future discussion. 

###### Energy as a Key Factor of Sustainability 

Javier Targhetta, Vice President, Freeport McMoRan, Phoenix, Arizona, USA 

Energy must be seen as the prime mover for development and is therefore vital for economic equilibrium and social welfare. Energy will continue to play a key role in the coming decades being not only an environmental challenge but also a fundamental issue in terms of the progress of humanity. Nevertheless, harmonizing several aspects related to energy management will be of essence for the 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

X 



near future and will make energy one of the greatest challenges of the 21<sup>st</sup> century. It is becoming increasingly important to maintain the appropriate equilibrium between environmental issues (global warming, the future of nuclear waste, the integration of renewable energies…), coordinated governments policies to ensure that global energy costs are kept competitive and companies finding a balanced, rational and fair model of energy utilization based on the review of ethical business aspects and the establishment of social responsibility principles. 

This paper develops the idea that the rules and procedures for future energy use must be based on a reasonable equilibrium between technical aspects mainly associated to environmental issues, political decisions made by governments and public administrations and social responsibility programmes that companies themselves must assume and implement. 

###### <mark>The Supply and Copper Producer Response to a Growing Demand Scenario</mark> 

Ricardo Alvarez, General Manager, Codelco El Teniente Division, Santiago, Chile 

<mark>The prospects for medium and long-term consumption of copper are promising. A recovery projected for developed economies, starting 2010, joins the growing impact on demand generated from the process of development and urbanization of emerging countries. The intensity of copper use will also maintain the positive growth started a decade ago based on factors such as providing solutions to combat global warming.</mark> 

<mark>The objective of this presentation is to analyze how supply may react and adjust to envisaged demand scenarios, bearing in mind some distinctive elements of the copper industry like:</mark> 

- <mark>Historical supply reaction to demand and price levels</mark> 

- <mark>Availability of resources and copper ore reserves, incorporating a dynamic analysis and the effects of geological exploration and possible technological changes.</mark> 

- <mark>Pipeline of probable and possible projects, analysing the effects of projects in less developed and riskier geographical locations</mark> 

- Technological changes under development that may posi

tively impact the amount of reserves available and the competitiveness of projects. - The growing role of scrap as a supply source for copper. The analysis of these points will allow us to confirm the capability of supply response to growing demand, ruling out revisited hypothesis of insufficient reserves ###### Implementation of Recent Global Copper Projects Tim J. XVI|_er 2010_| _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ # Electrowinning and -refining 1235 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1236 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ ### Measurement of Bubble Size Distribution in Copper Electrowinning Process by Image Analysis Reza Al Shakarji, Yinghe He Simon Gregory James Cook University Xstrata Technology School of Engineering and Physical Science, QLD 4811 Hunter Street, Stuart, QLD 4811 Townsville, Australia Townsville, Australia **Keywords:** Electrowinning, bubble size measurement, image analysis, acid mist #### Abstract During electrowinning of copper, oxidation occurs at the surface of the lead anode and oxygen gas is liberated. The size and the burst mechanism of the oxygen bubbles are known to have significant effects on the generation of acid mist. However, little is known about the actual size and its distribution of the oxygen bubbles that are generated under typical operating conditions of a copper electrowinning tankhouse. This paper presents a technique for the measurement of oxygen bubbles formed in a copper electrowinning process. Live images of the generated oxygen bubbles were captured by utilizing a high speed camera, super bright LEDs and a special viewing chamber. MATLAB-based software was developed to analyse the images and to determine the size of the bubbles. The effect of electrical current density on the size of the oxygen bubbles was experimentally investigated. Results show that regardless of the current density applied, bubbles were found in various sizes ranging from 33 to 278 µm. They also revealed that current density had a negligible effect on bubble size distribution. The mean bubble diameter for three different current densities was found to be between 65 and 68 µm. The experimentally measured amount of acid mist was found to increase linearly with the increase of current density. Based on Faraday’s Law, the total volume of oxygen generated at the anode is linearly related to the current density. Since the current density had a negligible effect on the bubble size, it was postulated that the total number of bubbles generated at the anode was also linearly related to current density. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1237 _Al Shakarji, He, Gregory_ #### 1 Introduction Electrowinning is an electrochemical process that is used to extract metal from its solution, and is extensively used in the production of copper. More than 20 % of the world’s primary copper is produced through electrowinning [1]. In electrowinning of copper, a DC electrical current is p

assed between an anode and a cathode which are submersed in a copper-rich solution (electrolyte) [2]. At the inert anode, water molecules are hydrolysed and oxygen bubbles are formed at the anode surface. These oxygen bubbles grow and eventually detach from the anode surface and rise in the bulk of the electrolyte. These bubbles burst at the free surface of the electrolyte and produce highly acidic electrolyte droplets of which the fine ones become airborne and form an acid mist throughout the tankhouse of the electrowinning plant. 

Acid mist is highly corrosive and results in the corrosion of cathode plates, anode hanger bars, and other tankhouse equipment and building structures. Acid mist also poses a serious health hazard and causes extreme discomfort to the skin, eyes and respiratory systems of the tankhouse workers. Although it is known that bubble size directly affects the amount of acid mist being generated [3], no publications could be found in relation to the size of the bubbles that are generated during copper electrowinning. Furthermore, current density is known to influence the amount of acid mist generated. However, there have been no studies to quantitatively relate current density to the amount of acid mist. 

This article presents a method for the determination of bubble sizes. The method combines the use of a high speed camera and super-bright LED lighting for the capture of live images of the oxygen bubbles with digital processing of the images to determine the size of the bubbles. The paper also examines, quantitatively, the relationship between the amount of acid mist generated and current density applied. The acid mist amount is further related to the number of oxygen bubbles based on Faraday’s Law. 

#### 2 Methodology 

###### 2.1 Equipment setup 

Figure 1 shows the pieces of equipment and their arrangement used in this investigation. Essentially, the copper electrowinning process was replicated in a bench-scale cell. The cell was 220 mm long, 200 mm wide and 210 mm high and was constructed of 10 mm thick clear acrylic. The cell had an inlet and an outlet to allow the circulation of the electrolyte solution and also to allow the addition of the makeup electrolyte by a peristaltic pump. Four submergible heaters were placed in the corners of the cell to maintain a constant temperature of electrolyte for the duration of each test. 

To replicate industrial operations, Ca-Sn-Pb alloy and 316L stainless steel were used as anode and cathode, respectively [4]. A clear acrylic frame was constructed for each of the electrodes to control 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

1238 

_Bubble Size Distribution for Copper Electrowinning Process by Image Analysis_ 



the exposure of the electrode’s surface to the solution. The use of these frames ensured a consistent and precise electrical current density for all the experimental runs. The electrodes were placed about 50 mm apart. A double junction reference electrode was placed near the a

node to monitor the anodic potential during each experiment. 

An electrolyte solution (45 g/L Cu, 180 g/L H2SO4, 15 mg/L Guar gum, 20 ppm Cl, 100 ppm Co) was prepared that replicated a typical electrolyte solution used in a copper electrowinning tankhouse [2]. 



###### Figure 1: Equipment setup 

Capturing live images of the generated oxygen bubbles proved to be an extremely difficult task because these bubbles were typically less than 100 µm in diameter and they were produced in very large numbers on the surface of the anode. 

A number of different approaches were tried. The successful method was based on the transfer of the oxygen bubbles from the original cell to a viewing chamber (VC). This method is similar in 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

1239 

_Al Shakarji, He, Gregory_ 



concept to the HUT method developed by Grau and Heiskanen [5]. The VC was a relatively small, narrow and fully sealable box made of 2 mm thick clear acrylic. A clear PVC tube connected the top end of the VC to a vacuum pump while a flexible silicon tube connected the bottom end of the VC to the main electrowinning cell (sampling tube in Figure 1). The end of the silicon tube was free and could be placed at any location near the surface of the immersed anode. 

When the vacuum pump was turned on, the bubble-containing electrolyte was drawn through the silicon tube and transferred from the main cell to the VC. Because the VC was very narrow and also slightly tilted from the vertical, oxygen bubbles usually formed a single layer, making photographing of the bubbles much easier. In contrast, the bubbles in the main cell formed multiple layers which made it difficult to obtain clear images. A control valve on the clear PVC tube enabled the control of vacuum power and hence the number of bubbles entering the VC. 

A 130-µm diameter copper wire was fixed inside the VC adjacent to the electrolyte entrance. The diameter of this wire was used as a reference to determine the size of the bubbles captured in each image. 

High speed photography of micro sized bubbles required a strong light source that could penetrate the electrolyte solution. Super bright blue LEDs were utilized to provide sufficient background light. A semi clear white acrylic sheet was fixed to the back wall of the VC to disperse the light of the LEDs and to provide even illumination for the region of interest. A high speed camera (RedLake MotionXtra HG-100K) was placed perpendicular to the surface of the VC. A constant current DC power supply (GW Instek, model: SPS-1230) was used to deliver the required electrical current for the electrowinning process. The cell voltage and current were monitored by high sensitivity multimeters (Digitek QM1538) connected to the anode and the cathode. 

###### 2.2 Experimental design 

The main goal of the present work was to determine the effect of electrical current density on the size of the bubbles as well as its effect on the amount of acid mist generated. Three diff

erent levels of current density were applied (200, 300 and 400 A/m<sup>2</sup> ). Two individual experiments were performed at each current density, or six independent experiments in total. 

Each experiment was run for 30 minutes and acid mist was collected for the entire duration of the experiment. Bubble size image captures were conducted approximately once every seven minutes, giving four independent observations for each experiment. The bubble sizing process and acid mist capture are explained in more detail in the following sections. 

###### 2.3 Acid mist measurement 

Nitro cellulose filters were used to capture acid mist. These filters were 47 mm in diameter and had a pore size of 0.45 µm which ensured the capture of very fine acidic droplets. For each experiment, a fresh filter paper was installed at 45 mm above the free surface of the electrolyte solution inside

1240

the cell. The filter was hold by an inverted funnel and connected to an air pump via a pneumatic tube. A flow meter with a built-in valve was installed on the pneumatic tube to ensure a constant air flow of 5 L/min through the filter for the duration of the experiment. 

At the end of each test, the used nitro cellulose filter was removed from the cell and placed in 25 mL of deionized water and then stirred for about 60 minutes. The pH of the solution was then measured and the amount of the captured acid was calculated as the grams of sulphuric acid per cubic meter of air flown through the filter. 

###### 2.4 Bubble size measurement: Image acquisition and processing 

For each electrowinning test, a set of images were captured approximately every seven minutes. A high shutter speed was used to ensure the clarity and sharpness of the bubbles in the images. Each set of images contained 750 photos captured at 250 frames per second. 

Manual bubble sizing was attempted by using the ‘Measure and Label’ Plug-in feature of the Image J software (version 1.40). In this method, a circle was drawn around each individual bubble. The software would then label each of the identified bubbles and measure the diameter of the corresponding circles. High accuracy and selectivity (i.e. ignoring the out-of-focus bubbles) were the main advantages of the manual bubble sizing technique. This technique, however, was time and labour intensive. The processing of a typical image containing, for example, 100 bubbles would take about 2 hours. 

As an alternative, a MATLAB-based code was developed (named ‘The Bubble Detector’) to automate the image analysis. The Bubble Detector, unlike Image J, was capable of processing grey scale bubble images without the need of converting them to binary format. The Bubble Detector analysed each image in the following steps: 

1. Improved image quality by eliminating uneven illumination effects and background noise 

2. Enhanced bubble contrast and sm

oothed out the image 3. Detected the edges of all the objects that appear in the image 4. Filled the holes of the detected enclosed objects and ignored the open or too small objects 5. Distinguished circular objects (i.e. bubbles) from other objects in the image 6. Calculated the area and the diameter for each of the detected bubbles based on the size of the reference wire 7. Highlighted the detected bubbles on the original image and exported the results to an Excel file The Bubble Detector was tested on several images. In all cases, the software successfully detected almost all the bubbles that appeared in each image. When measuring bubble size distribution through the viewing-chamber arrangement, a major issue is to ensure that no bubble breakage or coalescence occurs during the transfer process. The diameter of the sampling tube and the applied vacuum are two important factors in bubble size measurement. Incorrect setup of either of these two factors could lead to bubble coalescence or breakage in the transfer tube which would result in biased bubble size distribution measurements [8]. Tucker (1994) suggested that bubble breakage was significant when the diameter of the sampling tube was not large enough for the big bubbles to pass through easily [9]. The diameter of the sampling tube, shown in Figure 1, was three orders of magnitude larger than the largest bubble detected. Therefore, no bubble breakage was expected to occur at the entrance of the sampling tube. Through the valve on the PVC tube, the suction rate of the solution from the main cell was controlled at sufficiently low levels to ensure no breakage of bubbles during their transfer from the main cell to the VC. 

Literature suggests that bubble coalescence is highly unlikely in a solution where different ionic species are present at high concentrations [10]. Since the utilized copper electrolyte solution contained several ionic species at high concentrations, bubbles were not likely to coalesce while inside the solution. 

To confirm the measured bubble size in the viewing chamber was a true reflection of what was at the anode, video footage was taken from the surface of an operating anode. This confirmed that neither breakage nor coalescence took place in the electrolyte or during the transfer process.

#### 4 Conclusions 

Acid mist is a serious issue in copper electrowinning tank

houses worldwide. Although oxygen bubbles generated at the anode are known to be the major contributor to acid mist, no systematic studies have been conducted to investigate the nucleation, growth and burst mechanism of these bubbles. 

In the present work, live images of the ascending oxygen bubbles were captured. MATLAB-based software was developed to analyse the images and to determine the size of the bubbles. Bubbles were found in various sizes ranging from 33 to 278 µm. The heterogeneous surface of the anode was identified as the main factor for such wide bubble size distribution. 

Bubble sizing at different current densities revealed that current density had a negligible effect on bubble size distribution. The average bubble diameter at three different current densities was found to be between 65 and 68 µm. 

At higher current densities more acid mist was detected. The number of generated bubbles was accurately predicted at different current densities, based on the bubble size distribution data. Both the amounts of generated acid mist and the total number of generated bubbles were found to be linearly related to current density.

**Keywords:** Electrowinning, cathode, stripping, robotic, refining 

#### Abstract 

Copper cathode stripping machines and stainless steel cathode plates are critical elements determining the longevity, productivity and efficiency of modern tank houses. In the last decade notable innovations have been the ISA 2000 and Kidd robotic cathode stripping machines, and enhanced integration with the overall electrode handling system. The acquisition of Falconbridge by Xstrata in 2005 provided a unique industry opportunity to bring two competing technologies together and has led to the development of a new stripping system which accesses the successful IP, experience and know-how of both ISA and KIDD systems of the past. 

This paper presents a new copper cathode stripping system, developed and prototyped by Xstrata Technology in 2009, for the electro refining and electro winning industries. It features the use of robots for both the handling and stripping functions, providing a highly reliable, low-maintenance handling system. The flexibility that comes with robotic operation also offers shorter delivery time, simplified installation and high operational capacity. 

The performance, safety and efficiency features of the new Xstrata Technology Robotic Cathode Stripping system are presented, along with an introduction to flow on impacts for other areas of tankhouse design and operation.

Invented and commercialised by Mount Isa Mines, the ISA PROCESS<sup>TM</sup> was first implemented into Copper Refineries Limited (CRL), Townsville, in the 1970’s. The KIDD

###### 2.3 Electrode Handling Systems 

Efficient integrated electrode handling is paramount to a productively operating efficient tankhouse. The prime objective of the cathode stripping machine is to safely process the copper as quickly as possible, in order to minimise the downtime associated with cathode stripping operations. In business terms, asset utilisation and productivity comes through continuous plating of copper and this cannot occur unless blank SS Cathode plates are routinely returned to the electrolytic cells. Lost time efficiency from stripping operations generally accounts for around 4-6 % in electro-refining operations. 

The electrode handling system productivity depends on both mechanical and process factors. This section considers the main process related factors that affect overall cathode stripping machine throughput. Common causes of reject copper in the CSM are briefly given below: 

1255 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Aslin, Eriksson, Heferen, Sue Yek_ 



- **Thin copper deposits** are caused by short circuits, limited plating time, poor alignment or poor electrical contacts. Thin copper is difficult to separate from the stainless steel plate due to its lack of rigidity, and generally requires rejecting and manual stripping. 

- **Sticky copper deposits** are generally related to poor surface condition on the cathode plate, such as corroded surface or improper mechanical treatment. These are also problematic to separate in the flexing station. 

- **Heavily nodulated cathode** can often cause stoppages in the cathode stripping machine as the protruding nodules interfere with guides and other parts of the machine. It is generally more efficient to reject these plates than to attempt to strip them through the machine and risk long interruptions to the stripping. 

- **Laminated Copper** is a particular issue that occurs with ISA 2000 cathode stripping machines. This results when DC power supply to the electrodes is stopped during the growth cycle, then resumed again, causing a lamination in the cathode deposit. While these events are rare, they can have a significant impact on cathode stripping rate for the affected cathodes. 

ISA 2000 stripping relies on the separation of the ‘frangible’ portion of copper inside the bottom edge v-groove, see Figure 1. This portion has a natural line of weakness starting from the void inside the v-notch and travelling downwards vertically through the deposit. Laminated cathode has a secondary line of weakness along the lamination which often affects the ease with which the two sheets can be separated. The ISA 2000 cathode stripping machine successfully deals with this cathode by detecting splitting failure and automatically carrying out one or several repeat down-ending cycles (referred to as ‘flapping’), however does lead to slower overall stripping rates as reported at the Hitachi refinery [6].

###### 4.1 ISA 2000 CSM 

The ISA 2000 Waxless machine use

s hydraulics to drive a set of stripping knives downwards in between the copper cathode and stainless steel blade. This machine opens the copper envelope approximately 30 degrees each side (60 degrees total). The grippers then engage onto the copper sheets and the down enders rotate downwards about the bottom edge of the cathode until the copper sheets are taken just past horizontal position (approximately open to 195 degree angle). If separation does not occur, the downenders go up and down repeatedly (flapping) until the copper fatigues, cracks and separation occurs. The copper is then dropped onto a transfer conveyor where it is taken to be sampled, weighed, labelled, bundled and strapped. 

The ISA 2000 CSM’s have been operating successfully in refineries and electrowinning operations since 2001. They provide full control of copper sheets, produce a split sheet copper cathode product bundle and require minimal operator intervention during stripping.

###### 4.2 ISA 2000 Flexor Stripper 

This stripping system is a development based on the proven low capacity flexor stripper system patented by Xstrata Technology for use in electrowinning operations to allow operation without bottom edge strips or wax. The ISA 2000 Flexor Stripper uses a similar stripping function to that of the high capacity ISA 2000 Waxless machine. 

The hydraulically driven knives on this machine extended the full width of the plate. This allowed the support and application of the stripping force across the full width of the stainless steel blade and copper, respectively. It also worked well in helping maintain a straight copper cathode in addition to aiding the separation of the cathode in the corners where it is generally more difficult to separate as shown in Figure 4 and Figure 5 below. 





Figure 4: Thin Wedge, curved copper Figure 5: Full Width Wedge, due to separation issues on uniform copper separation edges due to faulty edge strips 

The first set of knives typically opened and split the copper. The secondary set of knives was used only when the bottom bond was strong or separation didn’t initially occur (by opening the copper to the horizontal position). If separation still did not occur, flapping arms raised the copper back up to approximately 45 degree opening (90 degree open envelope) and then the knives were used again to bring it back down. Both sets of knives were attached to a “cassette”

allowing the first set of knives to get closer to the bottom edge of the cathode (pivot axis of the copper envelope). The cassette moved up and down vertically and also had the flexing station attached. 

This design allowed a full function machine to be compressed into the size of a single station making it ideal for space or capital limited operations, although cycle time is extended.

#### 5 The New Concept 

It was apparent from the previous research and test work that the point of force application on the copper cathode had a substantial impact of the separation reliability. This was the main driving factor in the design and development of the new CSM process concept. 

The following design parameters for the new concept were set based on the test work and operational experience from both the ISA and KIDD stripping systems: 

- Small opening angle – Initially open the copper envelope as minimal as possible to prevent any bending of the copper in the sometimes weaker section just above the bottom edge of the envelope. 

- Full width mechanism – Support the full width of plate (eliminate risk of plate damage) and copper (maintain straight flat copper cathode). 

- Maintain or Increase Speed – Maximum speed to ensure fast cycle times. 

- Reliability – be able to strip the complete range of deposited copper from normal operating conditions to laminated. 

- Reduce Friction – to provide an efficient and lower maintenance machine. 

The following prototype was designed and constructed for initial testing on site at CRL. It comprised of four vertical members profiled in the shape of a wedge, it was designed to support the entire face of the copper cathode when rotating or stripping (Figure 8). The sharp angle allowed the wedge to reach the bottom whilst maintaining a minimal opening angle on the way down to prevent the copper bending as mentioned previously. The arms on either end locked in to a horizontal shaft to help keep the wedge in position during rotation, ensuring that the wedge made it to the bottom and guarantee that all forces were applied into the correct position on the copper cathode during separation.

###### 6.3 Stripping Process 

The process in which the wedge works is similar to the original ISA 2000 waxless stripping machines. However, in this case the knife, grippers and transport conveyor are all in the one apparatus. Figure 12a-c provides a snapshot view of the movements of the new Robotic stripping wedge and its flexibility. 

The permanent stainless steel cathode is presented in the stripping station already flexed and preopened, the robots then bring the knives in tip first until the blade is approximately 50 mm past the top of the copper. At this point, the wedges start rolling to a vertical position whilst they are travelling in a downwards motion (the tips of the knives only mm away from the blade on each side). Once the wedge is down far enough to clear the hanger bar (shown by recess in wedge profile) the wedge is completely vertical and the rollers are touching the stainless steel blade keeping the knife edge away and unable to cause damage. 

Figure 12b shows each of the wedges in the bottom position just before down ending. At this point the grippers are activated and the copper becomes clamped. Both wedges roll to horizontal about an imaginary axis which is perfectly aligned with the void in the copper envelope cause by the v- groove. Once horizontal, the wedges rise slightly and then pull away from each other separating the copper and transporting it away to a bundle, transfer conveyor, weighing device, reject bundle, sampling device or any ot

her station the customer desires.

###### 6.4 Performance and Results 

Testwork of separation efficiency to date has been outstanding. No flapping has been observed in the Robotic Stripping system when processing standard V- grooved stainless cathode plates, with laminated copper cathode. When processing stainless cathode plates prepared with significantly reduced V-groove condition and laminated copper deposit, a maximum 3 flapping motions were required. 

If the copper did not separate on the first attempt, the robots “flap” the copper in a specific program sequence. Importantly, there is no bending in the copper and all the forces are concentrated in the same location leading to the vastly reduced flapping frequency. 

With increased separation reliability, the average cycle times gets closer to the designed cycle times providing operators with satisfaction and guarantee that they will meet throughput and production requirements irrespective of copper deposit conditions. 

Testwork on the Robotic Stripping prototype is ongoing, and in parallel it is used by the Xstrata Copper operating refining to process stainless cathode plates rejected from the commercial stripping machines.

### Evaluation of Mist Suppression Agents for Use in Copper Electrowinning 

Jack T. Bender 

Cognis Corporation 2430 N. Huachuca Drive Tucson, AZ 85745, USA 

**Keywords:** Mist suppression agents, acid mist, surface tension, cathode quality, experimental 

#### Abstract 

Copper electrowinning systems generate corrosive sulfuric acid aerosols as a by-product of oxygen gas evolution at the anode during the electrowinning process. New mist suppression agents were synthesized that reduce the surface tension of the highly acidic electrolyte solutions decreasing the surface energy of the oxygen bubbles. The oxygen bubbles will then burst at the liquid surface with much less energy, thus ejecting smaller electrolyte droplets with less force. Three classes of suppressants were synthesized and tested: alkylbetaines, amidobetaines, and substituted TMP 7EO compounds. Although all of the compounds tested were able to suppress acid mist, the alkylbetaines were substantially more effective mist suppressants. In addition to reducing acid mist, these additives also resulted in smooth cathodes with no visible nodulation or dendritic growth. 

#### 1 Introduction 

In the industrial electrowinning (EW) of copper from electrolyte solutions, substantial amounts of sulfuric acid aerosol are generated which is a major concern. This aerosol is generated when oxygen bubbles, produced at the anode, rise to the surface of the electrolyte and burst, ejecting droplets of the electrolyte into the air. Typically electrolyte contains a high concentration of copper (>30 g/L) and sulfuric acid (160-200 g/L), along with other metals and chemical reagents. The aerosolized electrolyte is corrosive to operational equipment and can pose a health risk to anyone working in the tankhouse [1]. Various methods have been used to minimize acid mist including: chemical mist suppression additives [2, 3], physical barriers, extensive ventilation, combinations of these techniques [4], as well as other less conventional methods [5]. 

Controlling acid mist generation is essential to reducing the d

etrimental effects on plant infrastructure and remaining below the regulated exposure limits. Many tankhouses have either been built or 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

1271 

_Bender_ 



retrofitted with mechanical barriers or forced ventilation. Physical barriers are either placed in the electrolyte or are suspended above the surface. Plastic balls, screens and brushes have all been used with or without chemical additives to reduce acid mist. Additional ventilation is often used in conjunction with other mist suppression methods. Forced ventilation does not mitigate the acid mist; it pushes the mist out of the tankhouse into the surrounding area which can still result in adverse affects for plant equipment and personnel. 

The most effective means to reduce acid mist has been the addition of chemical compounds which reduce surface tension (ST) resulting in less energy on the surface of the oxygen bubbles which in turn reduces the amount of electrolyte ejected from the solution [6]. FC-1100 (Fluorad™) manufactured by the 3M Corporation is the current industry standard chemical additive for mist suppression. To a lesser extent, foaming chemical additives have been used in electrowinning systems [2-3, 7-10]. Mistop<sup>®</sup> (distributed by Fenix Hydromet), Dowfroth™, and alkylated ethoxylates patented by BASF [11], are foaming agents that reduce acid mist by trapping the oxygen bubbles and impeding the ejection of mist. One potential problem is that the foam can trap oxygen on the surface of the electrolyte and organic resulting from the entrainment of circuit organic. This organic has a substantial amount of a kerosene fraction that can become flammable in the presence of the high oxygen atmosphere at the air/electrolyte interface. Studies have shown that surfactant foams used in electrowinning systems can ignite if there is a spark in the presence of organic contamination from the solvent extraction system [12]. 

In this paper, we report the mist suppression capability of some surface tension modifiers. Small changes in chemical structure resulted in large differences in the quantity of acid mist generated. One of the compounds in this work, EnviroMC<sup>®</sup> 1000, has been tested in a large scale pilot plant (30,000 L electrolyte inventory) and a full scale plant [13]. Results of this testing are still being evaluated.

Oxygen bubbles reaching the surface will then burst with less energy, resulting in smaller droplets being ejected at lower velocity. In order to reduce the surface tension of the electrolyte, various chemical compounds (Figure 1) with surfactant like properties were synthesized and tested. The compounds in this work were chosen based on passing cr

In summary, we synthesized various surfactant like molecules that were compatible with the solvent extraction/electrowinning (SX/EW) system. These compounds were able to significantly reduce surface tension, albeit to varying degrees. As expected, the reduction in acid mist for these additives was relative to their ST re

### The Simulation of Current Distribution in Cells During the Electrowinning of Copper 

Dr. Anthony Blackett, Prof. Michael Nicol 

Murdoch University, Parker Center South Street Murdoch, Western Australia 

**Keywords:** Electrowinning, copper, current, distribution, simulation 

#### Abstract 

A common problem in the electrowinning industry is that of maintaining a uniform current density across both surfaces of each electrode, while also ensuring that the current is equally shared among all the electrodes and cells throughout an operating tankhouse. One way to study this problem is to model the current distribution both on each electrode and between electrodes and cells in a simulated tankhouse. 

A circuit analysis approach has been implemented to model the current distribution within a simulated tankhouse using off-the-shelf electronic circuit simulation software. An electrode model developed to incorporate the main characteristics of contact and solution resistance, overpotential and reversible potential provides the basic building block for the construction of a simulated electrowinning tankhouse. The resulting model is flexible and easily modified to allow the simulation of various conditions and changes in parameters so that their effect on the distribution of current in the tankhouse can be evaluated. 

Several examples will be shown which reveal the effects of poor electrode alignment, electrical shorts, poor contacts, removal of electrodes and busbar/contact system on the distribution of current in cell and the effects on adjacent cells. 

#### 1 Introduction 

An ongoing issue within the electrowinning industry is current distribution and its effect on deposition rates on individual cathodes and also among multiple electrodes in each cell throughout an operating tankhouse. Successfully modelling these aspects of the electrowinning process should lead to improvements in energy utilisation and optimising deposition rates, while minimising uneven plating, dendritic growths and short circuits. Uniform current distribution is becoming increasingly important as the trend to higher current densities in the industry continues. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

1281 

_Blackett, Nicol_ 



One can consider the problem in two parts. The first involves the distribution of current distribution on the faces of a single cathode which relates directly to the uniformity of deposition on the cathode. The second considers the current distribution in a cell of multiple elec

trodes and in a tankhouse of multiple cells, which affects the uniformity of plating across all the cathodes in an electrowinning operation. 

A full rigorous treatment of the current density distribution in a single electrochemical cell involves 2 the mathematical solution to Laplace’s equation, ∇ φ = 0 for the potential φ in the electrolyte under a given set of boundary conditions. Extension of this detailed mathematical approach to a model of an electrowinning tankhouse would require solving the Laplace equation simultaneously in many interacting electrochemical cells. The computational effort needed to solve such a large problem would not only be impractical, but unlikely to yield results that would significantly improve on a simpler approach. 

This paper describes a relatively simple but effective approach to the simulation of the second of the above current distribution problems. In this method, an electrical circuit analysis approach using commercially available software has been adapted to describe an equivalent electrical circuit of a cathode/anode pair and this,in turn, is used as a building block to simulate the operation of an array of cathodes and anodes connected in various configurations to emulate operating conditions in an electrowinning tankhouse. 

#### 2 Description of the Model 

National Instruments’ (Electronics Workbench) Multisim 10 has been chosen for the task of constructing and simulating the electrical equivalent of a small electrowinning tankhouse. Multisim is based on SPICE, a general-purpose circuit simulation program developed at the University of California. The program handles the design and simulation of complex electrical circuits, which can include both standard and customised linear and non-linear devices. Circuits can be easily modified and the operating states can be measured and logged to determine voltages and currents at any point in the circuit. 

###### 2.1 A DC Electrical Model of an Electrode

A realistic electrode model should include electrical equivalents for the reversible potential and the overpotentials at the anode and cathode. In addition to these electrochemical characteristics, the voltage losses associated with the busbar, the contacts between the electrode hanger bars and the busbar and that in the solution between the electrodes should be added. 

Contact/busbar and solution resistances can be modelled using fixed resistors with an appropriate value. For the reversible potential potential of each electrode, a simple DC voltage source provides a suitable model.

The reason for this is that in the first cell, cathode C10 is fed a higher current from anode A11 (end effect) and this then feeds directly into anode A10 of cell 2, increasing the current flow to cathodes C9 and C10 in t

One of the reasons proposed for implementing the segmented inter-cell busbar system over the Walker system is that it should localise short circuits [1] and thereby improve current efficiency. Thus, one can compare simulations of the effects of a shortcircuit on the two systems (right hand plots in Figures 7 and 8). In the Walker configured tankhouse (Figure 7), large current flows through the short circuit, resulting in a near uniform 40 % drop in current density on the remaining cathodes of the shorted cell. The same considerations apply to disruptions during cathode harvesting in that these can have a greater impact on other cells in a segmented bar than a Walker configuration. The Walker inter-cell busbar system remains an effective configuration for maintaining a near-ideal current density distribution. 

#### 4 Conclusions 

A circuit analysis approach has been implemented to model the current distribution in a simulated tankhouse using electronic circuit simulation software. An electrode model developed to incorporate the main characteristics of contact and solution resistance, overpotential and reversible potential provides the basic building block for the construction of a simulated electrowinning tankhouse. The resulting model is flexible and easily modified to allow the simulation of various conditions and changes in parameters so that their effect on the distribution of current in the cells can be evaluated. 

Several examples have been shown which reveal the effects of poor electrode alignment, electrical shorts, poor contacts and the removal of electrodes and busbar/contact system on the distribution of current in a cell and the effects on adjacent cells. A comparison has been made of the effects of short-circuits on the current di

stribution in a conventional Walker system with that using a segmented inter-cell bar system. Although the latter reduces the effects within the affected cell, the effect of a short-circuit is tranmitted to adjacent cells while the effect on adjacent cells is minimal with a Walker system.

**Keywords:** Thermodynamics of precious metals, decopperized anode slime smelting, dorй matte refining, dorй metal refining, Ag-Se-O chemical potential diagram 

#### Abstract 

The state of the art of the dorй metal fire refining process is reviewed from a theoretical point of view, particularly focused in the thermodynamics of the equilibrium as well as in solutions theory of the multicomponent diluted silver alloys at 1100 ºC. 

Considering the most recent information from technical literature, the main interest of this paper is oriented to obtain an update of the chemical potential diagram of the Ag-Se-O ternary system at 1100 °C. The exhaustive thermodynamical data of the Ag-Cu-O, Ag-Te-O y Ag-Cu-Se ternary systems are analyzed as well. In the same manner, a preliminary thermodynamical analysis of Ag-CuSe-O and Ag-Cu-Se-Te-O multicomponents systems at 1100 ºC and the relationship between metal and slag is also performed, verifying the thermodynamic deportment of Na2O-B2O3 type slags during the dorй metal fire refining process. 

Finally, according to the performed analyses, some operational considerations and implications are discussed and a better understanding of the dorй metal fire refining process is obtained. Particular attention to the equilibria of Ag-Cu-Se-O alloys by means of their chemical potential diagrams is given in this final discussion. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The anode slimes are a by-product of the electrolytic refining of copper. The processing of anode slimes has been previously analyzed [1, 2]; nevertheless, recently a significant advance in relation to the processing of these materials has been obtained [3] when incorporating a reactor that, besides producing a remarkable reduction of the process time, offers operational flexibility and is friendly with the environment, eliminating at the same time several unit operations of the old schemes of processes. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

1293 

_Devia_ 



The anode slimes, previously decopperized and des

elenized, can be smelted applying some of the reactors available commercially at present (Kaldo, TROF, TBRC). The smelting process of this material is done altogether with fluxes in an oxidising atmosphere in the reactor. In this way, a significant elimination of impurities takes place in the slag or gases of the process. At the end of the smelting process an alloy denominated dorй matte is obtained, which contains almost all the silver and gold, as well as residual impurities, such as copper, selenium and tellurium, initially present in the anode slimes, which did not oxidise to the slag and/or gases during the anode slimes smelting. 

The dorй matte fire refining to dorй metal involves the sequential elimination of impurities (M), which has been explained theoretically in the author’s previous publications [4-6] by means of the thermodynamics of Ag-M-O ternary solutions [4-6] and the use of an Ellingham diagram [5]. The technical difficulty of the refining is based mainly in the complex that turns out to obtain a dorй metal, which it fulfils the technical specifications for commercialisation or, for the further processing up to obtain electrolytic silver. 

Information about thermodynamics of solutions applied to diluted silver alloys is scarce, but that the available one has allowed fortifying the base of information for the analysis of the thermodynamic equilibrium during the dorй metal refining. From this point of view, the analysis of Ag-Se-O has been study from the late 80’s. Devia [1, 4] performed the first attempt to explain the equilibria of Ag-Se-O alloys by means of their chemical potential diagram. Later, Rankin et al. [7] conducted laboratory-scale smelting experiments using unleached anode slimes, with and without the additions of fluxes under three different atmospheres. Both authors coincide that during the anode slimes smelting selenium is readily removed as gaseous selenium dioxide and that molten Ag-Cu-Se-O matte form when fluxes are added. Further fire refining of the Ag-Cu-Se-O matte by oxidation with oxygen, or oxygen enriched air and addition of fluxes, result in the formation of dorй metal, that is appropriate for a further process to obtain electrolytic silver. 

Relatively recent studies, specifically related to the Ag-Cu-Se-O alloys, which are very important in the anode slimes smelting to dorй metal, were performed. Swinbourne et al. [8] analyzed the oxidation and deportment of Ag-Cu-Se mattes poor in silver. Swinbourne et al. [9] developed the chemical potential diagram of the Ag-Cu-Se-O system at 1100 °C. Swinbourne et al. [10] oxidised molten silver selenide matte with pure oxygen at 1100 °C establishing the thermodynamic basis of the chemical potential diagram of Ag-Se-O. Wiggett et al. [11] updated thermodynamic information of the miscibility gap of Ag-Se binary system, giving solubility limits of selenium and contributions of key information about activities and activity coefficients for selenium in liquid silve

r. Lamontagne et al. [12] investigated the effect of oxygen in the Cu-Se-Ag system for liquid alloys both rich in copper and rich in copper selenide between 1130 and 1223 °C. They concluded that for high oxygen potentials, the silver distribution ratio between Cu and Cu2Se phases diminish due to the oxidation of some of the Cu2Se to Cu2O. That is, increases the silver solubility in Cu2O (slag). Pickles [13], studied the oxygen refining of liquid copper-silver alloys with a borosilicate slag, concluding that is possible oxidise copper from copper-silver alloys with a very low silver loss to the slag. ###### 3.1 Thermodynamics of the Ag-Cu-Se-O System 

In Figure 3, the chemical potential diagram obtained by Swinbourne et al. [9] by mean of juxtaposition of the Ag-Se-O y Cu-Se-O systems chemical potential diagrams at 1100 °C, is shown. Several auxiliary lines can be ob

The importance of this diagram is that while the SeO2 partial pressure in equilibrium with the Ag-Cu-Se-O system at 1100 °C is known, the way that follows the anode slimes smelting process to matte and further dorй metal refining can be determined, that will be discussed later. 

###### 3.2 Thermodynamics of the Ag-Cu-Se-Te-O System 

Swinbourne et al. [14] concluded that the presence of tellurium in the Ag-Cu-Se ternary alloy during its oxidation process increases lightly the selenium concentration. In a period around 85 % as oxidation percentage (measured as % accumulated of copper, selenium and tellurium removed from the initial matte dorй), estimated that the selenium and tellurium oxidise fast. Also, in accordance with a previous study [1], it was concluded that the tellurium is reported completely in the slag. 

From the results of Swinbourne et al. [14] it is possible to suggest that, for the anode slimes smelting process at high oxygen potentials, the tellurium mass distributions are lower than 1 % in the matte/metal phase and the balance (> 99 %) is reported in the slag phase. Also, it is possible to be warned that for very low percentage of oxidation, part of tellurium distributes to the slag phase (~ 23 %), another part to the matte/metal phase (~ 72 %) and the rest to the gas phase (~ 5 %). 

Pйrez-Tello et al. [18] performed tests of dorй metal in an industrial Kaldo reactor. They verified that the oxidation of the selenium takes place from the start of the dorй metal refining, whereas the oxidation of tellurium only occurs when the selenium/tellurium ratio in the alloy reaches a value of 0.55. They concluded that this parameter seemed to be more a thermodynamical restriction of the system than a kinetical rate control. They also suggested that, probably, fluid dynamics parameters and oxygen potential associated to the Kaldo furnace operation can affect the global rates of reaction.

#### 4 Operational Implications 

###### 4.1 Operational Analysis of the Dorй Metal Fire Refining 

In accordance with the suggested and observed previously, clearly the tellurium oxidises quickly when a Se/Te ratio is appropriate. Also, in the presence of a suitable slag, it is possible to slagging tellurium effectively. The same can be said for copper, although this element can be eliminated rather well until to obtain content in the order of 1 % in equilibrium with the dorй metal at 1100 °C. 

In relation with tellurium removing, its oxide has an acid deportment instead, which causes that it can be removed rather well by interaction with a strongly basic slag, like Na2O [1]. During the dorй metal refining, it would seem to exist a type of competition by oxygen between Te and Cu, in the presence of a sodium slag [6]; nevertheless, when the contents of both elements in liquid silver are almost similar, in t

he order of 1 wt. %, the affinity of Te by oxygen is higher compared with the one of Cu, i. e., clearly the balance had to move towards the Te oxidation-slagging instead of Cu. 

On the other hand, it has been proposed [5] the use of slag based on SiO2 or B2O3 for an efficient copper elimination, i. e., slags more acid instead of typical alkaline based on Na2O·B2O3 and Na2O. These considerations have been confirmed in a study destined to consider the acid or basic character of some slags [21]. On the other hand, Swinbourne and You [20], analyzed the solubility of silver in slag based on SiO2·Na2O system at 1100 °C, concluding that for SiO2/Na2O = 2 ratio, with pO2 = 1 atm at 1100 °C, has a value of 5.6 wt. % (Ag like AgO0.5). 

In the (Ag+O)-Cu-Se pseudoternary system, shown in Figure 4, it can be noticed that in the Ag2SeCu2Se matte with low content in silver it is possible to dissolve big quantities of oxygen, presumably as Cu2O and Ag2O [9]. In this case, it has been proved that the great effect over the smelting process is the delay metallic silver apparition. Nevertheless, in Ag2Se-Cu2Se matte high in silver, the oxygen dissolution is less intensive and the progress of matte refining to dorй metal follow the expected route (Figure 4). At 1100 °C the route of matte refining to dorй metal is from the L2 region, i. e., homogeneous solution of Ag2Se up to achieve the other end where is stable L1, i. e., the homogeneous solution of liquid silver with dissolved selenium. 

Continuing with the refining process, once eliminated tellurium and copper reaching its equilibrium value (~ 1 %), the selenium has probably been in a higher value in comparison to the one of the dorй metal technical specifications (< 0.02 wt. %). The deportment of the selenium elimination can be continued considering the chemical potential diagram of the Ag-Cu-Se system at 1100 °C, shown in Figure 5, including the isopercent of oxygen and selenium in the stability zone of liquid silver. It can be noticed that, even though in strict theoretical sense, the separation line of Ag2O-Ag phases is displaced towards a higher oxygen pressure (~ 10,000 atm), the thermodynamics of Ag-O diluted solutions indicates that the saturation with oxygen in liquid silver is in the order of 0.3 wt. %, whose oxygen potential corresponds to log pO2 ~ - 0.2.

#### 5 Conclusions 

In this article, the operational conditions and sequence of elimination of impurities observed in industrial facilities of dorй metal production are justified and based on theoretical and operational aspects, as well laboratory tests. 

Related with the deportment of the impurities dissolved in dorй metal, as a conclusion of this work, it is suggested to undertake a kinetic analysis of selenium elimination from Ag-Se-O diluted alloy at 1100 °C, in order to identify the limitations that could affect the selenium oxidation rates at low dilution. The feasibility to assure the operational point for the efficient selective separation of selenium and tellurium in the industrial process would have altogether to be solved from the most exhaustive application of theoretical basis and industrial practice. 

The emissions of SeO2 to the environment and surroundings of Precious Metal Plants during roasting and decopperized anode slimes smelting processes, as well as of the dorй metal refining, is a subject that is still pending and had to be boarded in an integral and responsible way by the dorй metal producers.

In May 2006, started design preparation for new refinery in Pirdop Bulgaria. The civil design and design of electrolyte circulation equipment was made by the Bulgarian company “Chimcomplect”. #### 1 Introduction 

The production of electrolytic copper in the copper smelter and refinery Pirdop commenced in the year of 1958 when the plant for handling of copper concentrates was put in operation. The cathode period of the sections was 7 days. #### 7 Conclusions The conclusions for the operation of ISA 2000 in the Pirdop’s Refinery are based on the results from its work till the end of 2009: - The technology ISA 2000 operates optimally with current density above 325 A/m2 . - The technology ISA 2000 does not allow switch-off of the DC current to the electrolytic cells for more than 0.5 hours and in case it happens the flapping ratio increases significantly. - In the technology ISA 2000, an effect of corrosion of the copper layer which cover hanger bar and top part of the SS blank is observed. - During normal production operation mode, the flapping of FDSM is below 1.08 num/blank. - The Cu content in the solution should be within 42-48 g/l. - H2SO4 content should be within 165-185 g/l. - Content of the Cl ion should be within 35-50 g/l. 1325 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1326 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ ### The Effect of SPCC Smelter Modernization on Anode Quality and Electrorefining Process F. Fernandez, F. Begazo Southern Peru Copper Corporation Ilo Refinery Pampa Caliche Km. 9 Ilo, Moquegua, Peru **Keywords:** Copper, anode quality, smelter modernization, ISASMELTTM , impurities, electrorefining process, southern Peru #### Abstract Southern Peru Copper Corporation (SPCC), the main copper mining producer in Peru, has completed the biggest and most ambitious environmental project, the Ilo Smelter modernization, fulfilling the ca

pture of at least 92 % of the SO2 gases generated during the smelting process of copper concentrate. That concentrate comes from open pit copper mines in Toquepala and Cuajone. 

Before the SPCC Smelter modernization, anodes were produced in the Ilo Refinery; now anodes are produced directly at the smelter; changing the treatment of refinery recycling materials that cannot be treated in the new smelter. 

Also, due to the new processes applied in the modernization of the smelter, the chemical composition of the anodes now varies mainly in the content of Bi, Sb, Pb and Zn, which are different to the original design parameters of the Refinery. 

This paper presents revisions and adjustments for chemical and physical anode quality, coordinating between the Refinery and Smelter staff. It summarizes investigations, modifications on electrolyte control parameters, optimization of the electrolyte purification process, effect of electrolyte Bi concentration on Starting Sheet production circuit and treatment of the recycling materials; in order to maintain the current efficiency rates higher than 98 %, refining anodes of the highest weight and thickness in the world. All the changes have not varied the high chemical quality 100 % “A” Degree Cathodes that have reached the certification in Quality ISO 9001, Environmental ISO 14001 and Security and Occupational health OSHAS 18001 management systems.

#### 1 Introduction 

SPCC Ilo Refinery, with an original production capacity of 150,000 mt/y copper cathodes, was built and commissioned in 1975 by Minero Peru S.A., a Peruvian government owned entity, to process blister bars from the Southern Peru Copper Corporation (SPCC) Ilo Smelter. In 1994 SPCC purchased the Ilo Refinery from the Peruvian government, with increased production capacity of 199,000 mt/y copper cathodes. After the purchase, SPCC took on the task to increase production to process as much blister as possible from the Smelter (See Figure 1). The production increases up to 275,000 mt/y would come from an expansion project, which consisted of the installation of more and larger refining cells, a larger rectifier, and increases in current density (CD). 



Figure 1: Ilo Refinery flow sheet original design with blister bars treatment in its anode plant. 

In 1999, Grupo Mexico purchased the SPCC Ilo Refinery from ASARCO. The production increases up to 285,000 mt/y by using 29 kA (almost total rectifier capacity). According to the environmetal compliance and management program (PAMA), SPCC has completed the biggest and most ambitious environmental project, modernizing the Ilo Smelter fulfilling with a capture of at least 92 % of the SO2 gases generated during the smelting process of copper concentrate from its open pit copper mines: Toquepala and Cuajone. 

After SPCC smelter modernization, the Ilo Refinery now consists of an Electrolytic Plant, Precious Metals Plant, Sea Water Desalinizat

ion Plant, air pressure and steam generation, unloading anodes and spent anodes dispatching system; and other auxiliary facilities, such as an analytical SPCC central laboratory and maintenance shops. The products from the Ilo Refinery include high grade copper cathode, refined silver, refined gold, commercial grade selenium and crude nickel sulfate (until 2008). The Ilo Refinery flow sheet is illustrated in Figure 2. 

This paper will provide a description of the experiences of reviewing the electrorefining parameters, the anode quality, impurities controls in anodes, electroyte, starting sheets, anodic slimes, in order to maintain the cathode quality. The goal of the Refinery personnel was to overcome current variations of the new anode, maintaining the high grade A copper cathode quality at the Ilo Refinery [1].

###### 1.1 Smelter modernization effects on copper anode quality & electrorefining process 

The schedule below relates modernization of SPCC smelter and location of anode production: 

• Anode production at Ilo Refinery Since 1974 until January 2006 • Anode production at Smelter without modernization Since February, 2006 • Anode production after Modernized Smelter Since March, 2007 

Anodes at the refinery had been produced at its own anode plant by re melting blister bars coming from the smelter; then a new anode plant was built at smelter directly passing molten copper from converters to fire refining furnaces. After almost one year, the new Isasmelt furnace started operation in March of 2007 and the anodes coming from the new smelter showed a different chemical composition compared to that of the original design parameters of Ilo Refinery.

To better compare chemical quality of anodes before and after SPCC smelter modernization, data has been collected considering 5 steps for anode production: 

- Step 1 – At refinery regarding period of year 2005.

- Step 3 – With Copper coming from new Isasmelt furnace from March 2007 to December 2007.

- Step 5 – From January until July 2009.

###### 1.2 Behaviour of first group: As, Sb and Bi 

Monthly assays of As, Sb, Bi and molar relation in the anode are shown in Figure 3 for the five steps of evaluation. Behaviour of these elements in anodes and the effect on electrolyte and anodic slimes could be seen. Some high values, especially on Bi content, were reported due to the treatment of purchased

external copper concentrate; for this reason Step 4 is compared with Step 1 because only copper concentrate from SPCC was treated in both Steps 1 and 4. 

**For anodes** , the average chemical composition as well as standard deviation of As, Sb, Bi and molar relation (MR) by steps are shown in the Table 1. It can be seen that antimony content was 51 ppm for anodes produced at refinery (Step 1) and increased up to 58 ppm in Step 4 increasing about 14 %. The Bi content increased from 18 to 79 ppm for the same steps, representing the most important and high increment of about 440 %. During Step 3 anodes with an average of 122 ppm Bi were treated for the first time in Refinery history and promoted a big concern for cathode quality. 

In the case of As, the content was always lower than 200 ppm in blister copper bars processed at Refinery Anode Plant, and it continues being low in the molten copper received in the fire refining furnaces at smelter. Therefore to control the behaviour of the Bi and Sb, As2O3 is dosed in the molten copper to maintain the As content in the anodes in the range from 450 to 600 ppm. For example the As content was increased to 534 ppm (see Step 4) due to the high Bi value of 79 ppm in the anodes obtained when processing copper concentrate in the modernized SPCC smelter. 

Generalizing, the As / (Bi + Sb) molar relationship values have diminished 13 at 8 due to the increment of the Bi content and to maintain the As levels in the anodes.

#### 3 Conclusion 

The effect of SPCC smelter modernization on anode quality and its electrorefining process was reviewed after 3.5 years of anode production at smelter, and 2.3 years after new Isasmelt furnace started operation. Anode chemical composition has varied from those originally produced at refinery. For example, anodes produced at smelter which avoids copper remelting (Step 2) have varied mainly in content of Pb, Ni, Zn, and Fe. From Isasmelt furnace operation changes can be seen on Bi, Sb, Pb, Ni and Zn (Step 4). Sulphur and oxygen content were not considered because that depends directly on anode plant staff. 

Present and original refinery electrolyte purification system became insufficient to remove impurities. Therefore, plans to remove them included suspension of recycling materials with high impuri-

ties such as As, Sb and Bi to smelter, second liberator expansion, and electrolyte bleeding off to leaching plant and, Bi and Sb control by As increasing up 7 g/l. 

Bismuth control is undertaken and mainly by increasing As in electrolyte to form Bi (AsO4), compound reported at slimes. For this purpose team work with Smelter and mines staff is on going to maintain Bi content in anodes below 85 ppm, but also As, Sb, Pb,

and Zn under limited ranges. 

Bleeding off a small portion of electrolyte yet and together with low oxygen content in anodes, is resulting in reduction needs of first liberator allowing for power savings and using those cells for commercial cathode production. Plans include increasing the amount of electrolyte to be bleed off. 

The behaviour of Ni became in anode and electrolyte content reduction, as a result the evaporation system to purified soluble elements such as Ni, was shut down since 2008 and Ni sulphate production was stopped. 

Impurities such as Fe, Zn is building up in electrolyte deserving future attention for their impact on process and cathode quality. It is expected to be controlled by increasing the amount of bleeding. 

Because of the Pb, As, Sb, Bi content increasing in slimes, capacity of equipment such as Selenium roaster became too small for the amount of slimes generated by anodes from the modernized smelter. The reactor’s original capacity was 1.0 mt and at present year, after some improvements is working with 2.0 mt but selenium remaining in roasted slimes is increased. For this reason the treatment of gases coming from slimes melting furnace needs to be enhanced to control gas emission into the atmosphere. 

Finally, quality of refined copper cathodes maintains high A Grade, as well as current efficiency.

The lamination is an unique problem for the waxless ISA process, means a phenomenon where the bottom of stainless plate is covered with deposited copper when the energizing or electrolyte circulation is stopped during operation, or mainly due to the unexpected power shutdown. When the lam

ination occurs, the bottom of the deposit cannot be stripped by one motion and „flapping“ movements have to be repeated for several times to remove the deposits. It causes a serious problem for cathode stripping operation, and may result in production loss for several thousand tons. The interface of electrolytic copper with lamination was observed by EPMA and existence of chlorine and oxygen was found out. In order to clarify the mechanism of how lamination occurs, an investigation on a laboratory scale was conducted and it was found out that there is a formation of CuCl near the interface was found. It is assumed that in the process of electro-deposition of Cu, where it is reduced from divalent to univalent, an abnormal adsorption of Cl to Cu occurred to form this. In a normal electro-deposition, CuCl reacts further and CuCl is reduced to metal while Cl goes back to electrolyte. But when there is a power shutdown, the it reaction to reduce to metal stops and causes condensation of CuCl. Further, in the electrolysis cell, Cu concentration is not even and Cu concentration and Cl concentration are high at the bottom, Thus, the CuCl generation reaction tends to be promoted at the bottom. It was also found out that CuCl is dissolved if electrolyte circulation is started when re-energizing. Cu

The treated slime used to be recovered and dehydrated by a centrifuge, but there had been a problem of not being able to recover fine slime particles that overflew from the basket. Since these fine slime particles contained comparatively high precious metal, the particles, collected at the electrolyte „Ultra“ filter had to be recycled to the smelting plant and caused metal loss. The fine slime particles, floating on the surface of electrolyte in the cell, could cause short-circuiting and resulted in decrease of current efficiency. In order to solve these problems, a filter press designed and manufactured by Larox Co., Ltd. was introduced. This filter is a vertical type press and unlike ordinary filter press machines, the 1350 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Recent Improvements at Tamano Refinery_

filter plates are positioned horizontal to drive the filter cloth. It can efficiently recover fine slime particles and has good rinsing capability. Tamano Refinery introduced this filter press in 2009 and it has been operating satisfactorily. After introduction of filter press, the suspended solid concentration in the filtrate decreased from previous 200-300 g/L to 0.15-0.3 g/L. Sargento Cuevas 093 Rancagua, Chile **Keywords:** Multi-frequency current, AC + DC, electrowinning, electrorefining, current desity #### Abstract The use of composed electrical signals i.e. a high-multi frequency AC superimposed to a DC of set, improves the copper electrowinning (EW) and copper electrorefining (ER) processes. From a phenomenological point of view, the high-multi frequency AC superimposed to a DC of set, excite the electrochemical double layer, noticeably increasing the movement and displacement of the ionic species at the electrode/electrolyte interface. A charge transfer steps are always controlling the mechanisms of the electrochemical reactions, in copper EW and/or copper ER operation conditions, improving electrochemical behaviour of the electrodes. Specific energy consumption tend to decrease, and the physical and chemical quality of the copper electro-won, improves noticeably. Additionally, a better electrochemical behaviour of anodes in copper EW and E

R processes might be obtained, in the electrolytic cells. 

The aim of this paper is to compare the physical quality of copper electro won obtained under DC vs. DC+AC electrical signals. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Copper has been recovered industrially and commercially from Cu<sup>2+</sup> solutions by using the combined LX-SX-EW process for over 30 years. This technology has increased copper production thanks to the technical feasibility of purifying and concentrating Cu<sup>2+</sup> solutions with extraction and stripping technology in the SX steps. High grade cathodes are produced in the EW tank-house (reaching a degree of purity of "five nines", i.e. 99.999 %). This global process has an additional advantage of low capital and operational costs. At present, the Chilean copper production capacity through LX-SX-EW exceeds 3.0 million metric tons per year.
