The objective of copper electrowinning and/or electrorefinning plants is to produce the greatest number of high chemical and physical purity metal cathodes, at as lower specific energy consumption as possible. The EW/ER plants required an external electrical energy, and production is based on the level of the imposed continuous DC current. In order to reconcile cathode production with chemical quality, copper EW/ER plants operate normally with electrical DC current density levels that oscillate, by design, around 300 +/- 50 A/m<sup>2</sup> , with 92-94 % current efficiency, and with specific energy consumptions of 1700-2000 kWh/ton for copper EW. Some operational variables can be manipulated externally, including the concentration of cupric ions in the EEC solution; the electrolyte temperature, and the electrolyte flow into the cell; these should be established as a function of the imposed DC current (production), and the desired physical and chemical quality. 

###### 1.1 Copper cathode reduction 

The industrial process of copper cathode reduction uses a continuous electrical current and involves electrochemical reactions that take place at the electrode-solution interface over both the cathodes and anodes. 

Whether by EW or ER of copper in industrial plants, one of the most recurrent mechanisms for characterizing the cathode reaction of copper over a substrate of copper, titanium, or stainless steel, is generated by three kinetic steps leading from the reactive (Cu<sup>+2</sup> o<sup>) to the product (metallic Cu on</sup> the cathode): the transport of cupric ions by diffusion (stage 1) and two successive mono-electronic steps of electron transfer (stages 2 and 3). 

The simplest way to represent the electrode processes in an electrolysis cell is through an electrical circuit equivalent to that shown in Figure 1. The equivalent electrical circuit considers three elements (Rs, Cdc, Zf) from the cathodic and anodic sides. 

The faradic impedance is proper to each electrode process. In general, it i

s necessary to rely a phenomenological models to characterize the kinetic or the velocity of the reaction. This is generally obtained by establishing reaction schemes.

#### 2 Operational problems affecting production and quality 

In the industrial processes of Cu electrolysis, the key to increased production (given the same installed capacity) is increased current density. However, with the current cell designs and technology, indiscriminate increments in current density decrease the physical-chemical quality of the cathodes. As already indicated, copper EW and ER plants generally operate with current levels between 240 to 350 A/m<sup>2</sup> , not being able to surpass 320 A/m<sup>2</sup> in order to safeguard the quality standards of the cathodes. 

An increase of current density in conventional electrolysis cells must consider the following technical and economic aspects: 

- Appropriate technology for increasing the current density without experiencing a deterioration of the process control indicators, most notably the physical-chemical quality of the cathodes, current efficiency, and specific energy consumption; 

- An EW anode material able to withstand elevated currents without experiencing significant corrosion; 

- Control of the current passage through the intercell electrode/bar contact; 

- Control and removal of acid mist in the EW of Cu; 

- Control and removal of lead slime in the EW of Cu; 

- Control of anodic passivation in the ER of Cu. 

The quality of the cathode production must be also considered. The most important variables affecting cathode production and quality are the following: 

- Imposed current, 

- Electrolyte temperature, 

- Copper ions concentration in the electrolyte, 

- Flow of electrolytes to the cell, and 

- Electrochemical behaviour of the electrodes (cathodes and anodes) `.` 

In order to improve the electrolysis process, several technological developments have been created. The most important from a production and cathode quality point of view of are: permanent cathode technology, intercell equipotential bars, insoluble anodes in the EW, new electrolysis cells designs such as EMEW process and control in acid mist. With the objective of increasing the current density, ultrasound vibration and agitation through the injection of pressurized air (air sparging) are the main used techniques.

#### 3 The proposed technology 

The technology proposed in this paper consists of superimposing a sinusoidal AC multi-frequency signal over the continuous DC signal and applying this to the processes of electrowinning and/or electrorefining of metals, in particular copper, as shown in Figure 2. The amplitude and frequency of the alt

ernating signal depend on the faradic impedance of the cathode and anode processes described in Figure 1. ###### 3.1 Related technologies This type of super-imposed alternating signal at the continuous level has been used successfully in electroplating processes on sensitized surfaces of materials that are not conductive for currents (e.g., pressed circuit plates, plates for electronic components, or diverse geometric PVC bases metallized for practical and decorative uses in automobiles). These processes seek very fine, smooth electrolytic deposits of copper and chrome that are very adherent to the base surface, working at low current density. In fact, these processes are reported to benefit the super-imposed sinusoidal signal at the continuous level in terms of the quality of the metallic deposit by acting directly on the electrochemical double layer, although no further phenomenological explanations are given. Moats University of Arizona University of Utah Tucson, Arizona, USA Salt Lake City, Utah, USA **Keywords:** Copper electrorefining, anode passivation, oscillation, chronopotentiometry #### Abstract Commercial copper electrorefining accounts for the majority of refined copper produced worldwide. Anode passivation is often encountered in these facilities with dire effects on operational efficiency and cathode quality. Passivation results in an immediate increase in power consumption and possibility of floating slimes that can adverse affect the cathode quality. This paper presents research that investigates and analyzes the period just prior to passivation onset. Fast scan chronopotentiometry (FSCP) was used to obtain detailed information regarding potential oscillations in the pre-passivation region. The periodic oscillations indicate that the surface is fluctuating between unsynchronized and synchronized dissolution and formation of a sulfate salt-film. These results yield valuable information regarding the passivation mechanism involving commercial copper anodes. The kinetics of sulfate salt-film precipitation and dissolution are discussed. #### 1 Introduction This paper presents an analysis of the oscillations associated with the pre-passivation behavior of commercial copper anodes. There has been considerable work addressing the passivation of impure copper anodes [1-15]. Anode passivation can cause serious problems in the operations of copper electrorefining tankhouses. The research of Cheng and Hiskey [10] demonstrated the sensitivity and usefulness of chronopotentiometry as a technique for analyzing and characterizing copper anode passivation. A large number of commercial copper anodes have been investigated, and nearly all exhibit a region of periodic potential oscillation just prior to passivation

of copper dissolution. 

Oscillations have been observed with various metal electrodes experiencing anodic polarization. This behavior is directly linked to the instability of both porous and non-porous passivating films (i.e. the spontaneous and repeated precipitation and dissolution of a passivating film on the electrode surface). Periodic oscillations during the anodic dissolution of iron in 1N H2SO4 using constant potential were documented as early as the 1950s [16, 17]. Since then several different theories

have been developed to explain this phenomena [18-22]. Until recently, none were able to adequately predict reasonable time constants and behavior. Rush and Newman [22] showed that by using physical constants and carefully applied assumptions, oscillation could be generated using a computer model similar to those produced experimentally. Qualitatively, the cyclic phenomena for iron anodically polarized in sulfate solution was attributed to the precipitation of a non-porous ferrous sulfate film as a precursor to the formation of an iron oxide species. Both the sulfate and the oxide play a passivating role. These layers form and dissolve periodically with respect to time. 

Unlike the passivation of pure metals in sulfate media which involves only the formation of sulfate and oxide films, impure copper anodes entails the formation of an additional layer of slimes. The deportment of impurity elements is critical in establishing the phases present in the slimes layer. Some of the phases detected in anode slimes include various selenides and tellurides (i.e. Cu2(Se,Te), CuAg(Se,Te), Ag2(Se,Te)), euhedral NiO crystals, PbSO4, silicates, kupferglimmer, and complex oxides. The quantity, morphology, pore structure, and adhesion properties of the slimes are crucial factors which influence mass transfer processes at the anode/electrolyte interface. 

#### 2 Experimental Procedure 

The preparation of the working electrodes and the electrolyte have been reported elsewhere [23]. A standard electrolyte composition of 40 g l<sup>-1</sup> Cu and 160 g l<sup>-1</sup> H2SO4 at a temperature of 65 ± 0.5<sup>o</sup> C was used throughout the investigation. 

Test electrodes were allowed to equilibrate with the system by being held in the electrolyte at open circuit potential for five minutes. A constant current density of 3820 Am<sup>-2</sup> was then applied using an EG&G model 273 Potentiostat/Galvanostat controlled by HEADSTART software for the during of the test. Potential-time (E-t) responses were collected as averages of two-second intervals. The experiments were typically run for 3600 seconds. All tests were conducted in air under static conditions. 

Fast scan chronopotentiometry (FSCP) experiments were conducted in a very similar manner. The exceptions involved the control of the Potentiostat/Galvanostat and data acquisition. The EG&G model 273 Potentiostat/Galvanostat was programmed to ap

ply 382 mA of current using the front face controls. Data was acquired through the external port, which was connected to a National Instruments Lab-PC-1200/AI data acquisition card with 12-bit resolution. The data were streamed from the card into a spreadsheet format using LabView 4.0. Potential samples were taken at a rate of 500 per second compared to one every two seconds in the standard procedure.

Very shortly after the chaotic behavior shown in Figure 5, a more periodic response is observed. Periodic oscillations characteristic of this stage are shown in Figure 6. The activation/passivation events in this stage exhibit potential swings as high as 100 mV. The activiation is believed to be a result of the synchronization of copper sulfate dissolution over a large fraction of the anode surface. Electrolyte in these areas becomes concentreated with copper from the recently actived surface. The increasing copper concentration rapidly yields copper sulfate precipitation and growth of the sulfate film causes a potential rise that eventually lead to a temporary passivation peak. This is followed by gradual dissolution of the film to a period of asynchronous small amplitude oscillations noted in Figure 6. During this stage, the electrode appears to be fluctuating between unsynchronized and synchronized dissolution and formation of sulfate/oxide films. 

Once the anode becomes synchronized with respect to activation/passivation events, the oscillations exhibit a more uniform appearance as shown in Figure 7. An expanded view of the 0.72 sec cycle between 883.24 sec and 883.96 sec is shown in Figure 8.

A general description of this potential behavior can be generated by an analogous comparison to the model developed for the Fe/H2SO4 system. The cycle starts with minimum potential corresponding to the maximum active surface area. In the case of an impure copper anode, this surface area is still partially blocked by sli

mes, but most of the sulfate and oxide have been removed. This allows copper dissolution, which in turn causes saturation with respect to copper sulfate which precipitates. Copper sulfate crystals nucleate and grow within the pores of the slimes for approximately 0.35 sec and the anode approaches passivation. At the interface of the sulfate and anode surface, oxide starts to form. At the point of passivation, the sulfate will eventually dissolve, exposing the oxide film.

Depending on the acid concentration within the pores, the oxide may dissolve. Over time, the oxide dissolves until finally a massive dissolution event occurs resulting in the activation of the electrode surface. This completes one cycle. These cycles will continue with ever increasing potentials until a point is reached where the potential needed to maintain constant current is enough to stabilize the oxide in bulk electrolyte. It appears that potentials in excess of 0.8 V vs. NHE are sufficient to stabilize the copper oxide surface films. Once the oxide is stable, complete passiviation towards copper dissolution occurs. 

This qualitative description of the observed oscillations in Region II relies on the formation and removal of copper sulfate and copper oxide. Abe and Goto [2, 3] showed that CuSO4⋅5H2O is present during potential oscillations. Cheng, Hiskey, and Krusmark [9] observed massive layers of copper oxide on an anode surface during oscillations. More importantly, Chen and Dutrizac [8] displayed a photomicrograph in which a layer of CuSO4·5H2O is on top of a layer of copper oxide, which is in turn on top of the copper anode surface.

#### 4 Conclusions 

Several characteristic periods of potential oscillation are observed during the polarization of commercial copper anodes. Chaotic oscillations appear initially followed by a period of oscillations indicating a surface that fluctuates between asynchronous and synchronous formation and dissolution of copper sulfate and copper oxide surface films. Well defined periodic potential oscillations are observed from commercial copper anodes just prior to passivation.

### Understanding and Improvement of Electrowinning Current Efficiency at FMI Bagdad 

S. Joy, A. Staley, C. Perkins, J. Uhrie M. Moats Freeport McMoRan Bagdad University of Utah, Department of Metallurgical Engineering Bagdad, AZ, USA Salt Lake City, UT, USA 

T. Robinson Freeport McMoRan Mining Phoenix, AZ, USA 

**Keywords:** Copper electrowinning, tankhouse current efficiency, optimizing operations, iron, short circuits, improvements 

#### Abstract 

One of the key operational benchmarks for an industrial copper electrowinning operation is current efficiency, as it impacts both operating costs and metal production rates. Freeport McMoRan Bagdad Operations has optimized current efficiency through a systematic approach which included implementation of industry best practice, statistical monitoring and control of key process indicators. The details of this approach, including contribution of various inefficiencies in the tankhouse and the practices of implementation to minimize these inefficiencies, are presented. The use of fundamental evaluations, implementation of best practice, and statistical analysis of outputs to guide development has allowed Bagdad to achieve record levels of efficient cathode production. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The Freeport McMoRan Bagdad Solvent Extraction and Electrowinning (SX-EW) is the oldest plant of its kind currently in operation. The Bagdad plant was commissioned in 1969 and was the second SX-EW operation built following the Ranchers Bluebird SX-EW near Miami, Arizona. As an older tankhouse the operation employs smaller cells and starter sheet technology. The original Bagdad operation consisted of 52 cells containing 49 anodes and 48 cathodes. In 2005, the tankhouse was expanded to 108 cells due to the installation of the Concentrate Leach Plant. The new tankhouse consists of 56 cells having 48 anodes and 47 cathodes.

Until recently, the Bagdad SX-EW was operating at its capacity of 27 kt yr<sup>-1</sup> of rod grade copper cathode. To operate at the highest level, a systematic approach was applied to the optimizing of current efficiency in the electrowinning tankhou

se beginning with a thorough understanding of the fundamental principals governing the parameter. The method involved the implementation of industry best practices, process management, and the statistical monitoring of key process indicators. 

#### 2 Background

It is even more critically important if the Leach-SX-EW operation is tankhouse limited as current efficiency will limit the ultimate production of copper. ###### 2.2 Iron 

For a side reaction to consume electrons, it typically is thermodynamically more favorable than copper deposition. Since solvent extraction prohibits most impurities from entering the electrowinning process and the relative nobility of the copper deposition reaction, the only side reaction of consequence is ferric reduction. Ferric reduction is thermodynamically favored over copper deposition as shown by its more positive standard reduction potential. 





As ferric reduction is significantly more favored than copper deposition, the rate of ferric reduction is only limited by its mass transfer to the cathode surface. That is to say that the rate of ferric reduction occurs at its limiting current density. The limiting current density of any reducible specie is given by:

Thus, it is readily seen that the amount of current loss to ferric reduction is a functio

n of its diffusivity, concentration and the Nernst boundary layer thickness. 

Recently the diffusivity of ferric ion in simulated copper electrowinning electrolytes have been reported [1]. The diffusivity appears to be independent of copper and acid concentrations. Diffusivity would increase with increasing temperature in accordance to an Arrenhius relationship. 

Equation 5 indicates that the amount of limiting current will increase linearly with increasing iron concentration and thus current efficiency should decrease. This has recently been shown by several researchers using different conditions [1-4]. 

Boundary layer thickness is much more difficult to predict but will be a function of localized electrolyte flow and solution viscosity. Solution viscosity is a function of copper and acid concentrations and temperature [1, 5]. Localized electrolyte flow is dependent on total flow rate, electrolyte distribution system and gas lift caused by oxygen evolution at the anode.

In order to minimize current loss to ferric reduction, the desired properties are a thick boundary layer, low ferric concentration, and low temperature. Unfortunately, these parameters can lead to poor cathode quality and a higher frequency of short circuits. 

###### 2.3 Short Circuiting 

Short circuiting can also be a leading cause of current inefficiency. Short circuits are the direct contact between anodes and cathodes leading to some current by-passing the electrochemical reactions that should occur within the cell. Short circuits result from improper spacing of electrodes, improper positions of electrodes, bent anodes or cathodes and/or nodules/dendrites. Bent anodes or cathodes and improper spacing are all a result of poor operational practices. 

Dendrites or nodules form when an electrically conductive particle adheres to the surface of the cathode or localized concentration gradients begin subtle changes in the deposition rates. Once the dendrites are nucleated, they are self propagating catalyzed by increased thermodynamic driving forces due to their decreased relative proximity to the anode. Further localized encouragement of the growth can be generated by interaction of neighboring dendrites producing concentration gradients that results in diminished growth of some dendrites and enhanced evolution of other dendrites. 

However, this occurs only if the deposition rate exceeds the ability of additives to control the surface of the cathode. Inhibitor addition to copper electrowinning electrolyte is done to selectively increase growth on errant structures plated on the cathode surface. Inhibitor molecules tend to have polar heads and long organic tails. It is thought that inhibitors are attracted to the area of higher potential and, due to the higher local concentration of the additives; inhibition at that point is increased. The selective increase in surface inhibition at “hi

gh” points, allows “smoothing” of the copper deposition and influences cathode microstructure. This phenomenon is symbolically portrayed in Figure 1. Additionally, smoothing copper deposition dampens dendritic growth (nodulation) which reduces electrode short circuiting events and thus increases current efficiency. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1382 _Understanding and Improvement of Electrowinning Current Efficiency at FMI Bagdad_ Figure 1: Schematic Illustration of Inhibitor Interaction with Cathode Surface. If inhibitors are present in excess, the molecules cover a much larger part of the cathode surface and increase inhibition across the entire cathode surface affecting microstructure of the cathode and the general operation of the facilities in a negative fashion. Modifications to the microstructure can not only influence mechanical integrity and ductility but also, potentially of increased interest to electrowinners and rod mills, cathode density and solution/particle encapsulation in the cathode (impurity). ###### 2.4 Stray current Stray currents occur when current flows from the electrowinning system to ground or from one cell to another through electrolyte or salt bridge paths. Proper design and maintenance (e.g. housekeeping) of an electrowinning system minimizes the amount of stray currents. ###### 2.5 Analyzing Tankhouse Current Efficiency To determine how to improve current efficiency (CE), an operation needs to determine what its leading causes of inefficiency are. ###### 2.6 Misconceptions 

A common misconception is that the electrical resistance of the electrolyte or IR drop is responsible for a loss in current efficiency. When current passes through the cell, a voltage is needed to overcome the system resistance. The IR drop relates to power consumption and not current consumption. 

Along the same lines, it is often thought that bad contacts result in current loss. Although functionally this is correct, the existence of bad contacts in actuality drives to current inefficiencies indirectly. Bad contacts can lead to current inefficiency if they significantly redistribute current. The resulting uneven current distribution would lead to large variations of current density among cathodes within the same plating cell resulting in a distribution in the thickness of the cathodes. The thicker cathodes would have a higher likelihood of experiencing shorts circuits due to current density complications encouraging dendrite formation.

#### 3 Systematic Approach 

Using this background information, a systematic approach was taken to improving current efficiency at Bagdad. The procedure was a combination of processes developed from a sound understanding of fundamentals, process management, and implementation of best practices. Statistical monitoring was used to track key process indicators to ensure changes were having the desired effect. In this section, specific actions implemented are discussed. 

###### 3.1 Improve ear alignment and electrolyte level control in the cells 

Current distribution will occur preferentially at edges and corners due to higher fluxes at these points. This can lead to greater copper growth which on edges is called roping. In order to minimize cathode roping, and consequently decrease the probability of a short circuit, a focused effort was placed on the alignment of cathode ears (e.g. loops over the hanger bar). Following placement in the cells, a piece of string was used to align the cathode ears at a proper distance from the side of the cell. This drastically reduced the occurrence of roping on the side of the cathode by insuring proper side-to-side alignment between the anodes and cathodes. 

A procedure for changing the level of the electrolyte in the cell over the course of the plating cycle was also implemented to reduce the potential for roping on the top of the cathode and on the ears. 

###### 3.2 Installation of a cathode press 

As the Bagdad tankhouse uses starter sheet technology, cathode pressing is a n

ecessary element of daily operation. In the past, pressing involved “slapping” the cathode with plywood. The addition of a used cathode press from the Morenci property alleviated the labor intensive pressing technique of old and increased the quality and consistency of pressed sheets. 

The cathode press has been particularly valuable in limiting the number of bent and bowed sheets and thus reducing the short circuits caused by these defects. The cathodes are pressed on the second day of plating. This ensures that the cathodes are straight for the majority of the plating cycle. 

###### 3.3 Implementation of Ti blanks/edge strips, stripping racks, and improved rigidizer performance 

The quality of the starter sheets was drastically improved due to a complete makeover of the process to produce the starter sheets. Old stainless steel blanks were replaced with quarter inch thick titanium blanks. The titanium releases the starter sheet easier which improves the overall uniformity of the sheet both in general flatness and frequency of minute edge irregularity that can lead to dendrite

New stripping racks, shown in Figure 3a, were implemented to not only improve the process from an operator’s perspective but also generate a scenario which allows for a more uniform applied force for the removal of the sheet. Each starter blank hangs from an arm that can be swung out of the way once the blank is stripped. This allows the operator to face the blank and makes the task considerably easier and more beneficial in the effort to generate quality sheets (shown in Figure 3b). Finally, the rigidizer (shown in Figure 3c) performance was improved by increasing the number of individuals that were trained on the tuning of the machine. The rigidizer is responsible for rolling the starter sheets and pressing grooves (e.g. embossing) into the face to increase overall rigidity. The results of the changes were more consistent and straighter starter sheets. The improvement in the starter sheet quality gives the electrowinning process a higher probability of not experiencing shorts due to cathode issues.

###### 3.4 Short tracking and correction program 

The short correction program involved operators surveying the tankhouse with a Flir InfraCam SD infrared gun to identify potential shorts. When a potential problem was identified, the cathode or anode was removed from the cell and repaired. The

issues of interest included, but, were not limited to bent sheets, bowed sheets, slippers (e.g. electrodes that have fallen into the cell), top roping, bottom roping, ear nodulation, body nodulation, bad anode, insulators, double contact, and no contact. The corrective actions that resulted from the issue included, but, were not limited to straightening of the sheet, removal of the sheet, knocking off the nodulation, replacing the anode, replacing the insulator, making contact, and noting if contact was irreparable. A tracking system was created so that the data from the short correction program could be statistically analyzed to indicate recurring issues or recurring locations of issues. The new compression molded vinyl ester cell furniture was custom made for the hanger bars and the arrangement of the cells. The new inter-cell busses were notched which means that there are low spots on the _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1387 _Joy, Staley, Moats, Perkins, Uhrie, Robinson_ bus where the electrodes rest. This allows for the hanger bars to make more contact with the bus and therefore improve the current distribution. ###### 3.6 Implemented ISO 9000:2000 quality management system Bagdad became ISO (International Standards Organization) 9000:2000 certified in December 2007. ISO is a quality management system that serves to set clear expectations and accountability. Specifically, ISO is used to standardize procedures through the control of documentation. Additionally, the production process is monitored for consistency by tracking changes and revisions during standardized auditing procedures. When implementing best practices, it is imperative to ensure that directions are clear and concise and that procedures are being followed. An example of the ISO implementation at Bagdad is the building of work instructions by the individual crews with the assistance of management and the continual review and monitoring of these documents. ###### 3.7 Increased focus on training (peer mentoring program) At Bagdad, the peer mentoring program was implemented to increase the overall level of training. This

system has been effective as it introduces accountability into the training program. It stands to reason that more trained employees recognize and repair issues more effectively than their counterparts. Although the results were not realized immediately, a higher level of training will result in a more efficient operation. In the case of a tankhouse, this means a decrease in the amount of short circuits caused by operator carelessness. 

###### 3.8 EW process scorecard audits 

Process scorecard audits were implemented to ensure that operators were performing housekeeping and other daily tasks at an acceptable level. With quality training in place, it was important to follow up and confirm that best practices were continually followed. Some of the items of interest on the audit included correct cell levels, proper rigidizer performance, anode shields were in place, shorts were checked and repaired, and instances of no contacts were addressed. The crew was given a total score based on the variety of issues addressed in the audit. Following the audit, the results were discussed along with any areas in need of improvement. 

Beyond the obvious benefit of following up to ensure quality work, the scorecard audits have the additional impact of creating a competitive spirit between the crews. Each crew takes pride in its work and strives to be the best at Bagdad.

###### 3.9 Scheduled Preventative Maintenance on Electrowinning Cells 

The introduction of cell cleaning and cell maintenance on a 90 day target allowed for potential issues to be addressed and repaired before they became catastrophic. The 90 day target has proved to be appropriate for Bagdad. 

###### 3.10 Improved insulators 

Prior to 2007, the anode insulators at Bagdad seen in Figure 5a were attached with pins and were quite worn. Due to the attachment mechanism and the slow degradation of the anodes, the insulators fell off frequently and were ineffective insuring proper spacing. In addition, when the insulators became loose, they often caused the starter sheets to hang up and become bent while getting placed in the cells. The replacement insulators were PVC twist lock type hairpins (Figure 5b) which are considerably more stable and have been successful at reducing the resulting shorts.

**Keywords:** Hydrometallurgy, anode slimes, gold, wet chlorination, ORP 

#### Abstract 

The Rio Tinto Kennecott Copper Refinery, which began operating in 1950, was expanded and modernized in 1994. A fully hydrometallurgical process for recovering gold, silver, PGM, and other byproducts was simultaneously developed and has successfully operated in its state-of-the-

art Precious Metals Plant since then. Although the slimes process remains basically the same, new technology, associated with sustainable developments, plays a major part in continuous improving the end result of economic prosperity. Sustainable developments in slimes processing, with emphasis on optimization of leaching precious metals, specifically gold and selenium, are exhibited in this paper. The use of continuous monitoring of in-line Oxidation Reduction Potential (ORP), which enabled operations to determine the critical end-point of the leach reaction thus resulting in reduction in costly reagents, increased yield and improved efficiency, is also illustrated.

#### 2 Kennecott Copper Anode Slimes Process 

The KUC Refinery is located at Magna, approximately 16 miles west of Salt Lake City. In the Tankhouse at the Refinery, commercial anodes from the KUC Smelter are electrorefined. When a copper anode dissolves during electrorefining in the Refinery Tankhouse, slimes (in

soluble material) are continuously released from the anodes and fall to the bottom of the cells. These insoluble metals and compounds are comprised of various amounts of copper, gold, silver, selenium, tellurium, lead, bismuth, and barite, together with traces from the platinum group metals.

The slimes are then pumped to Precious Metals (PM) Plant as slurry in a mixture of drain electrolyte, cell and floor wash water, and anode/cathode wash water. In the PM Plant the anode slimes are initially thickened in three settling tanks. All three settling tanks are of 40,000 gallon capacity. Their purpose is to decant off the receiving tank and allow for continuous clarification of the return electrolyte in two plate and frame filters. The filtered decant solution is guaranteed clear enough and returned to the tankhouse as electrolyte makeup solution [3]. 

Electrolytic refinery slimes is <u>first leached with sulfuric acid and oxygen in two autoclaves to</u> achieve rapid and essentially complete oxidation of the copper present in the slimes. The decopperized slimes are then (second) processed in wet chlorination, which is accomplished by slurrying the decopperized slimes in an aqueous solution of hydrochloric acid, and oxidized with hydrogen peroxide. Leach solution, <u>third, is fed to solvent extraction that includes two stage countercurrent</u> extraction with dibutyl carbitol (diethylene glycol dibutyl ether) and multi-stage countercurrent scrubbing with 1-3 molar hydrochloric acid. Gold is reduced directly from the organic phase by contact with an aqueous solution of the reducing agent and crude selenium is recovered from the goldfree raffinate by reduction to element form. Fourth, wet chlorination residue is re-pulped in a dilute solution of sodium carbonate and leached with a solution of aqueous ammonia for lead and silver recovery, respectively.

#### 3 Wet Chlorination 

The slimes are pumped to the Precious Metals Plant (as shown in Figure 2) for recovery of the precious metals. It is a unique characteristic that Kennecott slimes have high gold content (gold to silver ratio is 1:10, compared to the gold to silver ratio of 1:100 in anode slimes at other Copper Refineries), so a hydrometallurgical process of chlorination was employed to allow for production of gold. 

Wet chlorination of decopperized slimes is performed by the metered addition of hydrogen peroxide to agitated slurry of slimes suspended in an aqueous solution of hydrochloric acid. The process of wet chlorination is to oxidize

and solublize the gold and selenium in the slimes. Hydrogen peroxide is used as the oxidant and hydrochloric acid provides the chloride for a gold complex solubility. Side reactions that occur during this leach include solubilization of some the slimes impurities and conversion of lead sulfate to lead chloride. Process chemistry occurs via the following reactions: 

PbSO4 + 2HCl → PbCl2 + H2SO4 (1) 





H2O2 → 1/2O2↑ + H2O (5) 

Although chlorine is a considerably cheaper oxidant than hydrogen peroxide, it was not chosen to be used in the wet chlorination, due to a fact that chlorine is an extremely dangerous martial to store, transfer, and deliver to the chlorination tank. 

###### 3.1 Continuous improvement 

The chlorination step is the heart of the precious metals recovery process. It is such an important operation in the PM Plant that it could affect the enterprise performance not only in gold in bar, but could also leave selenium in the leach residue creating a product quality issue. One of the main problems that can occur during chlorination is a rapid “foaming” of the tank contents. When foam rises to a certain level in the leach tank, addition of reagents must stop. This delays the chlorination cycle resulting in a bottleneck in the PM operation. In order to optimize this process, a Six Sigma project was carried out with efforts that focused on dosage of reagents and control of the temperature. This project solved the foaming issue and the reaction time was reduced. An automated control program for wet chlorination batch operation coupled with distributed control system (DCS) is illustrated in Figure 3.

#### 4 Technology Development 

###### 4.1 Fundamentals of ORP 

Other than temperature, a major control of the wet chlorination is through the monitoring of ORP. ORP stands for Oxidation-Reduction Potential (also referred to as Redox). An ORP reading provides an indication of the ability of a solution to support oxidation or reduction. As the name implies, this is a potentiometric (voltage/millivolt) method. Very similar to common pH measurement, as shown in Figure 5, ORP electrodes contain both a reference electrode and a measuring electrode. The reference electrode is identical to that used in pH, and as its name implies, serves as a stable reference voltage to compare the measurement electrode re

ading. The measurement electrode for ORP is most commonly platinum metal (in place of the glass sensing component of a pH electrode). The inert platinum electrode does not chemically react with the solution, but senses the electron “pull” of oxidizing solutions or the electron “push” of reducing solutions. The presence of oxidizing chemicals causes the millivolt reading to be more positive (+), while presence of reducing solutions cause a negative (-) reading. ORP measurement therefore provides a direct indication of the oxidative strength of a solution. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1398 _Sustainable Developments in Copper Anode Slimes – Wet Chlorination-Processing_ Figure 5: Illustration of fundamentals of ORP ###### 4.2 ORP measurement in-line The oxidation is monitored by ORP measurement and terminal ORP defined at which the reaction is considered to be complete. #### Abstract 

Mitsubishi Materials Corporation’s Naoshima Smelter & Refinery has operated the precious metals plant and refined gold, silver, selenium, and platinum group metals (PGM) from de-copperized slime produced in the copper refinery by the conventional smelting process since 1989. To the purpose of fast pass recovery of gold with minimal in-process inventory, the smelting process was replaced with new hydrometallurgical process in October 2004. 

The new hydrometallurgical process consists of 1) wet chlorination for dissolution of gold, selenium and PGM, 2) solvent extraction of gold using dibutyl carbitol (DBC) and direct reduction of gold from the organic compound, 3) de-chlorination of silver chloride bearing residue, 4) original silver refining using the silver smelting & cupellation process and 5) recovery of selenium and PGM from the gold raffinate. 

Due to increasing production of de-copperized slime caused by high lead content in copper concentrates and increasing recovery of copper concentrates, the original slime flotation system is maintained in operation prior to wet chlorination treatment. 

In addition, wet-type electrostatic precipitator was built in order to reduce the environmental impact, especially fugitive emissio

n to the atmosphere from the conventional silver smelting and cupellation process. 

In some period at the starting up, some technical initial problems had been encountered, for example, problems on equipment such as 1) corrosion troubles in the aggressive chemical environment by chlorine, and problems on process operation such as 2) low gold extraction at wet-chlorination, 3) chlorine remaining of silver residue at de-chlorination process, and 4) longer cycle time because of scale on cooling tubes in the wet-chlorination vessel. After resolving these problems, the new

#### 1 The conventional smelting process 

Mitsubishi Materials Corporation’s Naoshima Smelter & Refinery has operated the precious metals plant and refined gold, silver and PGM from de-copperized slime produced in the copper refinery by the conventional smelting process since 1989. The conventional smelting process is shown in Figure 1. 

De-copperized slime were first charged to the flotation process, and separated to concentrates and tales of removing lead sulfate. The concentrates removed lead sulfate were charged to the roasting and smelting furnace for oxidation roasted and selenium is volatilized as selenium dioxide. Volatilized selenium is recovered as sodium selenite by contacting sodium hydroxide solution in the venturi scrubber. The sodium selenite solution is reduced with the sulfur dioxide gas, and 99.9 % selenium is obtained. 

On the other hand, after oxidation roasting, the flux and the reducing agent were charged in the roasting and smelting furnace at 1200 °C in the smelting stage. After molten bath is left settling for several hours, it is separated to lead containing of slag and matte containing of silver in the furnace. 

The matte is charged to the cupellation furnace from the roasting and smelting furnace, and oxidized with sodium carbonate and sodium nitrate and blowing oxygen gas. Tellurium is removed as a slag, and the crude silver bullions are cast into anodes and electrolytically refined by the Moebius process. Refined silver is washed, dried, and cast into 30 kg-Bars. The slime from silver electrorefining is leached with nitric acid at higher temperature. Platinum and palladium are recovered from leaching solution as sponge products, respectively, in the PGM recovery process. The gold residue is separated from the leachant, molten and cast into gold anodes and electrorefined by Wohlwill process. Gold cathodes are cast into gold bullions such as large bars.

The amount of de-copperized slime treatment was 200 t/month, though it has greatly increased to 300 t/month compared to expected capacity of 240 t/month due to increasing treatment quantity of copper concentrate in the copper recovery process and increasing of lead content in copper concentrates. In order to overcome increasing quantity of de-copperized slime, it was decided to continue the operation of the flotation process. 

As a result, it has become possible to reduce the amount of the hydrochloric acid addition and to increase the amount of de-copperized slime input volume in the wet chlorination process due to removing of lead from its slime and reducing its slime volume. 

The concentrate separated by flotation process is leached as the main raw material in the wet chlorination process. Precious metals other than silver in the concentrate are leached into the solution. The residue consisting of silver and lead is recovered with filter press. The leached solution is purified by solvent extraction with DBC, a highly selective extractant for gold. 

The organic compound in extraction called crud is generated, and it interferes with separation of aqueous phase and organic phase.

The hydrochloric acid concentration is adjusted between 1.5 mol/l and 1.6 mol/l before extraction to prevent from crud generation and co-extraction of impurities such as iron and tin. 

The gold concentration in DBC is controlled to 40 g/l in order to maintain adequate phase separation. Otherwise, increasing specific gravity of DBC by higher gold concentration causes insufficient phase separation.

Reduced gold sands are washed with dilute hydrochloric acid and isopropyl alcohol to remove organic and sodium. After drying the gold sand is molten and cast into gold bullion such as large bar. Chlorination leach residue is de-chlorinated by reducing silver chloride to silver with iron and converting lead chloride to lead sulfate with sulfuric acid. The converted residue is charged to the roasting and smelting furnace to recover silver. 

It was capable of decreasing selenium input from silver recovery process to pyrometallurgical process, because lower selenium content of the residue. Recycled materials from selenium recovery process, however, were treated in the pyrometallurgical process, which has succeeded to install another wet-type electrostatic precipitator in order to reinforce the performance for environmental matters. The pyrometallurgical process and silver electrorefining continue in the same systems. The slime containing gold from silver electrorefining are re-charged to chlorination process. 

Selenium is recovered from gold free raffinate by reduction to elemental form with sulfur dioxide. The reduced selenium contains gold and PGM. Selenium is distilled to recover a pure product for sale. PGM is condensed in the still bottom from distillation from which PGM is recovered. 

#### 3 Troubles occurred and countermeasure 

When the hydrometallurgical process was constructed, following troubles were occurred and solved by adequate countermeasures to each: 

1. Corrosion on equipment, 

2. Low gold dissolution rate in wet-chlorination, 

3. High chlorine content in silver sludge, 

4. Longer cycle time of wet chlorination process. 

###### 3.1 Corrosion on equipment 

The polypropylene lining tank which treats the liquid including DBC was changed to the FRP lining, because the polypropylene lining was broken at weld by thermal expansion and it caused the leak. 

Though the chlorination tank was constructed with iron of FRP lining on the initial plan, FRP lining was peeled off from the iron support and cracked by the continuous heat cycle from 40 to about 80 °C. In addition, lined FRP itself was corroded and eroded between 4 and 6 month. Therefore the chlorination tank was replaced that of titanium in August 2008 and chlorination process has been operated without any troubles.

#### Abstract 

Tankhouse Information Management System (TIMS) is a new and modern data collection, reporting and management system to integrate Outotec’s tankhouse material handling, CellSense electrolytic cell monitoring and process control systems. The system is a modular, real-time and easy to access portal into tankhouse production and machinery events, performance reports, troubleshooting, preventive maintenance, quality control and material tracking. The focus of refinery information management approach in TIMS is to support faster and proactive operation decisions based on systematic and process oriented on-line analysis. Significant benefits are gained in increasing the energy efficiency, product quality and improving the maintenance and safety. First TIMS for the expansion of UMMC Uralelectromed Tankhouse in Russia demonstrates the benefits of the system. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Modern copper refinery is often highly automated process, where both discrete and continuous automation play critical role to ensure efficient operation and high quality cathode copper production. Often, inherent differences between the tankhouse material handling systems and continuous solution process lead often to the situation, where process information is stored locally by subsystems and information exchange is very limited between these. Usually _ProcessControl System_ (PCS) controls continuous solution process and _Programmable Logic Controllers_ (PLCs) carry out machine operations and safety. While material handling systems play critical role to ensure high capacity of the plant, the continuous process ensures the quality of the cathode copper together with plant operators and management. For quality control, there are often systems such as _Laboratory Information System_ (LIMS) and on-line analyzers. Also supplementary systems, such as Outotec CellSense System, can be used for real-time process quality and performance monitoring [1].

MES system ( _Manufacturing Execution System_ or _Manufacturing Enterprise Solutions)_ acts between the plant floor automation and ERP levels. #### 2 TIMS – Tankhouse Information Management System 2.1 TIMS architecture 

Main architecture of TIMS is presented in Figure 3. TIMS is connected to Outotec machinery and process control system, which guarantees seamless integration between automation and MES layers. Tight integration between PLC/PSC systems and TIMS is essential. Interfaces between TIMS and automation layer are carefully specified so that all required production events and process information would be delivered correctly. TIMS consists of different functional modules, which provide flexibility and expandability to meet different customer requirements. 

Modularity stands for possibility to provide reporting tools for individuals machine as well as integrating all plant production information together. TIMS _Machine modules_ provide specific reporting and analysis functions for Outotec Material Handling Machinery. Machine modules can be upgraded by optional modules, which provide additional featu

res such as tools for maintenance advisor or tracking the performance of individual cathode blanks. _Plant modules_ provide plant wide integration between different process areas and machinery, and allow also connections to other systems like ERP and LIMS.

#### 3 Utilization of TIMS in operation management of tankhouse 

It is not always clear, what are the actual benefits of new information. However, without proper information management, it is very difficult to analyze and optimize the activities of production and quality. Automated information management also decreases manual work, which can be vulnerable for errors. This chapter highlights a few possible approaches to use TIMS in tankhouse operation management. 

###### 3.1 Production tracking – from anodes to cathodes 

TIMS plant wide integration provides direct genealogy link from the copper stack to the source anode batch provided that anode batch number is entered or automatically available during APM anode loading. In APM, each individual anode is weighted and physical quality measured. Based on batch number, chemical analysis information is fetched from LIMS database. After APM cell load of anodes is followed to the cell and finally to ASW, which enables accurate scrap percentage calculation.

###### 3.3 Crane harvest scheduling 

Crane should be operated in fixed schedules in order to maintain steady operation of production. However, unavoidable and un-planned downtimes and changes take place every now and then. Furthermore, there is always risk, especially in EW plants, that cathodes are let to grow too long due to mistakes in production scheduling. To overcome these issues, TIMS can be used to automatically estimate and follow-up cathode cycle completion. This is carried out by monitoring cathode cycle start events and calculating cathode growing times based on rectifier current consumption. 

TIMS suggest daily harvest schedules based on production history and required production performance and set targets. Operators can modify the harvest schedule, before it is downloaded to the crane PLC. Furthermore, online screen shows current status of production and harvesting.

Manufacturing operation management is important in copper refineries in order to achieve higher production efficiency, better quality of production and lower operation costs. In order to improve the performance and quality of operations, it is required that information is collected, analyzed and reported in real-time and a systematic way throughout the plant. Additionally, collected data can be converted into practical information that can be used to manage operations in order improve opera

### Effect of Variable Current on the Current Efficiency in Copper Electrorefining 

S. M. Lee, S. C. Ahan, W. K. Lyu, S. G. Lee, H. K. Hong, S. H. Cho 

LS-Nikko Copper Inc. 70, Daejung-ri, Onsan-eup, Ulju-gun Ulsan, 689-892, Korea 

**Keywords:** Variable Current, direct current, current efficiency, copper electrorefining 

#### Abstract 

Experiments were carried out to investigate the effect of variable current on the current efficiency in copper electrorefining. Experimental conditions were cautiously chosen such as high and low current density, frequency of current change and high current time. Finally, variable current and direct current was compared with the current efficiency in the same experimental condition. According to the results, the variable current showed the better performance such as higher current efficiency and lower average electrical resistance than the direct current. The optimal conditions for variable current operation were defined by the frequency of current change. It was suggested that the more frequent frequency change could yield higher current efficiency. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Copper electrorefining has been used to produce electrolytic copper with copper sulfate electrolyte. But there are numerous production problems unsolved. The most important problem of those is anode passivity. Anode passivity makes decrease in productivity and increase in power consumption. Main reason of anode passivity is known to be impurities in anode; also other electrolytic conditions are equally important [1-6]. Periodic Reverse Current (PRC), one of the current conditions for electrorefining, is commercialized to increase current density and productivity [7, 8]. Some zinc companies have studied PRC to reduce electric power consumption and reported good results [9, 10]. They concluded that reverse current could reduce –OH complex on the surface of Pb-Ag anode in zinc electrowinning [11]. Limited informations on PRC, in copper electrorefining, stimulate our interest for this investigation. In this article, the difference of current efficiency was studied by adjusting direct current and variable

current to impure and pure copper anode.

#### 2 Experimental 

###### 2.1 Preparation of Specimens 

Anode specimens were prepared by adding main impurities to pure copper with high frequency furnace. Main impurities were added separately and compositively (Table 1 and Table 2). Anode specimens added impurities separately were added 1000 ppm oxygen and 20 ppm sulfur based on pure copper and melted at 1400~1500 °C. Specimens were casted on the mold 20 mm in diameter preheated at 450 °C. Casted specimens were sliced to 15 mm in diameter and 4 mm in thickness with oil cooling for electrolysis tests. Anode specimens added impurities compositively were added As, Sb, Bi, Pb, etc and made by the same method as anode specimens added impurities separately.

###### 2.2 Electrolysis Tests 

Prepared specimens were used for electrolysis tests to input the same electricity amount with different types of current – Direct Current (DC), Variable Current (VC) and Periodic Reverse Current (PRC). Conditionts for electrolysis tests for DC were current input 62 mA, time 3000 sec, anode as prepared specimen with surface 0.78 cm<sup>2</sup> and cathode as Pt net. The results were cell voltage and weight of anode and cathode before and after the test. Electrolyte conditions were Cu 45 g/l, H2SO4 175 g/l and 58 °C. Electrolysis tests for VC were input high current 80 mA, time 700 sec and low current 20 mA, time 300 sec continued for three cycles. Electrolysis tests for PRC were input positive current 62 mA, time 742.5 sec and negative current 62 mA, time 7.425 sec continued for four cycles. Additionally, electrolysis tests for VC were used pure copper anode and input high current, time and low current, time based on the Design of Experiments.

Alejandro R. Lillo

**Keywords:** Electrowinning, energy saving, current density, tankhouse design, productivity 

#### Abstract 

With increasing demands for energy savings, copper electrowinning is becoming exposed to energy restrictions, cost increase and demands for making the process more intense is one of the ways potentially available to respond to the challenge. Its electrochemical fundamentals remain unchanged until today since its beginning in the late 1800’s. Major changes in design have been focused on electrodes and material handling, such as the introduction of massive use of permanent cathodes, but plants still are designed on a conservative way. Other metals using similar technology have reengineered the conceptual design of tankhouses and this paper is focused in adjusting those changes to copper electrowinning. Main results indicate that copper electrowinning is feasible to operate using parallel plate technology over 550 A/m<sup>2</sup> generating cathodes of equivalent chemical quality to those generated under current conservative parameters. Physical quality is improved by high current density due to the introduction of hardware which improves the cell hydrodynamics. The combination of results suggests a change in cathode geometry to reduce foot prints and maximize the rate of material handling. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Copper electrowinning has a long history, with substantial production starting early in this century at major operations at Chuquicamata (1911) and Inspiration (1924). 

With the introduction of solvent extraction in the 1960s it became possible to consistently produce high quality cathode from a richer and purer electrolyte. While the basics of the electrowinning process have not changed since its beginning, plant design and operations have become more intense in recent years. These developments, however, have had a common restriction with the size of the electrodes and limiting current density and automation. 

Major changes in design have been focused on electrodes and material handling, such as the introduction of massive use of permanent cathodes, but plants still are designed on a conservative way.

### How Anodes Passivate in Copper Electrorefining 

M. S. Moats University of Utah Salt Lake City, UT, USA 

J. Brent Hiskey University of Arizona Tucson, AZ, USA 

**Keywords:** Anode passivation, impurities, slime, electrolyte composition, passivation mechanism 

#### Abstract 

Anode passivation can decrease productivity and quality while increasing costs in copper electrorefineries. After examining the effect of anode and electrolyte composition on passivation tendencies, a passivation mechanism has been developed that explains most of the observed phenomena. Anode passivation results from the formation of inhibiting films. Potential oscillation can occur just prior to passivation and demonstrate the importance of slimes, copper sulfate and copper oxide. Slimes confine dissolution to their pores and inhibit diffusion. This can lead to copper sulfate precipitation, which blocks more of the surface area. Copper oxide forms at the interface between the copper sulfate and anode a

s a result of increasing potential. Ultimate passivation occurs when the anode potential is high enough to stabilize the oxide film in the bulk electrolyte. The effects of anode impurities and electrolyte concentrations are related to the formation of at least one of these films. This presentation coalesces a large amount of experimental data and provides a unified interpretation of how copper anodes passivate during electrorefining. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Copper electrorefining is an age-old process. It was first demonstrated experimentally by von Leuchtenberg in 1847 [1]. Elkington patented the process in 1865 and developed the first successful plant in Pembrey, Wales in 1869. In 1876, Dr. Emil Wohlwill implemented the technology in Hamburg, Germany. This plant operated with 3000 amps and produced 800 kg of electrolytic copper per day [2]. The first commercial electrorefining plant in the United States was constructed by Balbach Smelting & Refining Co. in 1883. The Newark, New Jersey plant produced 1800-2700 kg of electrolytic copper per day during the first year [1]. 

While significant modernization has occurred over the past century, electrorefining still utilizes the electrochemical dissolution of an impure copper anode in an electrolytic cell containing a copper sulfate-sulfuric acid solution. Copper ions are transported to the cathode where they are deposited with suitable purity. The basic electrochemical reactions involved are:

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Moats, Hiskey_ 





The production of copper by electrorefining has improved substantially since it was established in the late nineteenth century in terms of scale and productivity. Improvements in current efficiency, materials handling, electrolyte purification, and automation of process and process control have led to substantial production increases, particularly in the last several decades. Operating conditions at 56 commercial tankhouses located throughout the world have been recently reviewed by Moats _et al._ [3]. Recent trends that have led to increases in production and cathode quality include reusable cathodes [4, 5], improved electrolytic bleeds, monitoring of additives [6, 7] and anode preparation machines. 

Even with these technological advances, passivation of commercial copper anodes still occurs occasionally in most modern electrorefineries. Passivation is the inhibition of the dissolution reaction caused by the formation of non-dissolving films. Anode passivation results in lost production capacity, increased power costs, and decreased cathode quality. Thus, the minimization of anode passivation could ultimately improve worldwide copper quality and decrease production costs. 

###### 1.1 Passivation of Pure Copper 

The passivation of pure copper in a synthetic industrial electrolyte containing nickel at 65<sup>o</sup> C was investigated by Ghali and others. Using potentiostatic and voltammetric techniques Garneau · _et al._ [8] generated a passivating

film and determined it to be mostly CuSO4 5H2O by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and scanning electron microscopy. Cu2O was also detected after multiple sweeps using cyclic voltammetry. Jin and Ghali [9] found similar results using chronopotentiometry followed by X-ray induced Auger electron spectroscopy (XAES). Gauthier, Manzini and Ghali [10] found copper sulfate and copper oxides by SEM and XAES after passivation in linear sweep voltammetry. 

###### 1.2 Passivation of Impure Copper Anodes 

Under normal industrial electrorefining operating conditions, pure copper will not passivate. Therefore, the ultimate cause of passivation is the impurities contained within the anode and electrolyte. Impurities in the anode are the result of the original ore or scrap feed. As the anode dissolves, some impurities report to the slimes; others to the electrolyte. Impurities in the electrolyte become concentrated over time in the closed electrolyte system. 

The effect of anode impurities has been examined by studying the passivation response of commercial copper anode samples. Abe _et al._ [11] studied thirteen anodes using CP. They illustrated that

time to passivation (tp) decreased with increasing oxygen and slimes. Abe and Gotoh [12], also using CP, illustrated that the susceptibility to passivate increased when nickel, oxygen, or silver levels were high in the anode. Baltazar _et al._ [13] investigated the effect of arsenic and antimony using twelve different anode samples with chronopotentiometry at near to industrial conditions. Anodes with a molar ratio of As to Sb greater than two resisted passivation. Cheng and Hiskey [14] revealed that increasing arsenic within commercial copper anodes inhibited passivation in CP experiments. Increasing oxygen in anodes with low arsenic (<400 ppm) decreased tp. Moats and Hiskey [15] examined forty-four commercial copper samples using CP and showed that selenium, tellurium, silver, lead and nickel accelerated passivation, oxygen accelerated passivation when increased from 500 to 1500 ppm, but further increases did not have an effect and arsenic was the only impurity found that inhibited passivation. 

To fully realize the effect of each impurity within the electrorefining system, the behavior of that impurity during casting and electrorefining must be understood. With this in mind, the mineralogy and microstructure of anodes will be reviewed. The deportment of the impurities during electrorefining will then be discussed in terms of slimes, non-slime elements, and impurities in the electrolyte. 

###### 1.3 Slimes 

The understanding of the secondary phases present in the anode and slimes layer has been greatly enhanced by Chen and Dutrizac [16-32] and Forsen’s group [33-36]. The important phases that were detected were (Cu,Ag)2Se rings, euhedral NiO crystals, PbSO4, silicates, kupferglimmer, and various complex oxides. Mo

st of these phases were formed during prior pyrometallurgical processing. During dissolution they are released from the anode. Several phases, however, are formed or transformed during the electrorefining process. Selenium occurs predominantly as a metal deficient copper selenide (Cu2-xSe) along the grain boundaries of the copper matrix. During electrorefining, silver ions have been shown by Scott [37] to rapidly react with the selenides causing a transformation from Cu2Se to Ag2Se. Hiskey _et al._ [38] illustrated that this reaction causes a 20 % increase in the volume of the selenide phase. This could explain why Abe and Goto [12] noted that an anode with high silver exhibited a thicker and denser slimes layer than other anodes. The presence of lead sulfate is another indication of a reaction occurring within the slimes layer. Lead typically occurs as a complex lead oxide associated with various elements. These inclusions usually dissolve upon exposure to the highly acidic electrolyte. The resulting lead ions precipitate with the sulfate contained within the electrolyte to form PbSO4 within the slimes barrier. 

An understanding of the slimes chemistry and morphology is imperative because the slimes layer can inhibit diffusion, which leads to passivation. Abe and Gotoh [39] illustrated that pure copper, which did not passivate, passivated when masked with an artificial slimes layer (Millipore filter paper). It was also demonstrated that the tendency to passivate increased with decreasing pore size.

###### 1.4 Non-Slime Impurities 

There are impurities in the anodes that are not usually involved with anode slime formation that can also affect passivation. These elements, even at low concentration, can affect the complex copper dissolution reaction. Stankovic, using pure copper, illustrated that Fe [41] slightly accelerated, As [42] significantly increased, and Sb [42] slightly hindered the dissolution reaction of copper when present in the electrolyte at concentrations ranging from 10<sup>-5</sup> to 10<sup>-1</sup> M. In commercial anodes, the most significant impurities appear to be oxygen and the Group VB elements (As, Sb, and Bi). However, Abe, Burrows, and Ettel [11] had previously indicated that oxygen content in commercial anodes was detrimental from chronopotentiometric results. This latter viewpoint of oxygen accelerating passivation was repeated confirmed by Hiskey’s group [14-15, 43-44]. 

Arsenic,

antimony, and bismuth are very troublesome elements in copper electrorefining. Their reduction occurs at nearly the same voltage as copper, which can cause cathode contamination during periods of passivation. Another problem caused by the Group VB elements is their accumulation in the electrolyte, which can lead to the formation of floating slimes. Floating slimes, which are SbAsO4 and BiAsO4 [45], form by precipitation typically away from the anode surface. In the electrolyte, they can float to the cathode where they can be entrapped; thus causing contamination. However, none of these reasons overtly affects anode passivation. Hiskey _et al._ [38] demonstrated using chronopotentiometry on commercial anodes, that arsenic inhibits passivation, antimony accelerates it, and bismuth has a complex interaction. Finally, arsenic has been reported by Demaeral [46] to cause a decrease in the adhesion of slimes, which would hinder passivation by the removal or sloughing of the diffusion barrier. 

Hiskey _et al._ [38] proposed that the effect of Group VB elements and oxygen could be explained by using a _bi-layer passivation model_ . It is theorized that the slimes layer, because of its hindrance to diffusion, creates a substantial boundary layer adjacent to the anode surface. The concentrations of ions can be extremely different in this boundary layer than that in the bulk electrolyte. As oxides, particularly of As, Sb and Bi, dissolve, they either cause acid consumption or generation. Samples of possible reactions are as follows:

###### 1.5 Electrolyte 

Electrolyte composition and temperature play a critical role in passivation. Numerous researchers have shown that passivation is aggravated by increasing the copper concentration, the acid concentration, or decreasing the temperature [11, 47, 48-50]. Noguchi _et al._ showed that time to passivation decreased with increasing Sb<sup>3+</sup> , As<sup>3+</sup> , Bi<sup>3+</sup> and dissolved O2 in the electrolyte [13]. Abe _et al._ demonstrated that passivation time decreased with increasing nick

Moats and Hiskey [51] showed that the effect of nickel sulfate was more related to the sulfate addition than the nickel ion as sodium sulfate addition produced similar passivation results. Moats and Hiskey [51] also studied a wide range of electrolyte composition variables; examined were copper, acid, nickel, arsenic, chloride, thiourea and glue using several commercial copper anodes. This investigation revealed that electrolyte parameters that inhibit copper dissolution through copper sulfate precipitation, copper oxide stabilization and/or absorbed species lead to accelerated passivation. Species that prevent passivation have the ability to complex cuprous ions. 

Others have examined the effect of additives on passivation in laboratory experiments. Hiskey and Cheng illustrated that time to passivation is a function of thiourea [52]. For small addition, 1-5 ppm, thiourea improves the passivation behavior, but for large addition, greater than 15 ppm, passivation times decreased. Moats and Hiskey [53] found that 1) chloride concentration has a significant positive effect by extending the times to passivation for most anodes, 2) both glue and thiourea appear to be an optimal concentration (approximately 1 ppm) at which an increase in tp is observed, 3) there was an anode compositional interaction when chloride, thiourea and glue were all present. 

All of the additive compounds listed above have the ability to stabilize cuprous ions [52-54]. Therefore, it would appear that increasing the cuprous concentration increases the time to passivation. This coincides with the combined observations of Noguchi _et al._ [13] and Bombach _et al_ . [55]. Recall that Noguchi showed that passivation time decreased with increasing dissolved O2. Bombach _et al._ demonstrated that Cu<sup>+</sup> ion decreased with increasing dissolved O2. Combining these two observations would seem to indicate that increasing the cuprous content might be beneficial to passivation. Therefore, cuprous stabilizing compounds might be interesting to study. #### 2 Mechanistic Approach to Passivation 

While all of the aforementioned information is critical in understanding the complex issues involved in anode passivation, none fully elucidates the cause of passivation in impure commercial copper anodes. Passivation is the result of something stopping the ability of copper to dissolve and thus the flow of current. Numerous authors [8-10, 11, 16-18, 39, 43-44, 47] have reported observations of passivating films, such CuSO4·5H2O, Cu2O and CuO. Though no completely satisfactory passivation mechanism has been introduced, Abe and Gotoh [12, 39] have presented the most complete model in descri

bing oscillations during CP experiments. This mechanism associates the oscillations with the precipitation and re-dissolution of CuSO4·5H2O. The oscillations are believed to be caused by the instability of a CuSO4 phase. However, this mechanism is lacking because it disregarded copper oxide formation, which was noted by Abe and Gotoh during the oscillations. 

To explain anode passivation in a commerical electrorefining environment, the response of commercial copper anode under constant current conditions (e.g. chronopotentiometry) are thoroughly analyzed. Laborotory CPs exhibit four distinct regions as shown in Figure 1. The regions that are present lead to passivaiton will be thoroughly analyzed and discussed in this paper. Particular emphasis will be placed on developing a comprehensive mechanism for anode passivation. Information from other electrochemical techniques will be introduced as clarifying or supporting evidence. The analyis of post-passivation reactions during CP of commercial copper anodes have been previously reported [57].

The initiation of the applied current causes the dissolution of the commercial copper anode to commence, resulting in the first region of the chronopotentiogram. At first glance, the potential seems reasonably stable while slightly increasing. Compared to the large potential anomalies found in subsequent regions, this region appears to be rather well behaved and uneventful. However, the evidence deduced within the active dissolution region clearly foretells of the passivation that will eventually occur.
