Therefore the mechanism seems plausible. #### 3 Passivation Mechanism From the analyses of Regions I and II, a mechanism for the passivation of commercial copper anodes can be developed. When the dissolution of an impure copper anode commences: 1) the copper concentration of the electrolyte at the anode surface increases and 2) slimes are released. The slimes will reduce the active surface area of the electrode. This causes an increase in the current density and a subsequent increase in the copper concentration in the electrolyte within the pores of the slimes. Depending on the applied current density, amount of slimes, electrolyte composition and rate of diffusion, the copper concentration at the anode surface can reach the saturation limit of cop- per sulfate. The electrolyte will probably become supersaturated before the formation of CuSO4·5H2O nuclei occur in the pores of the growing slime film. The formation of the CuSO4·5H2O leads to a decrease in the copper concentration in the pores where it forms as the surface becomes blocked. This will eventually cause the copper sulfate to re-dissolve. Until that occurs, the s

ulfate layer will allow the formation of copper oxide between the sulfate and anode. When the sulfate does dissolve, if the potential and electrolyte conditions are not sufficient to sustain the oxide film, then it will also dissolve. 

The slimes layer and sulfate/oxide deposits continue to grow with time leading to the rise in potential noted in Region I. When the surface becomes increasingly covered, oscillations are detected as the dissolution/formation of the sulfate/oxide film become synchronized. The oscillations will continue until the electrode becomes suitably covered with slimes and oxide. This results in a high enough potential that a return to bulk electrolyte conditions at the anode surface will not dissolve the oxide. This potential appears to be between 0.8-0.9 V vs. SHE based on the analysis of the commerical anodes tested. Passivation is then complete. 

Simply stated, passivation occurs when the anode surface is completely covered with nonconducting or weakly conducting films. This causes the anode to stop dissolving copper. During the electrorefining of impure copper anodes, it has been shown that films of slimes, copper sulfate, and copper oxide can form at the anode surface. Thus, the formation rates of these film components will cause differences in passivation times. 

###### 3.1 Factors Affecting the Formation of Slimes 

The formation of refractory secondary phases or slimes is completely dependent on anode chemistry and prior pyrometallurgical history. The amount of slime formers is not greatly affected by electro- 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

1473 

_Moats, Hiskey_ 



refining conditions. The formation rate of slimes on the anode surface is related to the applied current because the release of slime components occurs as copper dissolves. Homogeneity of the anode structure and chemistry will affect the reproducibility of the formation rate of the slimes. 

Most of the elements shown to affect passivation in our previous study [15] can be classified as slime formers. The common slime-forming elements are selenium, tellurium, nickel, lead and silver. Selenium and tellurium has been shown by several researchers to occur in copper anodes predominantly as copper selenide and copper telluride. These phases dissolve very slowly in the electrolyte and thus form a portion of the slime film/layer. Therefore, increasing the selenium and tellurium would decrease the time to passivation. 

Nickel will be contained as a solute element in copper up to 2500 ppm. Above that, nickel will form two different oxides, NiO and kupferglimmer. Kupferglimmer will only form in the presence of antimony or tin. Both of these oxides are corrosion resistant to the electrolyte and will block the active surface causing a decrease in tp. Kupferglimmer is believed to be especially troublesome because of its platelet morphology. 

Lead is usually found as a complex oxide with copper and the Group VB elements. These oxides typically dissolve into the

electrolyte. Lead ion, however, is extremely insoluble because of the high sulfate concentration in the electrolyte. This causes PbSO4 to precipitate at and near to the surface, which will block the surface of the electrode. 

Lastly, silver is typically found in solid solution within the copper matrix. As the copper grains dissolve, the silver releases as an ion. The Ag<sup>+</sup> then reacts in three ways: 1) it will cement on to the anode and/or selenide features as small crystallites by reacting with cuprous ions, 2) cementation will occur with small copper crystallites which formed due to the disproportionation of cuprous ions or 3) the silver will react with the copper selenides and tellurides resulting in silver enrichment of these features. Obviously, the silver crystallites, which occupy surface sites, will block the dissolution of copper. The transformation of selenides and tellurides has been shown to result in a volume increase, thus covering more surface area. 

###### 3.2 Factors Affecting the Formation of Copper Sulphate 

The formation of CuSO4·5H2O is dependent on the ability of the electrorefining system to supersaturate the electrolyte adjacent to the anode. Supersaturation is caused by the copper anode dissolving at a rate faster than the diffusion rate of cupric ions. Thus, anything that affects the dissolution rate will influence the formation rate of copper sulfate. This indicates that current density, electrolyte temperature and composition, and anode impurities will significantly affect CuSO4·5H2O formation and time to passivation. 

Oxygen is the only anode impurity that can increase the rate of cupric ion generation. Oxygen has a low solubility in copper and will form numerous oxides. The most common oxide is cuprous oxide.

1474

This oxide will dissolve chemically when exposed to the electrolyte . That means the copper dissolution rate is the sum of the electrochemical reaction driven by the applied current and the chemical dissolution of copper oxide. Therefore, the formation of CuSO4·5H2O will occur more rapidly with increasing oxygen content. This should lead to a decrease in tp as oxygen increases, which is the observed trend from the CP data. 

Copper sulfate will form on impure anodes after the concentration at the anode surface exceeds the solution's solubility with enough supersaturation to overcome any nucleation barriers. Supersaturation occurs more rapidly when the bulk electrolyte content is closer to the saturation limit and the rate of concentration build-up at the anode increases. Anything that hinders diffusion will decrease the time to saturation. The copper and acid concentrations in the electrolyte affect both the proximity to the solubility limit and the rate of diffusion. Since the solubility of CuSO4·5H2O is controlled by the copper and sulfate concentrations in the electrolyte, increasing these would move the

solution closer to the saturation limit. The diffusion rate of copper is also adversely affected by increasing the copper and acid concentrations of the electrolyte [57]. Thus, increasing the copper and acid concentrations will lead to faster precipitation of CuSO4·5H2O on the anode surface. Any compound that adds more sulfate (NiSO4, Na2SO4) to the total sulfate content of the electrolyte will have a similar effect, at least on the initial proximity to the saturation limit [51]. 

###### 3.3 Factors Affecting the Formation of Copper Oxide 

From the qualitative analysis of Region II, the formation of copper oxide is dependent on the formation of CuSO4·5H2O. Copper oxide only forms after copper sulfate has blocked the surface. However, the stability of copper oxide after the copper sulfate is removed is dependent on the potential and pH at the anode surface. Copper oxides will not dissolve until the potential and pH allow for its thermodynamically feasiblity. 

Elements that can affect the localized acidity of the electrolyte are Group VB (arsenic, antimony, and bismuth) and oxygen. This was theorized by Hiskey _et al._ [38] to describe the effect of oxygen, arsenic, and antimony on time to passivation of impure copper samples. Examination of the chemistries of each of these impurity elements indicates that oxygen, antimony, and bismuth should be acid consumers and arsenic should generate acid. This would cause oxygen, antimony, and bismuth to promote passivation and arsenic to hinder it. In our investigations, increasing oxygen did lead to decreased passivation times and anodes with higher arsenic exhibited longer times to passivation [15]. Because of experimental scatter and the extreme variation in anode chemistry, the effect of antimony and bismuth was not observed in this study. However, as stated earlier, the effect of antimony to decrease tp was shown by Hiskey _et al._ [38]. 

Examination of the effect of the additives [53] reveals that compounds that extended the time to passivation (chloride, polyethylene glycol, glue, thiourea) exhibit an ability to complex cuprous ions. Complexation of cuprous ions could be beneficial by: 1) inhibiting the generation of copper

particulates within the slimes resulting from the disproportionation reaction, 2) slowing the cupric concentration build-up at the anode and 3) decreasing the stability of Cu2O. The dissolution of copper at the current density utilized in this investigation will involve the disproportionation reaction of the cuprous ion. With this reaction, copper particulates are formed which can join the slimes layer. By complexing cuprous ions, this reaction will be hindered causing a decrease in the amount of slimes generation. The disproportionation reaction also generates cupric ions which lead to the saturation and precipitation of copper sulfate. By inhibiting the reaction, the formation of CuSO4·5H2O will occur less rapidly. Fi

nally, the stability of Cu2O can be influenced by complexing cuprous ions. The dissolution of cuprous oxide in acid can occur by the following reactions: 

Cu2O + 2H<sup>+</sup> → Cu<sup>2+</sup> + Cu<sup>o</sup> + H2O (13) 



The effect of stabilizing the cuprous ion is not easily seen in either (13) or (14). The chemical dissolution of the copper oxide (13) becomes more favorable with Cu<sup>+</sup> stabilization because the reaction implicitly involves the disproportionation reaction of cuprous. The electrochemical dissolution (14) of Cu2O also involves the cuprous ion. Reactions rarely involve a simultaneous two-electron transfer as indicated in (14). Therefore, an intermediate step could include the cuprous ion, which would be affected by the presence of a complexing agent. Regardless of the mechanism, the complexation of cuprous ions appears to extend the time to passivation. 

###### 3.4 Adsorbed Species 

While organic additives, such as thiourea and glue, exhibited a positive effect at low levels, at higher concentrations these same compounds accelerated passivation. This phenomenon is thought to be caused by the adsorption of these compounds or their degradation products on the anode surface. The adsorbed film would block active surface sites just like slimes or copper sulfate, leading to passivation. In the case of thiourea, it is believed that formamidine disulfide (FDS), and ultimately elemental sulfur, act as the blocking species. However, for glue and its degradation products, it is unclear at this time how the adsorption occurs or what species are responsible for the passivating effect. There does appear to be an optimal concentration at which passivation is hindered for both glue and thiourea, but exceeding that level can be detrimental.

A thorough review of the open literature and the extensive experimental work conducted by our group has led to a description of the passivation mechanism for anodes in copper electrorefining. As anode dissolves, slimes are released. This concentrates the current density to open areas within the slimes matrix and hinders diffusion. As more of the anode surface passivates, the surface potential increases. Total passivation occurs when the surface potential is high enough (typically 0.8-0.9 V vs. SHE) to stabilize the cuprous oxide at bulk electrolyte conditions. Anode elements that generate (arsenic) or consume (oxygen, antimony) acid at the anode surface affect the stability of cuprous oxide and thus affect the rate of passiva

tion. Additives that complex cuprous ions can extend the time to passivation by affecting copper sulphate precipitation, slimes generation and copper oxide stability. Compounds that can absorb on the surface act as a de-facto slime layer. This descriptive mechanism can explain all of the observed research by our group and others.

### MnO 2 Deposition on Coated Titanium Anodes in Copper Electrowinning Solutions 

M. S. Moats University of Utah Department of Metallurgical Engineering Salt Lake City, USA 

**Keywords:** Titanium anode, electrowinning, manganese dioxide, copper 

#### Abstract 

As energy prices and concerns about sustainability increase, the need to reduce power consumption in copper electrowinning will become more acute. Replacing lead alloy anodes with coated titanium has the potential to reduce power consumption of a cell by 15 %. Unfortunately, the service life of coated titanium anodes is sensitive to deposits of foreign materials such as MnO2. Using factorial designs of experiments, industrially relevant electrolyte components and electrolysis parameters were investigated to determine their effect on MnO2 deposition on IrO2-Ta2O5 coated titanium anodes. It was observed that the rate of MnO2 deposition increases with increasing manganese, decreasing iron and decreasing acid concentrations. MnO2 deposition also increased with increasing temperature. Current density an

d cobalt concentration were not found to be statistically significant. Interactions existed between Mn and other cations. The laboratory results are examined with a focus on methods to reduce the likelihood of MnO2 formation on coated titanium anodes during commercial operation. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Due to increasing demand and environmental pressures, energy prices have generally increased recently. The electrowinning of metals from solution is an energy intensive process and thus sensitive to energy prices. Marsden [1] reported that for Freeport-McMoRan operations the energy consumption of electrowinning for standard hydrometallurgical processes was 1749 kJ kg<sup>-1</sup> of copper cathode. Electrowinning was the second highest energy consumption process behind the actual mining of ore. Marsden [1] also stated that two technologies to increase the energy efficiency of copper electrowinning had been developed by Freeport-McMoRan. These were alternative anodes and ferrous oxidation. These two technologies have the potential to reduce energy consumption by 13 % and 42 %, respectively.

The implementation of ferrous oxidation into a commercial copper electrowinning operation, while holding the most potential for energy savings, is also much more complex then replacing a lead alloy anode with a precious-metal coated titanium anode. Thus, it appears likely that the replacement of anodes may be the next step in energy reduction at electrowinning facilities. 

Numerous attempts have been made over the past 30+ years to replace lead with coated titanium anodes (CTAs). In 1984, a symposium of nine papers [2] was devoted to electrowinning anodes; about half of the papers were related to coated titanium in one form or another. More recently, a hybrid coated titanium-lead anode was developed and commercially demonstrated for copper electrowinning [3-6]. The so-called Mesh-on-Lead (MOL) anode reduced cell voltage by 10-17 %, produced grade A cathodes without the addition of cobalt and had a lifetime of 3.25 yrs. Even with these performance advantages over lead anodes, the MOL anode has not found acceptance on a commercial basis. A recent analysis of lead alloy and coated titanium anodes [7] indicated that the conversion to CTAs would be driven by energy prices and material costs. 

In addition to these overlaying economic concerns, the implementation of CTAs has also been hindered by technical issues such as the deposition of foreign materials onto the anode surface. One of the main foreign deposits of concern to CTAs is electrodeposited MnO2. The deposition of MnO2 on CTAs in zinc electrowinning was extensively studied by Nijjer [8]. Pajunuen et al. [9] examined the effect of manganese concentration on anode activity and found that MnO2 deposition significantly inhibited CTA activity. In both of these studies, the Mn<sup>2+</sup> concentration was ≥ 1 g l<sup>-1</sup> , which is entirely appropriate whe

n examining zinc electrowinning. However, in copper electrowinning the Mn<sup>2+</sup> concentration of the electrolyte is typically <200 mg l<sup>-1</sup> [10] as the solvent extraction process utilized to produce the electrolyte minimizes the transfer of manganese. Furthermore, copper electrowinning operates at lower current densities and in the presence of iron ions which could affect MnO2 deposition [11]. 

In this study, parameters in ranges that are more typical of industrial copper electrowinning were examined to determine their effects on the deposition of MnO2 on CTAs. 

#### 2 Experimental 

###### 2.1 Materials 

All experiments were performed using IrO2-Ta2O5 coated titanium anodes. Titanium anode samples were provided by DeNora Tech and Freeport McMoRan Copper & Gold (FMI). No details were provided concerning the manufacturing of either anode material. Electron dispersive spectroscopy was used to confirm the presence of Ir and Ta on the parts. The DeNora Tech material was used for the short-term electrowinning experiments. The Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold material was used for the longer-term experiments.

All solutions were prepared using reagent grade chemicals except as later discussed. The water used was de-ionized (>18.2 MΩ cm). All metal ions were added as sulphates except lead which was added as an acetate. Iron was added as ferric. Chloride and nitrate were added as sodium chemicals. Sulfate ion was added as MgSO4⋅7H2O. For the longer-term electrowinning experiments, the cathode smoothing agent, acid mist suppressor, and solvent extraction chemical used were commercial products provided by Freeport McMoRan Copper & Gold. 

###### 2.2 Electrowinning 

The electrodeposition of MnO2 on coated titanium anodes was studied using laboratory copper electrowinning experiments. Two different experimental set-ups were used during this study. Short term experiments were conducted to examine the effect of electrolyte and electrolysis conditions on the rate of MnO2 deposition. Longer term experiments were examined to again study electrolyte and electrolysis conditions on MnO2 deposition and cell voltage behaviour. 

###### 2.2.1 Short Term Electrowinning 

Short term electrowinning experiments were performed in a small glass reactor. The reactor was filled with 200 ml of synthetic copper electrowinning electrolyte. Two electrodes were placed into the cell with 4.5 cm spacing. The anode was a 2.5 cm<sup>2</sup> coated titanium sheet. The cathode was grade 1 Ti sheet of the same area. Each electrode was welded to a grade 1 Ti rod to facilitate electrical connection. The Ti rod was wrapped in non-conductive Teflon tape. The cell was heated using a hot plate to the set temperature and controlled at +/- 1<sup>o</sup> C. Constant current was applied using a Gamry PCI4/750 potentiostat. The cell voltage was recorded througho

ut each of the 6000 second long experiments. 

Two 2<sup>3</sup> full factorial designs of experiments were employed during the short term experiments to examine the effects and interactions of electrolyte and electrolysis conditions. The conditions employed and the factors and levels studied are shown in Table 1. Each condition was performed with two replicates.

###### 2.2.2 Longer Term Electrowinning 

Longer term electrowinning experiments were also performed to examine MnO2 deposition and cell voltage behaviour. These experiments were conducted for six-days to simulate one electrowinning harvest cycle. Four replicate cells of design similar to that used in the short-term experiments were connected to an electrolyte reservoir. Electrolyte in the reservoir was heated using a quartz heater. Temperature in one of the four cells was measured and used to control the heater in the reservoir insuring 40<sup>o</sup> C +/- 2<sup>o</sup> C in each cell. The total electrolyte volume used for each experiment was 7 litres. The electrolyte was pumped from the reservoir to each cell individually using a 4-channel peristaltic pump. The flow rate through the cells was high (119 ml min<sup>-1</sup> ) to insure that the electrolyte constituents were not depleted. 

Each cell contained one anode and one cathode. The anode was a coated titanium mesh. The cathode was a grade 1 titanium sheet. The size of the electrodes was 6.2 cm<sup>2</sup> . The electrodes were spaced 4.5 cm apart. Each cell was connected in series electrically with a constant current provided by a digital power supply. The cell voltage for each cell was recorded individually using a National Instruments data acquisition voltage card (USB9201) connected to a PC computer for data recording. Anode potential was measured every 12 hours versus a Ag/AgCl reference electrode positioned halfway between the electrodes using a hand-held voltmeter. 

The electrolyte composition was maintained by checking the copper and acid concentrations twice daily using titration methods provided by FMI. Copper was replenished using a 97 % copper hydroxide that was prepared in our laboratory. The copper hydroxide was prepared by precipitation from a copper sulphate soluti

on using NaOH. Using the copper hydroxide, no additional acid neutralization was needed and copper concentrations were maintained at +/- 1 g l-1 . The effect of electrolyte composition and electrolysis parameters was examined using a Taguchi L12 experimental design. The factors and levels used are shown in Table 2. Characterization consisted of examining the anode using scanning electron microscope (SEM), energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and/or X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy (XRF). The net intensity of the Mn peak measured by EDS was analyzed by ANOVA methodology. It should be recognized that the four replicates of each condition are not truly independent as they were operated on the same electrolyte by the same power supply. Any variation observed would be based on differences in CTA specimens or individual cell set-up. Thus, the full ANOVA results will not be presented as they are compromised by the experimental design. 

Even so, the results of the long-term experiments provided some strong indications: 

- 1) Higher Mn surface content was observed at the high (150 mg l<sup>-1</sup> ) Mn concentration, 

- 2) Not all high Mn concentration tests resulted in large amounts of Mn on the anode surface, 

- 3) Conditions that promoted heavy MnO2 deposition also included low Fe (1 g l<sup>-1</sup> ), high nitrate concentration (1000 mg l<sup>-1</sup> ) and the presence of SX chemicals. 

While the results of these tests are less conclusive, they do indicate that Mn<sup>2+</sup> and iron concentrations interact on the likelihood of MnO2 deposits on CTAs as previously indicated by the short-term experiments. The results also indicate that solution ORP (or EMV) is probably important as nitrate and/or iron had effects on MnO2 deposition. Finally, the effect of the SX chemical on MnO2 deposition should be investigated further. 

The longer-term (six-day) experiments also provided insight into the voltage response caused by MnO2 deposition. During the experiments, the cell voltage in general decreased due to the plating of copper on the cathode. The average decrease for all of the experiments was 30 mV. The anode potential typically exhibited a small increase (average 20 mV) with a range of -30 mV (decrease) to 80 mV. 

The cell voltage and anode potential responses were analyzed with respect to the presence or quantity of Mn on the anode surface and no correlation

was found. This finding is very interesting since the SEM images indicate that some anodes were heavily covered with MnO2 and yet no response to anode potential or cell voltage was detected. This appears to indicate that the surface of CTAs can become significantly contaminated by Mn deposits and still perform adequately at least for a short term. With that said, the long term effects of these surface deposits on ultimate lifetime would have to be studied further to determine if they were truly harmless to the CTAs. 

#### 4 Conclusions 

This research has shown that MnO2 can deposit on IrO2-Ta2O5 coated titanium anodes in conditions typical of commercial copper electrowinning. Short-term experiments revealed that MnO2 deposition rate increases with increasing Mn<sup>2+</sup> , decreasing iron, decreasing acid and increasing temperature. Longer-term experiments revealed that nitrate concentration and the presence of SX chemicals may also promote MnO2 deposition. During the six-day electrowinning experiment, no correlation was found between the change in cell voltage or anode potential and the presence or amount of

As surface deposits are known to affect CTA lifetime, more research should be performed to understand the long term effect of MnO2 deposits grown during copper electrowinning. Since it appears that the likelihood and rate of MnO2 deposition on CTAs during copper electrowinning operation is dependent on electrolyte composition, operators should evaluate this potential problem for their system before making a significant investment in new anode technology.

#### Abstract 

This article presents the results of a three year research project funded by the “Sponsor Group Copper Electrorefining”. Investigated were passivation behaviour, anode dissolution, anode sludge formation and distribution coefficients of impure copper anodes with linear independent target contents of Sb, As, Bi and O processed at three current densities. The experimental setup is shown as well as the obtained results. Mathematical modelling of the results was done, analysing the influence of these factors and their interdependencies on the electrolysis process. All significant effects are

displayed using scaled and centred coefficient plots describing the influence of the critical elements. #### 1 Introduction Copper refining electrolysis is the essential process step to produce high-purity copper and precious metals. The anode copper used in the electrolysis process contains impurities, most frequently Ag, As, Au, Bi, Fe, Ni, O2, Pt, S, Sb, Se, Te, and Zn. Their content depends on the raw materials used (ores or scraps) and process conditions. During electrolysis impurities, ignoble to Cu, are dissolved into the electrolyte and the insoluble residue based on noble and insoluble components is collected as anode sludge. The accompanying elements cause different, mainly negative effects during the electrolysis process by reacting with each other or with the electrolyte components. These effects range from anode polarisation, copper losses in precipitation products up to cathode inclusions. Normally the content of certain impurities in industrial copper anodes is correlated as they derive jointly from complex resources. Such it is hard to separate the effects of the impurities on electrolysis parameters. 1495 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Mцller, Bayanmunkh, Friedrich_ The target of the present study is the systematic investigation of impurity interactions in copper anodes in respect to their dissolution/passivation behaviour, anodic current efficiencies and distribution coefficients. Lab-scale produced anodes with various impurity combinations of the Cu-Ag-NiAs-Sb-Bi-O-system are tested, with linear independent target contents of Bi, As, Sb and O. The use of synthetic anodes allows for separation of the effects of the different elements by using multivariante statistical methods. Trials have been carried out in series, each of 6 different anodes at identical conditions and were conducted at constant temperature. This publication presents the results of a 3 years research project funded by the “Sponsor Group Copper Electrorefining”, showing the experimental setup as well as the effect of anode composition and anode current density on the electrolysis process. #### 2 Experimental setup In order to investigate the “interaction of anode impurities”, 87 anodes are cast with linear independent compositions (Figure 1). Among the seven potential alloying elements only the content of Bi, Sb, As and oxygen are altered. Target contents are in the case of oxygen 1000 ppm, 2000 ppm and 4000 ppm, for Bi 0, 250 and 500 ppm, for Sb 0, 500 and 1000 ppm and for As 0, 1500 and 3000 ppm. The silver concentration is kept constant at 1000 ppm for all trials, the same applies for nickel with 2000 ppm. The combinations are illustrated in Figure 2. #### 6 Effect of arsenic 

Arsenic has a huge influence lowering the passivation tendency (Figure 5) and except for the combination factor Bi*As, which seems to have a small contrary effect, all other factor combinations containing As also have a strong trend to lower the passivation tendency, partly annulling the heightening effect of these single components. This explains why no anodes containing arsenic passivated during our investigation, independent of their chemical composition. Reason for that is that the oxidation of As<sup>3+</sup> is reported to be more preferable and faster than that of Sb<sup>3+</sup> . Therefore, the oxidation of Sb<sup>3+</sup> to Sb<sup>5+</sup> , which causes an exceeding of the much lower Sb<sup>5+</sup> saturation limit in front of the anode, will not preferentially occur as long as sufficient amount of As<sup>3+</sup> is dissolved in the electrolyte [1]. The second reason for the lowered passivation tendency of anodes containing arsenic is the precipitation of antimony and bismuth as hardly soluble compounds in the anode sludge [2]. This formation does not cause passivation because with rising As concentration at the phase boundry metal/electrolyte the pH value in front of the anode decreases leading to an increased solubility of the components in front of the anode and their precipitation happens mainly inside the electrolyte [3]. Furthermore the sludge adhesion gets lower during this process [4]. 

Arsenic has also the characteristic to decrease the dissolved specific anode mass (Figure 5). It is partly dissolved in the anode copper matrix (20-30 % according to [5, 6]) and gets electrochemically dissolved even before copper due to its ignoble character. Unlike copper it is forming trivalent ions whilst consuming more electrons and therefore the dissolved mass per Ah is declining. The contrary effect of As*O is due to the formation of As2O3 which forms at the grain boundaries and dissolves chemically into the electrolyte. 

Figure 6 reveals that the amount of anode sludge is dependent on a lot of factors and the strongest influence can be determined as that of As, having the effect to lower the amount of anode sludge produced. The factor combinations As*O and As*i slightly increase the amount of anode sludge, but this is negligible compared to the single effects which do the contrary. Mechanisms accounting for this result are the same as for the prevention of passivation. 

All distribution coefficients analysed (Figure 6, Figure 7) are influenced by the As content in the anode for the same reasons as it is lowering their precipitation to ano

de sludge. It is the main factor influencing the As and Bi distribution to sludge and is also a strong factor in the Sb distribution. Furthermore the factor combination Sb*As is lowering the As and the Sb distribution to anode sludge and As*i slightly increases the distribution of As. The reasons for the lower Sb distribution have already been explained. Regarding the distribution of As it is assumed that, for a fixed amount of impurities, in particular lead and antimony, a fixed amount of As is bound as insoluble complex oxides, leading to decreasing percentages of arsenic reporting to the anode slimes at increasing arsenic concentrations in the anode (if all other components stay the same) [7]. No satisfying explanation was found for the effect of As on the Bi distribution.

#### 7 Effect of antimony 

The anode antimony concentration is a strong factor influencing anode passivation (Figure 5). It shows interdependencies with the anodic arsenic and oxygen concentration as well as the current density, whereas the first factor combination leads to a decrease in the passivation probability (as explained before) and the other factor combinations to an increase. It was already examined by various authors [8] that antimony primary dissolves into the electrolyte in the trivalent form and gets then oxidised to Sb<sup>5+</sup> in the presence of oxygen. By exceeding the much lower Sb<sup>5+</sup> saturation limit in front of the anode passivation occurs. Figure 5 also shows that Sb itself has no significant influence on the anode dissolution degree in the analysed range. 

The effect of Sb on the amount of anode sludge is quite forward (Figure 6). Antimony mainly reports to the anode sludge in form of various oxide components [12], so the higher the concentration of Sb in the anode the more anode sludge is produced. 

All distribution coefficients analysed are influenced by Sb (Figure 6 and Figure 7). The antimony distribution to anode sludge (Figure 6) is decreasing with increasing anode Sb concentration and it is assumed that the same mechanism accounts as for As. In case of the other distribution coefficients (Figure 7) an increase in the anode Sb concentration results in an increase of the Bi and As distribution to anode sludge, due to the formation of insoluble Bi-Sb, As-Sb containing compounds. In combination with As resp. Bi this effect is reduced by interactions. The following figure shows the transfer mechanisms and interactions for As, Sb and Bi to electrolyte/anode slime.

#### 8 Effect of bismuth 

The bismuth concentration of the anode has no significant effect on the anode passivation probability, the anode dissolution degree as well as

the Sb and As distribution coefficients within the analysed parameter range (Figure 5 to Figure 7). Bi is only slightly influencing these parameters in combination with other anode impurities as already mentioned. Figure 6 shows that Bi has a slight increasing effect on the amount of anode sludge formed, which is, like for Sb, due to the formation of various oxide components [12]. Compared to the other factors Bi has only a minor influence on its own distribution coefficient (Figure 7) based on the same mechanisms as for arsenic on the As distribution coefficient . A fixed amount of Bi is bond as insoluble and complex oxides, leading to decreasing percentages of Bi reporting to the anode sludge at higher anode bismuth concentrations. 

#### 9 Effect of oxygen 

Oxygen in the anode is mainly present in form of various oxides (Cu-, Ni-, As-, Sb-, Bi-) depending on the amount/type of impurities in the anode. The anode oxygen concentration significantly influences the passivation behaviour, the anode dissolution degree, the anode sludge generation as well as the metal distribution coefficients, especially Sb. As can be seen from Figure 5 oxygen is promoting passivation, as it impacts the anode slime structure and porosity. The higher the anode oxygen content the lower is the slime settling rate [7], thereby increasing the anode passivation tendency. This effect is further intensified by increasing current densities. The effect of As*O and Sb*O has already been explained and is due to their increased oxidation potential. 

Figure 5 also shows high oxygen contents lead to an improved anode dissolution degree, as oxygen is forming oxide phases with the metal impurities, which extensively dissolve chemically or go to the anode sludge un-dissolved. No electrical current is needed for their removal and such the dissolved anode mass per Ah is rising. Components dissolved into the electrolyte lower the amount of anode sludge produced at the same time which can be seen in Figure 6. Combinations of oxygen with As and/or the current density reduce this effect slightly. 

A rising oxygen concentration in the anode leads to an increased antimony distribution to anode sludge (via oxidation of Sb<sup>3+</sup> to Sb<sup>5+</sup> see Figure 8.) and is the only possibility to increase the Sb distribution coefficient (Figure 6). An increasing current density has only negative effects which can be partly compensated by combination with certain impurities.

#### 11 Summary 

In this research project the passivation behaviour, anode dissolution, anode sludge formation and distribution coefficients of impure copper anodes were experimentally investigated in labscale. Synthetically produced anodes with linear independent target contents of Sb, As, Bi and O were processed at three current densities. Mathematical modelling of the results was done, analysing the influence of these factors and their interdependencies on the electrolysis process. Significant effects can now be displayed using scaled and centred coefficient plots describing the influence of the critical elements. The results of this investigation can be summarized as follows:

### Smart Anodes for Electrochemical Processing of Copper Production 

M. Morimitsu, N. Oshiumi, N. Wada 

Doshisha University, Department of Environmental Systems Science 1-3 Tatara-miyakodani 

Kyo-tanabe, Kyoto, Japan 

**Keywords:** Copper production, oxygen evolution anode, amorphous coating, energy saving, anodic deposition 

#### Abstract 

Production of thin copper foils applied for printed circuit boards of electronic devices is based on electrodeposition of copper in acidic CuSO4 solutions, in which copper is deposited on a rolling cathode and continuously pulled out as a thin copper film from the cathode surface, while the anode reaction is oxygen evolution. 

This paper presents a novel anode for copper foil production, which consists of a binary oxide coating formed on a titanium substrate. The oxide coating comprising amorphous IrO2 and Ta2O5 developed in this work possesses higher catalytic activity for oxygen evolution compared to commercially available lead alloy electrodes and noble metal oxide coated titanium electrodes. 

The amorphous coating is also effective to suppress anodic PbO2 deposition by the oxidation of Pb(II) ions contained as an impurity in the electrolyte. The amorphous IrO2-Ta2O5 coated Ti electrode is a smart anode which can reduce the energy consumption and work for cont

inuous and longterm electrolysis for copper foil production. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Copper foil production uses acidic aqueous solutions containing CuSO4, in which copper is deposited by reduction of Cu(II) on the cathode as a thin film and the thin film is continuously pulled out from the cathode's surface. The anodic reaction is oxygen evolution, and lead or lead alloys are usually utilized as the anode's material in the electrochemical process of copper foil production. However, lead is consumed during the electrolysis and the dissolution of lead into the electrolyte causes a contamination of copper foil, although lead or lead alloys are low cost and show an acceptable lifetime for a long-term operation. A titanium electrode coated with a mixture of IrO2 and 

1511 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Morimitsu, Oshiumi, Wada_ 



Ta2O5, which is known as DSA (dimensionally stable anode) [1], is more preferable as an oxygen evolution anode than lead alloys, because of insolubility of the anode's material, low oxygen overpotential, and high durability in acidic media [2]. IrO2-Ta2O5/Ti electrodes have been already applied for the anode in electrogalvanizing of steel [3, 4], which uses an electrolyte based on sulfuric acid solution containing ZnSO4. It has been proven that a long lifetime more than 3 years is possible even under high current density operation such as 1 A cm<sup>-2</sup> or more and a high temperature between 40<sup>o</sup> C and 60<sup>o</sup> C [4]. 

From the background mentioned above, one can presume that IrO2-Ta2O5/Ti electrodes are applied for the anode in copper foil production, and the electrodes show low oxygen potential and high stability in acidic CuSO4 solutions as similar as the situation observed in electrogalvanizing process. Unfortunately, this is not the case of practice in copper foil production. The reason is related to the anodic reaction of Pb(II) ions dissolved in CuSO4 solutions. The electrolyte of copper foil production contains Pb(II) ions as an impurity, and the oxidation of Pb(II) in the acidic solution produces solid PbO2. The PbO2 deposition proceeds on the anode surface, if IrO2-Ta2O5/Ti electrodes are used, which results in IrO2-Ta2O5 catalytic layer covered with low activity PbO2 for oxygen evolution. This causes a large increase in the anode potential and the accumulation of PbO2 on the anode surface. A more detrimental matter is that PbO2 on the anode surface is reduced to PbSO4 when the electrolysis is stopped. The reduction of PbO2 to PbSO4 is occurred by a local electrochemical cell reaction, in which PbO2 is a local cathode and IrO2-Ta2O5 catalytic layer is a local anode because oxygen evolution is less noble than Pb(IV)/Pb(II) redox couple. Once non-conductive PbSO4 is produced on the catalytic layer, the electrolysis can not be restarted and continued. 

Recently, a novel electrode concept utilizing a valve metal oxide topcoat over a standard electrocatalytic material ( _i.e._ , IrO2-Ta2O5)

has been reported, which can inhibit some unwanted side reactions; _e.g._ , the oxidation of brightener compounds used in printed wire board (PWB) plating and anodic MnO2 deposition in copper electrowinning cells [5]. We have been also developing a new class of titanium electrode using the same electrocatalyst to inhibit unwanted side reactions during oxygen evolution with a different concept from the above electrode; _i.e._ , our developed electrode can distinguish between favorable and unfavorable reactions by only IrO2-Ta2O5 catalyst coated on a titanium substrate. Our original concept is to control individually the overpotentials of oxygen evolution and the unfavorable side reaction by modulating nano- and micro-structures of IrO2 in the oxide coating. The IrO2 structure can be easily modulated with the preparation conditions of the thermal decomposition process. This "Smart Anode" having a positive electrocatalysis to the main reaction, _i.e._ , oxygen evolution, and a negative electrocatalysis to the unfavorable one is obtained by choosing the appropriate conditions of thermal decomposition temperature, the oxide composition, and both of them [6-11]. 

In this paper, the electrochemical behaviors of IrO2-Ta2O5/Ti electrodes prepared at different thermal decomposition temperatures are presented. It is shown that low thermal decomposition tem-

#### 2 Experimental 

A titanium plate (1 cm Ч 5 cm Ч  1 mm, 99.9 % purity) was degreased in acetone and etched in 10 % oxalic acid solution at 90<sup>o</sup> C for 60 min. A precursor solution was prepared by dissolving H2IrCl6･6H2O and TaCl5 into 1-butanol with 6 vol. % HCl, in which the Ir:Ta ratio was 80:20 or 50:50 mol % and the total metal concentration was 70 g dm<sup>-3</sup> . The titanium plate was dipped into the precursor solution, dried at 120<sup>o</sup> C for 10 min, and heated at a temperature between 360<sup>o</sup> C and 470<sup>o</sup> C to coat the plate with a mixture of IrO2 and Ta2O5. This process was repeated five times and the average amount of the coating was _ca._ 0.7 mg/cm<sup>2</sup> . The crystallographic structure of IrO2-Ta2O5 coatings was characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD) with Cu Kα radiation. Electrochemical measurements were conducted using a three-electrode cell equipped with a platinum counter electrode and a KCl saturated Ag/AgCl reference electrode. The working electrode was IrO2-Ta2O5/Ti mounted in a PTFE holder to limit the exposed surface area to be 1 cm<sup>2</sup> [12]. At least three electrodes prepared under the same condition were used in the experiments. Reagent grade chemicals, conc. HNO3 and Pb(NO3)2, and distilled water were used to prepare HNO

3 solutions with and without Pb(NO3)2. The experiments were conducted at 30o C or 70o C without stirring. #### 3 Results and Discussion Commercially available IrO2-Ta2O5/Ti electrodes are usually produced through thermal decomposition of a precursor solution at 450o C or more, and the coating consists of a mixture of crystalline IrO2 and amorphous Ta2O5, in which Ir ratio is 70-80 mol %. First, our experiments were conducted to compare the IrO2-Ta2O5/Ti electrode comprising 80 mol % Ir with that comprising 50 mol % Ir. For both the electrodes, thermal decomposition temperature was set to be 470o C. Figure 1 shows XRD patterns of the IrO2-Ta2O5/Ti electrodes. The electrode of 80 mol % Ir has two clear diffraction peaks corresponding to IrO2 (110) and (101), indicating that IrO2 in the coating is crystalline. The diffraction peaks of IrO2 are also seen for the electrode of 50 mol % Ir, although the peak intensity, especially of IrO2 (110), is reduced compared to that of 80 mol % Ir. The result indicates that low Ir ratio induces less crystallinity of IrO2, even when the decomposition temperature is as high as 470o C. The reduced diffraction intensity also suggests that IrO2 in the coating of 50 mol % Ir is partly amorphous. The difference in crystallographic structure of IrO2 with Ir ratio affected oxygen evolution behaviors of the electrodes. #### Abstract 

The Toyo Copper Refinery of Sumitomo Metal Mining commenced operation in 1973 with a cathode copper production capacity of 100,000 TPY, and has been continuously increasing its capacity through expanding facilities and technical improvements since then. 

Currently, the Toyo Conventional tankhouse and the Niihama Refinery have achieved cathode copper production of 135,000 TPY and 165,000 TPY respectively. In addition, a new tankhouse was constructed and it started operation using the ISA process, in May 2005. It was designed to operate with an electrode distance of 95 mm and a current density of 350 A/m<sup>2</sup> with a 2 crops operation in order to achieve a total cathode copper production of 450,000 TPY. 

This paper describes details of the recent operations of the new Toyo Tankhouse. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The Toyo Copper Refinery of Sumitomo Metal Mining has three tankhouses - the Toyo Conventional tankhouse (Tankhouse #1), the new Toyo tankhouse (Tankhouse #2) at the Toyo site, and the Niihama Refinery (Niihama Tankhouse) at the Niihama site. Tankhouse #1 started operation in 1973, following the Niihama Tankhouse, which started in 1919. The Toyo site has a smelter complex and a starting sheet manufacturing operation in addition to the commercial tankhouse, and it supplies the Niihama Tankhouse and Tankhouse #1 with anodes and starting sheets. 

The Toyo Copper Refinery has been continually increasing its cathode copper production capacity through expanding facilities and technical improvements. The cathode copper product

ion and current density over the last thirteen years are shown in Figure 1. Recently, at Toyo Tankhouse #1 and the Niihama Tankhouse it has become possible to continue the operation using a high current density of over 300 A/m<sup>2</sup> . At this level, anode passivation is avoided and high quality products can be

#### 4 Operation performance 

Tankhouse #2 has had a gradual increase in cathode copper production using a current density of over 300 A/m<sup>2</sup> since 2007. By using the high current density, anode passivation didn’t occur and a high quality of cathode copper could be maintained. In addition, we were able to confirm the production capacity of cathode copper of over 430,000 TPY in the three months from October to December 2008. 

However, there were some problems using a current density of over 330 A/m<sup>2</sup> . The current efficiency was lower than expectation. The recent operation performance of Tankhouse #2 is shown in Fig

ure 7. Because of the adjustment of production levels, the operation hasn’t been done in the planned maximum current. But we have continuously operated at a high current density of over 330 A/m<sup>2</sup> . It originally aimed at a current efficiency of over 96 % at 350 A/m<sup>2</sup> in Tankhouse #2. However, the present current efficiency using a current density of over 330 A/m<sup>2</sup> is 92 % to 95 %, and it is not stable. As a result, the target hasn’t been achieved. 

The low current efficiency at high current density is caused by a high short circuit ratio. The reason why the short circuit ratio increases is that the blank cathode plate strikes against the anode when the cathode is being inserted into the cell, and as a result cathode strain increases. 

Since 2008 August, in order to decrease short circuit ratio, we have begun to rectify the strain on the cathodes and to improve the shape of the anodes.

#### 5 Conclusion 

Tankhouse #2 has operated since 2005 and has produced high quality cathode copper. However, Tankhouse #2 still has the problem of low current efficiency. 

The lower current efficiency was caused by an increase in the short circuit ratio caused by the unstable shape of the anode and an increase in the cathode strain. Cathode strain increases when the blank cathode plate strikes against the anode. Therefore, we think that decreasing cathode strain and maintaining a lower cathode strain is important. We are aiming at a stable operation using a high current density and by lowering the cathode strain.

### Synergistic Effects of Thiourea, Polymer Additives and Chloride Ions on Copper Electrorefining 

H. Nakano, S. Oue, H. Fukushima S. Kobayashi Kyushu University Kyushu University Faculty of Engineering Department of Materials Science and Engineering Department of Materials Process Engineering 744, Motooka Nishi-ku Fukuoka, Japan 744 Motooka, Nishi-ku, Fukuoka, Japan 

K. Tomioka Mitsubishi Materials Corporation Central Research Institute 1-297, Kitabukuro-cho, Omiya-ku, Saitama, Japan 

**Keywords:** Copper, electrorefining, thiourea, polymer additive, polarization 

#### Abstract 

The synergistic effects of thiourea, polymer additives and chloride ions on copper electrodeposition have been investigated by measuring the cathodic polarization curves for aqueous H2SO4-CuSO4 solutions and observing the surface morphology of deposited Cu. The cathode potential for Cu deposition was depolarized by the addition of less than 0.1 mmol/L of thiourea, whereas it was significantly polarized by increasing the concentr

ation of thiourea greater than 0.1 mmol/L. Thus, thiourea showed effects of both depolarization and polarization on Cu deposition, depending on its concentration. The grain size of deposited Cu decreased linearly with the addition of thiourea. In the presence of both thiourea and gelatin, the polarization effect due to gelatin decreased with addition of less than 0.1 mmol/L of thiourea. The grain size of deposited Cu appeared to be smaller in the presence of both thiourea and a polymer additive such as gelatin or PEG than in that of thiourea alone. On the other hand, in a solution containing both thiourea and Cl<sup>−</sup> ions, the synergistic effect of thiourea and Cl<sup>−</sup> ions on the polarization for Cu deposition was observed when the concentration of thiourea was increased to 1 mmol/L. However, at 0.1 mmol/L of thiourea, the cathode potential was depolarized irrespective of the coexistence of Cl<sup>−</sup> ions.

#### 1 Introduction 

In electrorefining Cu, certain additives such as glue [1-3] and thiourea are generally added to conventional electrolytes to maintain a smooth surface and a high purity of the cathode metals. The solution also contains chloride ions (Cl<sup>−</sup> ) to facilitate the formation of slime at the anode. These additives shift the cathode potential to the less noble direction to reduce the grain size of the deposit. Nakano _et al._ reported the effect of polymer additives such as gelatin and polyethylene glycol (PEG) on Cu electrorefining and the synergistic effect of polymer additives and Cl<sup>−</sup> [4, 5]. Additionally, thiourea [6] has been used to increase the gloss of Ni and Cu electroplating [7, 8]. However, there are many ambiguities in the effect of thiourea on Cu electrorefining. Since, in the electrorefining of Cu, glue and Cl<sup>−</sup> coexist with thiourea, it is important for practical reasons to elucidate the synergistic effect of these additives [9]. 

In this study, the synergistic effect of thiourea, Cl<sup>−</sup> and polymer additives such as gelatin and PEG on Cu electrodeposition has been investigated by measuring the cathodic polarization curves and observing the surface morphology of the deposited Cu. 

#### 2 Experimental 

The electrolytic solution was prepared by dissolving reagent grade CuSO4 (0.708 mol/L) and H2SO4 (2.04 mol/L) in distilled and ion-exchanged water. Thiourea and Cl<sup>−</sup> ions were added in amounts of 0.001-10 mmol/L and 0.1-10 mmol/L to the electrolyte, respectively. Gelatin or PEG of mean molecular weight 2Ч10<sup>4</sup> was added in amounts of 0.01 g/L to the electrolyte as a polymer additive. Copper sheets 1Ч2 cm<sup>2</sup> in size were used as cathode and anode. Electrodeposition was conducted in 0.5 L of unagitated solutions under galvanostatic conditions of 1-2000 A/m<sup>2</sup> at 40 °C. The cathode potentials were measured at each current density for 3 mi

n by using a Ag/AgCl reference electrode (saturated KCl, 0.199 V vs. NHE, 25 °C). The potentials were plotted with reference to the NHE. The relationship between the cathode potential and the concentration of thiourea was investigated by measuring the cathode potential for Cu deposition at 200 A/m<sup>2</sup> for 5 min in solutions containing various amounts of thiourea. The morphology of Cu deposited at 200 A/m<sup>2</sup> was observed by SEM. The crystal orientation of deposited Cu was determined using Wilson and Rogers’ method [10] at an X-ray diffraction intensity of 111 to 222. The grain size of deposited Cu was calculated by Scherrer’s equation [11] using half-width of the X-ray diffraction pattern of 110.

#### 3 Results and Discussion 

###### 3.1 Effect of thiourea on the deposition potential and surface morphology of Cu 

Figure 1 shows the total polarization curves during electrolysis in the Cu electrorefining solutions containing thiurea alone as an additive. At a low concentration of thiourea (0.1 mmol/L), the polarization curve changed insignificantly, but the somewhat of depolarization was observed at 200 A/m<sup>2</sup> . At high concentrations of thiourea (1 and 10 mmol/L), the potential for Cu deposition was evidently polarized in the region above 10 A/m<sup>2</sup> . 

Since the effect of thiourea on the potential for Cu deposition was expected to depend on its concentration from Figure 1, the deposition potentials of Cu were measured at 200 A/m<sup>2</sup> in solutions containing various amounts of thiourea. The potential for Cu deposition was somewhat depolarized by the addition of thiourea at a concentration less than 0.1 mmol/L (Figure 2). However, at concentrations exceeding 0.1 mmol/L, the potential for Cu deposition was significantly polarized as the concentration of thiourea increased. Thiourea had depolarization and polarization effects on Cu deposition when the concentration of thiourea in solution was low and high, respectively. Thiourea [SC(NH2)2] is likely to be reduced to HS<sup>−</sup> on the cathode [12]. It has been reported from the potential distribution model in the inner Helmholtz layer that the potential at the inner Helmholtz plane shifted to the less noble direction due to specific adsorption of an anion on the cathode, resulting in a decrease in overpotential for the cathodic reaction [12, 13]. On the other hand, the adsorption of non-reduced thiourea molecules is reported to suppress Ni deposition. In this study, depolarization for Cu deposition at low concentrations of thiourea is attributed to the decrease in potential at the inner Helmholtz plane due to specific adsorption of HS<sup>−</sup> on the cathode. However, at high concentrations of thiourea, the potential for Cu deposition was polarized with increasing concentration of thiourea, because of the polarization eff

ect by the adsorption of non-reduced thiourea molecules.

### Copper Electrowinning with High Current Density 

Dr. Ville Nieminen, Henri Virtanen, Eero Ekman Lauri Palmu, Eero Tuuppa Outotec Research Oy Outotec Oyj Kuparitie 10 Kuparitie 10 Pori, Finland Pori, Finland 

**Keywords:** Copper, electrowinning, high current density, gas sparging, solvent extraction, space-time yield 

#### Abstract 

High current densities are desirable in copper electrowinning (Cu EW), since higher current densities lead to a better space-time yield performance, thus reducing required capital investment. However, electrowinning conditions must be modified to inc

rease the limiting current density above a certain level in order to obtain a smooth deposit.  One possibility is to decrease the Cu<sup>2+</sup> boundary layer (Nernst diffusion layer thickness δ) around the cathode by enhancing agitation e.g. using gas sparging. Another possibility is to modify the electrowinning parameters in a significant way to increase the diffusion of copper ions. In this study these two methods for achieving higher current densities are compared with each other. 

Copper electrowinning experiments were carried out at a current density of 450 Am<sup>-2</sup> . Bench–scale experiments were done with a 120 cm high cell to obtain a representative vertical profile for the deposited copper cathodes. With typical electrowinning conditions only nodular and dendritic copper cathodes were deposited. A specially designed manifold was used to provide different sizes of bubbles and by means of gas sparging good surface quality copper cathodes were obtained. Optimal EW parameters (with respect to temperature, sulphuric acid and copper concentrations) without gas sparging were tested and good surface quality copper cathodes were also obtained. Different EW parameters also affected the copper crystal growth. 

In practice, using the optimal EW parameters would require changes in the solvent extraction EW flow sheet, especially in the solvent extraction (SX) part, since solvent extraction places some limits on the electrowinning parameters. In process optimisation, both SX and EW should be considered together, not as separate units. The implementation of modified electrowinning parameters in practice is discussed.

#### 1 Introduction 

A major objective in copper electrodeposition is the improvement of the space time yield performance in order to produce the largest possible quantity of high-quality copper with the lowest space requirements, or conversely, in an existing refinery per unit of time to reduce required capital investment. Higher space-time yields can be obtained by increasing the current density (CD). However, the current density cannot be increased indefinitely, since the reduction reaction is mass transfer (diffusion) limited. At a certain current density, namely at a limiting current density, the diffusion of ions on the reactive surface, i.e. the cathode, has increased to the maximum value and cannot increase further and thus, reduction of cations cannot occur any faster. The maximum rate of transport is achieved according to Fick's first law of diffusion. In practice, much lower current densities must be applied, because at some fraction of the limiting current density the deposit starts to be dendritic, decreasing the cathode quality. This is the point at which cathodes become unacceptably rough, porous, and impure and is known as the critical current density [1]. When the current density is above this limit closer to the limiting cur

rent density, dendritic growth on the cathode changes to powder formation. 

At the limiting current the maximum rate of transport is achieved according to the Fick's first law of diffusion, which can be expressed by the current and expressing it in its limiting form as follows [2]:

It appears to follow from Equation (1) that the limiting current density can be increased by raising the temperature or bulk copper concentration or by decreasing the viscosity or Nernst diffusion layer thickness. In practice, the most suitable way to increase the limiting current density is by decreasing the Nernst diffusion layer thickness, which can be achieved by employing various means of agitation such as enhanced circulation of electrolyte, use of tapered anodes, ultrasonic agitation, air sparging, insertion of turbulence promoters, and improving cell design. However, the limiting current density is increased by high temperature, increased copper concentration, as well as by decreased sulphuric acid concentration.

The results of the copper electrowinning (Cu EW) experiments at a current density of 450 Am<sup>-2</sup> are presented here. These results are compared to those obtained with modified Cu EW conditions, namely higher temperature and increased copper concentration as well as decreased sulphuric acid concentration. The comparison is made by evaluating the quality of the deposits. Finally, some discussion is given on how to achieve these conditions in practice.

#### 4 Discussion 

The idea of using gas sparging to increase the limited current density has been known since the 1970s, see e.g. a review by W. C. Cooper [3] and the references therein. It is well known that anodically generated oxygen enhances mass transfer at the top of the cathode, but the effect is not that pronounced at the bottom. This is well demonstrated in Experiment 2 at 450 Am<sup>-2</sup> , in which the copper surface is porous and rough at the bottom, but smooth and dense at the top. The porous and nodular surface apparently increased the impurity level on the cathode; the lead level was 5.7 ppm, although the calculated copper content was at a level of 5N. No cobalt was used in the experiments as an additive that would hinder anode corrosion. It is interesting to note that in Experiment 4, with higher temperature, higher copper concentration and lower sulphuric acid concentration, the deposition is rather even at the bottom of the cathode despite minor porosity. The lower sulphuric acid concentration decreases the viscosity [4] of which the diffusion coefficient depends. The diffusion coefficient also increases as a function of copper concentration, although rather mildly from 40 to 60 g/l copper concentrations at 150 g/l of sulphuric acid [5]. The diffusion coefficient, on the other hand, affects the mass transfer coefficient, which is detrimental to the limiting current density [6], see Equation 1. When comparing Experiments 2, 3 and 4 it can be concluded that under the reference conditions a CD of 450 Am<sup>-2</sup> is too high to obtain a good qua

lity copper deposit, but increasing the temperature improves the deposit quality considerably. This is essentially because of the temperature effect on the diffusion coefficient, and the consequent increase in the limiting current density, see Equation 1. It is to be noted that temperature has also a strong effect on the viscosity in a typical Cu EW electrolyte [7]. When the conditions are further improved, (higher copper concentration and lower sulphuric acid concentration) an even better deposit can be obtained at a CD of 450 Am<sup>-2</sup> (Experiment 4) than with the reference conditions at a CD of 300 Am<sup>-2</sup> . The copper concentration affects linearly the limiting current density, see Equation 1. Thus, it is strongly advisable to optimise the electrolyte for electrowinning. 

However, air sparging seemed to be superior with respect to the cathode quality produced. The enhanced mass transfer under the reference conditions is well evidenced in the SEM images, see Figure 4. It is to be noted that similar enhancement in mass transfer cannot be obtained simply by increasing the electrolyte circulation; one cannot afford or utilise such a high increase in the circulation rate [1, 6]. These experiments indicate that gas sparging is the most significant way to improve mass transfer and thereby utilise higher current density in copper electrowinning. However, increasing the temperature has a significant effect on the cathode quality at higher current densities as well and further improvement can also be obtained by modifying the copper and sulphuric acid concentrations to resemble copper electrorefining more. Utilising these improved parameters is by no means a simple matter, since the electrolyte is typically provided to the tankhouse by the solvent extraction (SX) plant. Below it is discussed how these parameters could be obtained and what may be the limiting values.

###### 4.1 Temperature 

In principle, it is straightforward to provide a higher electrolyte temperature into the cells by utilising heat exchangers between the solvent extraction plant and the tankhouse, and in fact this is typically utilised [8]. Heat is also generated more in the cells at higher current densities due to the ohmic resistance. The lean (or spent) electrolyte must be cooled to below 40 °C before being routed back to solvent extraction to prevent the degeneration of the organic phase. Typically, the inlet temperature is 45-55 °C in Cu EW, but for instance in the electrorefining of copper it is typically over 60 °C. Here the benefit of a high temperature in the tankhouse was clearly demonstrated. However, a higher temperature also leads to some disadvantages, such as the higher degradation of guar. More guar should be used in any event to keep the guar amount with respect to the amount of copper produced. Furthermore, heating and cooling the electrolyte possibly combined with

isolation increases the operating expenses. 

###### 4.2 Copper and sulphuric acid concentrations 

One practical obstacle to using a higher copper concentration is that it may crystallise. However, solubility increases with increasing temperature, which is limited to below 40 °C in the solvent extraction plant. In practice, the temperature is typically lower. Another reason why high copper concentrations are not practical is that a higher copper concentration leaving the tankhouse (lean electrolyte) to the solvent extraction plant may lead to higher copper concentrations in the raffinate, which is not economical. Solvent extraction also sets some limits on the sulphuric acid concentration, because typically 145-185 g/l or more is needed in the stripping depending on the extractant. In practice, the copper concentration leaving solvent extraction is mostly up to around 50 g/l. Some theoretical calculations were carried out with some unconventional copper concentrations values (over 50 g/l) at two sulphuric acid concentrations using copper solvent extraction circuits with one or two strip stages. The calculations were made using MEUMTM CuSX prediction software by Cytec Inc. The copper content of the extraction system pregnant leach solution (PLS) was 6 g/l at pH 2. In the extraction an Organic to Aqueous ratio of 1 was used (A/O = 1) and the organic phase was 26 % (v/v) Acorga M5640.

Using gas sparging means that a higher current density can be applied in copper electrowinning and very good quality copper cathode can be produced at 450 Am-2 . A fairly high current density can also be achieved without air sparging by modifying the electrolyte concentrations together with temperature, but the concentrations in particular are limited by solvent extraction. Even an increase in the copper concentration and decrease in the sulphuric acid concentration would help the tankhouse to use a higher current density, but the effect of temperature is also important. In an economic optimisation the whole flowsheet should be taken into account from leaching to the SX plant and the EW tankhouse and it should be considered what the optimal solution is; with an improved electrolyte a higher current density may be used without gas sparging and corresponding capital investment on it. On the other hand, e.g. temperature and pumping control may lead to higher operating expenses, also in the SX plant. However, if a current density of 450 Am-2 can be utilised instead of 300 Am-2 , the savings in the capital costs of the EW plant are significant, since only 2/3 of the cells are needed to produce the same amount of copper. This would be reflected directly in the capital costs of the cells, electrodes, hoods, bus bars, and so on.

In fact, optimisation of the electrolyte parameters in the tankhouse has already been utilised in practice, e.g. in Cerro Verde [10]. Finally, it is worth mentioning that utilising a high current density may not be straightforward, since other limitations may exist than those discussed here, such as additive usage, increased anode corrosion just to mention few, but these topics are out of scope of this study. 

#### 5 Conclusions 

Copper electrowinning experiments were carried out at a current density of 450 Am<sup>-2</sup> . Bench-scale experiments were carried out with a 1.2 m high cell to obtain a representative vertical profile for the deposited copper cathodes. Under typical (reference) electrowinning conditions without gas sparging the bottom of the cathodes were porous, nodular and dendritic, but acceptable at the top due to the mass transfer improvement by anodic gas evolution. Increasing the temperature to 60 ºC improved the cathode quality, but some porosity remained in the bottom. The quality was further improved by using a higher copper concentration and a lower sulphuric acid concentration. A specially designed manifold was used to provide different sizes of bubbles by gas sparging and good surface quality copper cathodes were obtained throughout the cathode without the need for using optimal electrolysis conditions. The quality of the cathodes with air sparging was very good and deposits were dense and smooth with long crystals even at the bottom. 

Utilising a high current density without sparging is typically limited by the rich electrolyte provided by the solvent extraction plant. Theoretically, the rich electrolyte copper concentration from solvent extraction could be increased to some extent without serious reduction in copper recovery, but solubility of copper places some limits. Increasing temperature is somewhat easier with heat exchangers.

In process optimisation, both the solvent extraction and electrowinning should be considered together, not as separate units, when looking at the economics of the process. Utilizing a high current density, either by optimising the electrowinning conditions or using air sparging, leads to a smaller number of cells and savings in the capital expenses of the tankhouse.

### Managing the Passivation Layer on Lead Alloy Anodes in Copper Electrowinning 

Aleks Nikoloski, Michael Nicol Alan Stuart Murdoch University, Parker Centre formerly BHP Billiton Western Australia Newcastle Technology Centre, NSW 

**Keywords:** Anode, protection, passivation, electrowinning, copper 

#### Abstract 

During copper electrowinning, a layer of PbO2 forms on the surface of the lead-calcium-tin alloy anodes that are most commonly used in modern copper tankhouses. The PbO2 layer is important for many reasons such as passivating the Pb metal to attack by acid and having a reasonable exchange current density for oxygen evolution. However, the electrochemical behavior of PbO2 under upset or open-circuit conditions is one cause of anode degradation and can lead to high levels of lead contamination of the copper cathodes and to more frequent shutdowns in order to remove the accumulated anode mud from the bottom of cells. Upset conditions arise when power is lost to the cell, which occurs in electrical blackouts and when cells are taken off-line for cleaning. Some tankhouses deploy back-up rectifiers of limited capacity which are used during such periods. This paper describes a study of the mechanisms for formation and breakdown of the PbO2 layer and establishes the minimum current density required in order to maintain the integrity of the PbO2 layer on the anode surface. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Lead alloys which are typically lead-calcium-tin are used as anodes in the electrowinning of copper. However, these materials have several shortcomings that pose a series of problems for commercial tank houses. Thus, electrochemical corrosion and mechanical degradation of the anode surface increases the cell operating voltage, increases the lead contamination of the copper cathode, increases the frequency of cell cleaning, and restricts anode life under standard operating conditions to around 5 years. These problems are exacerbated by localised current density fluctuations during harvesting and loss of power during cell cleaning and unintended power outages. Some operations have back up power supplies installed to minimise anode degradation as recommended by Winand et al. [1], but commercial experience has shown these to be inadequate fo

r prevention or even minimisation of anode degradation.

_Nikoloski, Nicol, Stuart_ 



It is well known that when lead or lead based alloys are exposed to sulfuric acid solutions, a passive PbSO4 layer is established on the surface. Under electrowinning conditions this layer is oxidised to the more electrochemically active PbO2 by the reaction 



Prengaman and Siegmund [2] characterised the microstructure of the PbO2 layer on a Pb-Ca-Sn anode, and showed it to contain a dense brown α-PbO2 layer close to the surface of the anode and dark flaky porous β-PbO2 at the solution interface. Highly conductive needle-like SnO2 particles extend from the lead substrate into this combined PbO2 layer. 

Maintenance of this microstructure is crucial for the prevention of passivation and minimisation of anode degradation. The EH-pH diagram in Figure 1 shows that the minimum “safe” potential for maintenance of the PbO2 layer under copper electrowinning conditions (150-190 g/L H2SO4 or pH ~ 0) is about 1.75 V. Any interruption to the flow of electrical current exposes the PbO2 layer to rapid degradation through interaction with metallic lead (Pb) and the electrolyte to produce a PbSO4 product. 

PbO2(s) + Pb + 2HSO4− + 2H+ = 2PbSO4(s) + 2H2O

The breakdown begins within the porous β-PbO2 layer followed by reduction of the α-PbO2 layer. The resulting PbSO4 species is less dense and this results in the formation of cracks and pores in the layer and accelerates the breakdown [2]. As a consequence of this process, the anode surface is covered in flaky material that is subject to spalling. The spalling can expose areas of the lead anode substrate that rapidly convert to the passive PbSO4 species. When the current is reapplied, the relatively sparse SnO2 needles provide a surface for electron transfer, at very high current density, while the PbSO4 layer undergoes oxidation to PbO2.

The key to preservation of the PbO2 layer is to provide sufficient operating current density at the anode during interruptions to compensate for the equivalent current associated with the reduction of PbO2 by lead. This is accomplished by use of a back up power supply to maintain a “trickle current” through the electrodes. Published literature [4] suggests 1.70 V as the safe potential for anode protection, while Winand et al. [1] suggested that maintenance of the potential above 1.65 V with a current density as low as 10 A/m<sup>2</sup> is sufficient. Others however, have recommended much higher current densities. Thus, Cifuentes et al. [5] reported on relatively short term experiments which showed that a current density of about 60 A/m<sup>2</sup> was required to minimize anode mass loss due to spalling in both synthetic and industrial electrolytes. 

Rudi

mentary test work carried out at BHP Billiton’s Newcastle Technology Centre showed that a trickle current density of 30 A/m<sup>2</sup> over a short period (<1 day) prevents spalling of the anode. Unfortunately, back up power supplies at commercial operations supply a trickle current to the whole tankhouse of as low as 1 A/m<sup>2</sup> , and upgrading of a system to provide even 30 A/m<sup>2</sup> cannot be justified economically. 

A more systematic examination was required in order to establish 

1. The minimum current density required to protect the PbO2 layer on the anode 

2. The effects of trickle current density on the extent of degradation of the oxide layer with time 

3. The maximum delay before application of a trickle current 

#### 2 Experimental 

In initial tests, the potential at which reduction of PbO2 occurs under typical copper electrowinning conditions was investigated. A portion of a commercial rolled Pb-Ca-Sn anode was fabricated into small disk electrodes which were polarised at a potential of 2.2 V for 100 seconds in a stirred solution of 180 g/L H2SO4 maintained at 40 °C using a EG&G 273 Potentiostat/Galvanostat. The potential of the electrode was then scanned in the cathodic direction at different scan rates. The scan rate was progressively reduced in order to confirm the potential for reduction of the oxide layer under pseudo- steady state conditions. 

In subsequent experiments, the electrodes were oxidised in a synthetic electrolyte containing 38 g/L copper, 175 g/L H2SO4, 1.2 g/L iron, 80 mg/L cobalt and 20 mg/L manganese which is similar to the composition of a typical copper electrowinning electrolyte. The temperature was controlled at 50 °C and all potentials were measured against a mercury/mercurous sulfate reference electrode but are quoted against the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE). Unless stated otherwise, a current density of 400 A/m<sup>2</sup> was used.

#### 4 Conclusions 

The results of this testwork have shown that the PbO2 protective layer on anodes used for copper electrowinning begins to breakdown almost immediately after the current is interrupted to the cells. The length of time before complete reduction of the oxide layer takes place depends on the thickness of the oxide layer and therefore on the period of oxidation prior to the open circuit event.

Anodic protection with a trickle current density of 4 A/m<sup>2</sup> is not sufficient to preserve the PbO2 layer and will not adequately protect a commercial anode from self-corrosion. The oxide layer is temporarily protected when the trickle current density is increased to between 20 and 40 A/m<sup>2</sup> but loss of anodic protection takes place gradually over a period of days. More permanent protection of the anode oxide layer was observed at a trickle current density of 50 A/m<sup>2</sup> . These current densities are probably beyond what is economically possible in commercial tankhouses and the basis for the use of very small trickle currents which are applied in some cases must be questioned.
