### Optimization of a Tankhouse Harvesting Plan 

Mats Nikus, Mikko Korpi Jukka Rantala Outotec Research Oy Boliden Harjavalta Oy Kuparitie 10, PO Box 69, FI-28101 FI-28330 Pori, Finland Pori, Finland 

**Keywords:** Tankhouse, copper, optmization, crane operation, harvesting plan 

#### Abstract 

In the present work the harvesting plan of the Boliden Harjavalta Pori tankhouse was optimized in order to be able to perform the daily cathode stripping and anode change in two shifts. After the raise in production capacity in 2007, the plant had been exceptionally run in three shifts. 

Based on the knowledge of the plant layout, the constraints such as crane and stripping machine speeds, as well as the operating times of the different cell sections, it is possible to optimize the harvesting plan with respect to operation time and/or production rate. A measurement campaign was performed in order to obtain the necessary information of the operating times for the different sections. A major decrease in operation time can be achieved by noting that the operations at the sections in the tankhouse can be performed not only in sequence, but also partly in parallel by combining the strip and scrap and strip only operations. The optimization gives as a result the harvesting schedule for the tankhouse sections and also which sections should be combined. It was shown in an example case that it is indeed possible to go from the three-shift operation to two shifts. The optimization method used was based on a genetic algorithm. 

Besides the optimization also a bottleneck analysis of the plant was performed. The bottleneck analysis showed that the stripping machine speed is well optimized for the plant, but that even a small reduction of the time taken for the crane to tune its position on the cells will result in a significant improvement in the total operating time. 

#### 1 Introduction 

As the last step in the production of cathode copper, copper anodes from the copper smelter undergoes an electrorefining phase. In electrorefining Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions migrate from the anode of 99 % purity and deposit on the cathode forming a >99.995 % pure copper layer. The electrolytic process takes place in cells containing a solution of sulfuric acid and copper sulfate. The anodes and cathodes form an alternating set in the cell where they are immersed. Several tanks are serially connected

together in sections. The electrorefining process is driven by an electric current to the sections. A fairly detailed, albeit c

oncise description of the electrorefining process, can be found in chapter 16 of the book “Extractive Metallurgy of Copper” by Davenport et al. [1]. 

In Boliden Harjavalta’s Pori tankhouse the permanent cathode technology of Outotec is employed. The raw copper anodes are transported from the Harjavalta Smelter to the Pori tankhouse by train. Each cell holds 35 anodes and 34 cathodes. The tankhouse comprises 28 sections with varying number of cells (Table 1).

The tankhouse is over 300 m long and the numbering of the sections and layout of the tankhouse is illustrated in Figure 1. The stripping machine is located approximately in the middle of the tankhouse whereas the anode handling machines are located at the northern end (left side in the figure). 



Figure 1: Section numbering of the tankhouse layout The tankhouse is run in a three-week anode cycle meaning that each cathode is stripped three times and each anode is changed once during the cycle. 

In conjunction with the stripping, the cathodes to be stripped are replaced with clean permanent cathodes. During anode change the scrap anodes (three-week-old very thin anodes) are removed, the cells are emptied and cleaned and new anodes are placed into the cells. As cathodes are always stripped at the same time as anodes are changed, this operation is called strip and scrap operation. During a typical working day strip and scrap will be performed in two sections and strip only operation in four sections. 

The stripping is performed in the stripping machine, where the copper layer deposited on the permanent cathode is mechanically removed. The stripped copper cathodes are subsequently bundled together. The incoming anodes are heated in a heating tank by hot water, if necessary, and handled in the anode preparation machine to improve the physical quality of cast anodes. The scrap anodes 

1570 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Optimization of a Tankhouse Harvesting Plan_ 



are washed and bundled in the anode scrap washing machine and then transported back to the smelter to be recycled. 

Three main overhead cranes are used in the process. The first crane takes care of the transfer of anodes from the train to the heating tank and further to the anode preparation machine. The second crane transports raw copper anodes from the preparation machine to the cells and scrap anodes to the anode scrap washing machine. The cathodes are moved between the stripping machine and the cells with the third crane. When a section is being stripped the third crane is used. During strip and scrap operation crane No. 2 is used in addition to crane No. 3. Because

the cranes travel on the same rails they cannot pass each other. An additional challenge is a consequence of the layout: the anode handling machines are located at the end of the tankhouse and not in the middle like the stripping machine, crane No. 2 has, on an average, to make much longer trips than crane No. 3. 

The goal is that the first crop should last for 6 days, the second for 8 days and the last for 7 days (a so-called 6-8-7 sequence). The constraint of the duration for the first crop is quite strict. On the one hand the duration of the first crop is preferably short because of a low current efficiency, but on the other hand there has to be enough time to form a thick enough copper deposit on the permanent cathode for a successful stripping. The durations of the second and third crops can deviate from their target values. 

At the start of this project the pulling work at the tankhouse was performed in three shifts. The aim of this work is to optimize the tankhouse harvesting plan and crane traffic in order to reduce the total cathode stripping and anode change times so that the daily operations can be carried out in two shifts. An important remedy is the combination of strip and scrap operation with strip only operation so that they are carried out simultaneously, in which case the capacity of the stripping machine is better exploited during the strip and scrap operation. 

#### 2 Measurement Campaign 

To find out the durations of the cathode stripping and anode change operations for different cell sections, a measurement campaign was performed, where the cycle lengths for cranes No. 2 and No. 3 were recorded. The cycle includes the operations performed at the cell section, the movement from the cell section to the stripping machine/scrap washing machine as well as the operations at the stripper (crane 3) or the preparation machine/scrap-washing machine (crane 2). The cycle lengths for the studied sections were measured repeatedly in order to obtain a representative average. The results were compared to computational durations and the comparison indicated a good fit.

Finding a good plan is a challenging integer-based combinatorial optimization task. In fact, there exists no unequivocal optimum, but different alternative solutions can be sought under different conditions. The final choice between different these options has to be made based on sound engineering judgment. At first there was an attempt to solve the problem using a purely stochastic approach, but this was abandoned in favor of a genetic algorithm (GA) due to the formers long computation times. 

GA is classified as a heuristic global optimization method and is a subclass of evolutionary computation. GA exploits the methods of inheritance, mutation, selection and recombination. An introduction to the field of evolutionary algorithms in general and generic algorithms in particular can be found in chapter 8 of a fairly recent book by Karray and De Silva [2]. In the beginning of the optimization the population is typically initialized randomly. The optimization proceeds in generations. Each individual’s fitness is evaluated and from the best individuals a new generation is formed through recombination and mutation. 

When attempting to minimize the time, also other means are possible. As examples the following can be mentioned 

1. The crane leaves as soon as the load is lifted high enough and without the drip protection tray yet being closed (measured time save 16 s). 

2. Lower the load as much as possible in advance before the crane arrives at the cell. 

3. Faster tuning of the crane’s position at the cells.

In this way the bottlenecks of the process can be quantitatively studied. The analysis was performed on a previously optimized harvesting schedule so that one bottle-neck at a time was studied by calculating the total operational time for a set of times associated with the bottleneck. The following bottlenecks were studied: stripping machine, scrap washing machine, crane tuning and crane speed. The results are illustrated in Figure 7. The stripping machine, which has a design speed of 270 s/cell is quite well designed for the tankhouse since smaller times hardly improve the total time at all. Note however that slowing down the stripping machine would have quite catastrophic effects. A speedup of the scrap washing machine (present value 400 s/cell) would influence the total time somewhat. The main bottleneck of the tank house is the crane tuning time. A moderate improvement of a few seconds has dramatic effects on the total operation time. Also the crane speed has a large effect, but due to safety reasons it is not desirable to raise the speed of the cranes. Furthermore regarding the process’ bottlenecks it can be noticed tha

t the plant is rather well balanced, meaning that there is not one sole bottleneck that limits the capacity, but rather the active bottleneck is determined based on the section being processed. During cathode stripping the bottleneck is the stripping machine, when stripping sections 7-20. For the remaining sections the speed of crane three is the limiting factor. During strip and scrap sections 1-10 the scrap washing machine is the bottleneck and for the other sections it is the speed of crane two. The situation gets more complicated when combining cathode stripping with strip and scrap. If both of the combined sections are relatively close to the stripper and the section to be stripped is farther away from the scrap washing machine, the stripping machine acts as the bottleneck. Otherwise in the combination case the crane three determines the processing time. Both the physical speed of the crane and the tuning time directly affect to results. 

It was concluded that it is not useful to combine sections 1-14 during strip and scrap operation, because they can be handled quite fast in the normal fashion without combination. During strip and scrap operation of sections 15-28 the benefits of combination outweigh the downsides.

The research showed that by optimizing the harvesting schedule and combining strip and scrap operation with cathode stripping it is possible to do the work in two shifts during workdays plus an additional shift during the weekend. ### Incorporation of Copper Solvent Extraction into a Copperbelt Cobalt Refinery 

Andrew Nisbett, Nathan Emmerich, Angus Feather, Gift Chisakuta 

Cognis Corporation 2430 N Huachuca Drive Tucson, Arizona, USA 

**Keywords:** Copper electrowinning, solvent extraction, cobalt refinery, copper cathode, cost saving, leaching 

#### Abstract 

Older generation cobalt refineries in the Copperbelt region of Zambia and the Democratic Republic of

Congo utilise electrowinning/electrostripping to remove copper impurity from the leach liquor. When the original flowsheets of these plants were designed, the available copper extractants were not able to readily extract copper down to acceptable levels from the relatively high acid environment. With the advent of the stronger oxime based extractants, the inclusion of copper solvent extraction into these flowsheets became a viable alternative. 

The electrostripping process produces a combination of low quality cathode plus sludge/powder and represents a poor revenue source for the operator. Copper solvent extraction offers the opportunity to produce saleable grade copper cathode, often at a reduced operating cost which is of significant economic benefit. This technology has already been successfully implemented at one of the Copperbelt operations. 

This paper describes the older generation flowsheets together with details and strategies of incorporating copper solvent extraction into an existing somewhat complex older generation process. Results of laboratory scale testwork and computer simulations are also presented. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Several cobalt refineries were constructed in the Copperbelt region of Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in the 1970’s and early 1980’s. Some of these are still operational today, either with the original flowsheet in place or with slight modifications to accommodate changes in feedstock or to incorporate newer technologies. 

1585 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Nisbett, Emmerich, Feather, Chisakuta_ 



The feedstock for the majority of these refineries is a cobalt sulphide flotation concentrate with the cobalt associated with copper as a carrollite [1]. This mineral type contains appreciable amounts of copper which must be removed during the cobalt refining process. When the original flowsheets of these plants were designed, the commercially available copper solvent extraction (SX) molecules were not able to readily extract copper down to acceptable levels in a reasonably high acid environment. Therefore, most of these older refining facilities utilised a combination of direct electrowinning and electrostripping to remove copper impurity from the leach liquor. The advent of stronger oxime based extractants has allowed copper solvent extraction technology to become an economically viable alternative in these cobalt refineries. 

The electrostripping process produces a combination of low quality copper cathode and sludge/powder and results in higher costs and lower revenue for the operator. Copper SX offers the opportunity to produce a saleable grade copper cathode, often at a reduced operating cost, which can be of significant economic benefit. This technology has already been successfully implemented at one of the Copperbelt operations [2]. 

Cognis conducted a series of laboratory tests and computer modelling studies to evaluate the inclusion of copper SX into the flowsheet of a compl

ex cobalt refinery as an alternative to the traditional electrostripping process. #### 2 Existing Process Description The general flowsheet of the roast-leach-electrowinning plant is shown in Figure 1. The sulphide concentrate is roasted under sulphating conditions at around 700 °C in a fluid bed roaster. The copper and cobalt are converted to soluble sulphates and the calcine is quenched and leached in spent electrolyte. The resultant pregnant leach liquor (PLS) contains both copper and cobalt together with other impurities such as iron, nickel and zinc. Copper is first removed by electrostripping and a bleed of the spent electrolyte reports to the cobalt circuit for further impurity removal ahead of final metal production. A secondary source of high grade cobalt material, also containing significant amounts of acid soluble copper, is treated in a pressure leach process and the resultant PLS is added to the calcine leach product prior to copper electrostripping. 1586 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Incorporation of Copper Solvent Extraction into a Cobalt Refinery_ Cu/Co Concentrates

Figure 1: Existing Refinery Flowsheet As mentioned earlier, the copper electrostripping process produces a low quality cathode which is usually sold as scrap and is used for doping in converters at a smelting operation. The realised price obtained by the operator is usually well below the prevailing copper price. In addition, the current efficiency obtained during electrostripping can be as low as 50 % in comparison with efficiencies of 90 % that can be obtained in a SX electrowinning tankhouse. If the amount of copper impurity entering the process increases, the existing rectifier capacity in the tankhouse becomes the limiting factor and this in turn may impose a ceiling on final cobalt production. #### 3 Proposed Copper SX Circuit During the electrostripping process the net reaction is as follows: Cu2+ + H2O → Cu0 + ½ O2 + 2H+ (1) By calculation, 1.5 grams of acid are generated for every 1 gram of copper removed from solution either as metal or in sludge. In the process flowsheet of the cobalt refinery, the copper tenors of the leach solutions are typically in the 30-40 g/L range and copper is electrostripped down to a targeted value of about 0.5 g/L. In the subsequent downstream purification steps, this generated acid has to be neutralised prior to the pH based precipitation stages to remove impurity species like iron. These purification steps typically operate in a pH range of 2.5-4.0. 1587 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Nisbett, Emmerich, Feather, Chisakuta_ The overall chemical reaction during the copper solvent extraction process is as follows: 2RH + Cu2+</

sup> ↔ R2Cu + 2H+ (2) From the two chemical reactions above it can be seen that the same amount of acid is stoichiometrically generated in the electrostripping process as in the copper extraction process. This means that the total amount of acid to be neutralised in the subsequent downstream purification stages would be similar if either copper removal process was employed. However, the copper extraction reaction is a reversible equilibrium reaction and it is not practically possible to extract the copper from 30 g/L down to 0.5 g/L in one “step” without an intermediate acid neutralisation stage. The conceptual flowsheet design of the proposed copper SX plant to be included in the refinery involves a primary copper SX stage to recover around 80 % of the copper. The raffinate, or a portion thereof, is then subject to an acid neutralisation step where the pH is raised to a targeted value of 2.0-2.3. This neutralised stream is then processed in a secondary copper SX circuit where a very low tenor copper raffinate is produced. This raffinate then reports to the existing cobalt purification plant where the remainder of the acid is neutralised. A schematic of the conceptual process is illustrated in Figure 2. #### 6 Discussion 

The isotherm results and Isocalc simulations predict copper raffinate tenors that exceed the expectations of the initial theoretical modelling. The primary copper SX circuits are able to attain recoveries in excess of 85 % with an acceptable net transfer on the organic phase. The neutralised composite primary copper SX raffinates that constitute the PLS to secondary copper SX are predicted to be around 4.5 g/L compared to the initial estimate of 6.3 g/L. The copper tenor in the raffinate produced by the secondary copper SX circuit is around 50 ppm which is quite acceptable ahead of subsequent downstream purification stages. 

The two reagents tested provided similar results. There had been some debate prior to the testwork that the stronger modified aldoxime based reagent may be better suited to the higher copper tenor

PLS streams. However, the lower strip point achieved with the non-modified aldoxime/blend compensated for its marginally lower extractive strength. At extractant concentrations of above 25 volume %, the low density and viscosity of a non-modified reagent will result in better phase separation, lower entrainment losses and less crud generation than when using a modified reagent. This reagent has also met the design criteria at a neighbouring cobalt refinery that has already successfully incorporated copper SX into their refinery flowsheet [2]. ve been used for copper electrowinning for many years. Prengaman developed the first rolled lead calcium tin alloy anode in the early 1980’s. The addition of cobalt to the electrolyte in the amount of about 50200 ppm has also increased life. #### 1 Background 

In the use of lead alloys for electrowinning of metals from sulphuric acid solution is attributed to the lead becomes an insoluble, oxide producing stable on anode surface. The property of lead which accounts for this use is the ability of lead to form an insoluble PbO2 corrosion film which can repair itself if damaged and prevent further corrosion of the lead anode. 

In metal electrowinning oxygen is produced at the anode. Oxygen is either evolved as oxygen gas, oxidizing materials in the electrolyte, or corrodes the lead anode. The main goal of anode lead alloy research is to develop anode materials which resist corrosion by the evolved oxygen.

When a new anode is placed into a copper EW cell a layer of PbSO4 is formed on the surface. This layer is converted via the applied potential in the cell to PbO2. The oxygen generated at the anode surface reacts with the lead alloy to form PbO and converts both the PbO and the PbSO4 to PbO2. 

For optimum performance of the anode, the alloy should form a thin, hard, dense, compact, adherent layer of PbO2 on the surface. Such PbO2 layer will not spall off, deteriorate or contaminate the cathode product. 

#### 2 Rolled Lead Calcium Tin Alloys 

Prengaman [1] developed a rolled lead calcium tin alloy for copper electrowinning. The anodes produced from this alloy resist oxidation and enhance oxygen evolution by the unique grain structure which is imparted to the corrosion films. These anodes have been used in copper electrowinning service since the early 1980’s. The combination

of calcium and tin along with the mechanical working produced by rolling creates a material with high mechanical properties. The high mechanical properties and the stability of the microstructure produced by precipitation of strengthening calcium tin intermetallic particles prevent distortion of the anodes in service. 

The combination of calcium and tin as well as the anode grain structure reduces the rate of corrosion and promotes the formation of a thin, stable, conductive PbO2 corrosion layer on the anode surface leading to improved anode life. Prengaman [2, 3] developed methods to attach the rolled alloy sheets to copper bus bars to produce an anode and protect the copper bar from corrosion by coating the bus bar with a layer of electroplated lead to improve the resistance to acid attack. 

Anodes must have high corrosion resistance, structural integrity, and mechanical properties a service life time is greater than 5 years. Tin additions to the lead-calcium alloys is instrumental in developing the unique rolled microstructure of the anode which leads to corrosion resistance, long life, high conductivity through the corrosion layer and improved oxygen evolution. The rolled lead calcium-tin alloy anodes have remained virtually uncharged since their development in the early 1980’s. 

#### 3 Anode Corrosion 

Understanding the relationship between anode chemistry, structure, and mechanical properties has lead to gradual improvements of the anodes. Despite the improvements and understanding of the corrosion mechanisms the anodes are still corroded by the oxygen evolved in the electrowinning process. Prengaman et al. [5] described the anode corrosion process and methods to reduce it. 

The anodes are corroded by oxygen evolved at the PbO2 surface which diffuses through this corrosion layer to the lead surface where it reacts with the lead anode alloy to produce the PbO2 corrosion

layer. It is important to produce a complete PbO2 corrosion layer on the anode surface so that oxygen can be evolved efficiently. 

As the corrosion product becomes thicker it begins to develop small cracks parallel to the anode surface. These cracks eventually expand and result in the development of non-adherent flakes on the surface of the anode. These flakes can then be dislodged from the surface of the anode by oxygen generated at the anode surface beneath the flake. The rate of corrosion is related to the electrolyte temperature and the current density of the electrowinning cell. The higher the current density and the higher the electrolyte temperature the more rapid is the corrosion. 

#### 4 Manganese Effect 

In addition to the electrowinning cell conditions the electrolyte often contains manganese. Manganese can react with the PbO2 surface corrosion product by reacting with the corrosion layer surface forming MnO2 and reducing the PbO2 to PbSO4. 

The reconverting of the PbSO

4 to PbO2 causes structural changes in the stable corrosion layer making it thicker, softer, less stable, less adherent and more susceptible to shedding. This trend was described by Prengaman [6]. 

#### 5 Cobalt Additions to the Electrolyte 

To reduce the deterioration of the PbO2 on the anode surface caused by the deposition of MnO2 and the improve oxygen evolution, cobalt has been added to copper electrowinning electrolytes. Cobalt additions were first described by Hyvarinen [7] and more recently by Yu and O’Keefe [8]. The beneficial mechanism of cobalt on the anodes is due to a reduction in the oxygen evolution potential of the anode leading to easier oxygen evolution. Cobalt ions are adsorbed onto the PbO2 lead corrosion product. This results in reduced anode corrosion, reduced or elimination of MnO2 deposition on the anodes, longer anode life and improved copper cathode quality. Analysis of the cobalt content of the PbO2 corrosion product varies between 50 and 2500 ppm depending on the concentration of cobalt in the electrolyte. 

Cobalt is added to the electrolyte in most copper EW tankhouses. Jenkins et al. [9] surveyed the operating conditions of 34 copper EW tankhouses. In the survey the cobalt added to the electrolyte varied between 50 and 300 ppm. To maintain the cobalt content of the electrolyte, cobalt must be continuously added to the electrolyte to make up for the bleed of electrolyte from the system to control impurities in the electrolyte. Cobalt additions vary between 100 and 800 g/l ton of copper cathode in the plants. Loss of cobalt to the bleed is a major cost in operating copper tankhouse. During the high cobalt price spike in 2008, some tankhouses reduced bleed and allowed the iron content to

**Keywords:** Copper, electrolytic refining, arsen, antimony, bismuth, nodulation, bleed treatment, solubility, precipitation 

#### Abstract 

The Atlantic Copper Refinery (Huelva, Spain) has operated the ISA permanent cathode technology since 1995, with a capacity of 260,000 t/y. Throughout this period, the control of the concentration of minor impurities (As, Sb, Bi) in the electrolyte has been a major challenge. It was found that concentrations of these impurities have to be kept within an optimum operating region in order to prevent the occurrence of different cathode nodulation phenomena. This paper describes recent developments to increase the removal capacity of the electrolyte treatment plant, aimed at maintaining these impurities within this region. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The Atlantic Copp

er Metallurgical Complex in Huelva (Spain) was commissioned in 1970 with a capacity of 40,000 t/y of copper from concentrate. In 1975, the old blast furnaces were replaced by the Outokumpu FSF technology and the copper refinery capacity was increased to 108,000 t/y. Between 1994 and 1996 an expansion project was carried out to increase the copper from concentrate and cathodes to 250,000 t/y and 215,000 t/y respectively. This expansion basically consisted of a new sulphuric acid plant, replacement of the anode furnaces by two 400 t units, an increase of the electrolytic cells up to 1,120 and implementation of the ISA permanent cathode technology. 

Furthermore, a debottlenecking project has led to a concentrate capacity of 1,000,000 t/y of fresh concentrate since 1997. Meanwhile between 1995 and 1998, a cathode production rate of 260,000 t/y was reached as a result of a progressive increase in the current density in the refinery.

In 2001, with the closure of Atlantic Copper’s mining operations, to deal with the weak acid from the smelter and the daily electrolyte bleed from the refinery that had been used as reagents in its mines for leaching certain ores, the following measures were undertaken: 

- Reduction of the amount of spent electrolyte bleeds by redesigning the decopperisation unit into an electrolyte treatment unit. 

- Commissioning of a Gypsum Plant in which the aforementioned streams are treated so that no acid streams are sent outside the Huelva Metallurgical Complex. 

As a result of these changes in the refining process, and a progressive increase in the As content of the concentrates fed to the smelter since 2004, it was found that the control of As, Sb and Bi concentrations was critical in order to prevent the occurrence of cathode nodulation phenomena. This paper describes the developments of the control of impurities that have been made to fit this new situation, such as the increase in the removal capacity of the electrolyte treatment plant. 

#### 2 Management of Electrolyte Impurities at Atlantic Copper 

###### 2.1  Behaviour of Impurities during the Copper Electrorefining Process 

During the copper refining process, impurities in the anode either dissolve in the electrolyte or form an anode slime which settles at the bottom of the cells. Gold, silver, selenium and tellurium, being more noble than copper, remain undissolved and report to the anode slimes. Nevertheless, it should be noted that the presence of dissolved selenium and tellurium in the electrolyte has a deleterious effect as they cement onto the copper cathode, so, care is taken to avoid electrolyte contamination by sources such as anode slimes leach liquors [1]. 

Those elements less noble than copper, such as iron and nickel dissolve almost entirely in the electrolyte. Iron decreases the current efficiency since reoxidation of the cathode copper by Fe(III) and O2 takes place [2], so its concen

tration in the electrolyte should be kept as low as possible. Nickel, on the other hand, does not have a detrimental effect and its presence in the cathode is only due to electrolyte entrapment; nevertheless, very high concentrations of this element (25 g/l) in the electrolyte can depress the solubility of copper sulphate resulting in anode passivation. 

Calcium is an element which may enter the electrolyte from different sources such as leaching from concrete to which the electrolyte is occasionally exposed [3] or the animal glue used as additive to control copper cathode growth. Calcium has to be removed from the electrolyte because when present it precipitates from solution as gypsum at the electrolyte cathode interface. 

Arsenic, antimony and bismuth are often considered as a group when their influence on the copper electrorefining process is studied because, depending on operating parameters such as anode and electrolyte compositions, they can report either electrolyte or anode slimes. 

1600 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Management of Electrolyte Impurities at the Atlantic Copper Refinery_ 



When arsenic, antimony and bismuth enter the electrolyte, they can undergo a number of different reactions depending on their respective concentrations, as well as on the presence and concentrations of other elements. Arsenic enters the electrolyte as As(III), and is gradually oxidized to As(V) [4]. In this instance, because of solubility product considerations, at a sufficiently high arsenate ion concentration insoluble antimony and bismuth arsenates are formed [3]. When they precipitate from the bulk of the electrolyte, they have a detrimental effect on cathode quality. But when As (V) is above 15-20 g/l, the Bi and Sb are depressed to less than 0.1 g/l in the electrolyte so that this risk is minimized. 

Furthermore, the presence of As(V) prevents the oxidation of Sb (III) into Sb (V) [5]. The presence of Sb(V) is commonly linked to the occurrence of floating slimes [6] that consist of amorphous antimonious and antimonic acids [7]. Additionally, Bi forms oxysulphates and slightly soluble sulphates, and have similar behavior to Sb [3]. Bi is also reported as a constituent of the floating slimes [1]. These slimes give rise to a severe top nodulation of the cathodic copper, negatively affecting current efficiency and cathode quality. 

It is necessary to keep the concentration of these elements in the electrolyte below certain levels, as well as at a proper ratio, such as As/(Sb+Bi) among others. This is achieved through electrolyte treatment and through controlling these impurities in anodes. 

Finally it should be considered that the anodes contain up to 0.1-0.3 % oxygen, mostly as Cu2O which dissolves chemically during the electrorefining process as contacts the sulphuric acid in the electrolyte. As a result of this dissolution, copper tends to built up in the electrolyte and should be removed in order to maintain a constant copper concentrat

ion to avoid undesirable phenomena such as anode passivation. 

###### 2.2  Electrolyte Treatment at Atlantic Copper 

The Atlantic Copper tankhouse consists of 7 circulation systems. Each one has a collecting tank of 60 m<sup>3</sup> . The number of cells of each circuit is different and hence effective cell volume is as depicted in Figure 1. The total volume of electrolyte in the plant is 4790 m<sup>3</sup> .

### Demonstration of the Ferrous/Ferric Anode Reaction for Copper Electrowinning 

S. Sandoval, P. Cook, C. Morales, T. Robinson 

Freeport-McMoRan Mining Company 4521 U.S. Highway 191 Morenci, USA 

**Keywords:** Electrowinning, energy, acid mist, anode 

#### Abstract 

In 2003 the Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc. Technology Center converted its SX-EW Test Facility to be able to continuously electrowin copper using the ferrous/ferric anode reaction. Conversion of the pilot-scale tankhouse was accomplished by adding up to 30 g/L Fe<sup>2+</sup> (as ferrous sulfate) into the copper electrolyte, incorporating an electrolyte distribution manifold into the electrowinning cells, installing additional unit operations, and replacing the conventional Pb-Ca-Sn anodes with stainless steel anodes. A solvent extractant that co-extracted copper and iron from PLS solution was utilized in the SX plant in order to maintain copper and iron make-up in the electrolyte circuit. 

Three separate unit operations were added external to the tankhouse. An

absorption tower was built for continuous introduction and absorption of sulfur dioxide into the lean copper electrolyte. From the absorption tower the lean electrolyte passed through an activated carbon bed where the reduction of Fe<sup>3+</sup> to Fe<sup>2+</sup> was catalyzed and the sulfur dioxide was converted to sulfuric acid. An acid recovery unit was utilized to remove sulfuric acid from the electrolyte circuit for use in copper leaching. This paper describes the results of the continuous demonstration as well as the economics for application of this process. A 46 % reduction in electrowinning voltage was achieved and acid mist was completely removed from the tankhouse. 

#### 1 Introduction 

In the early 1990’s the U.S. Bureau of Mines (USBM) Reno Research Center undertook research to evaluate options for electrowinning copper without acid mist generation. This would require that the conventional anode reaction in copper electrowinning, the decomposition of water to form oxygen gas, be replaced with an alternative anode reaction that was free from gas evolution. In 1995, USBM published a pilot plant study where-in copper electrowinning was carried out using the 

1617 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Sandoval, Cook, Morales, Robinson_ 



ferrous/ferric anode reaction in conjunction with reduction of ferric iron external to the cell using sulfur dioxide and an activated carbon catalyst [1]. The sulfuric acid generated by this reaction was extracted from the circuit using solvent extraction. This pilot plant work showed several benefits for copper electrowinning: 

- Cell voltage was decreased from 2 to 1 volt by virtue of the ferrous/ferric anode reaction and utilization of a metal oxide-coated titanium anode. 

- Acid mist generation in the electrowinning cell was eliminated. 

- Lead contamination of the circuit from lead anodes was eliminated as well as cobalt additions to copper electrolyte for stabilizing lead anodes. 

- Sulfuric acid was generated, although at a relatively low concentration. 

The alternative anode reaction technology (AART) also added cost to copper electrowinning in several areas: 

- Because copper electrolyte became stagnant in the cell in the absence of oxygen evolution, additional electrolyte pumping was required for mixing the electrolyte and to minimize build-up of ferric iron in the cell in order to maximize current efficiency. 

- The presence of larger quantities of iron in the electrowinning cell lowered current efficiency to about 85 %. 

- The metal oxide-coated titanium anode required to reap the full voltage reduction benefit was more expensive than a conventional Pb-Ca-Sn anode. 

- Additional capital cost would be required to support sulfur dioxide absorption and production of sulfuric acid, although the sulfuric acid produced would be a credit to the project. 

The Freeport-McMoRan Technology Center became interested in AART in 2002 because of the potential for decreasing energy consumption in

copper electrowinning (due to voltage reduction in the tankhouse and the potential to generate electricity from burning sulfur to provide sulfur dioxide for the process). Co-generation of sulfuric acid was also of interest for use in copper leaching. In 2003, the Technology Center’s SX-EW Test Facility, a pilot-scale demonstration plant, was converted for continuous demonstration of AART. #### 2 Methods and Procedures The SX-EW Test Facility is an integrated SX-EW pilot plant with four electrowinning cells, four solvent extraction stages, and a tank farm that receives pregnant leach solution (PLS) feed from Morenci’s Modoc PLS pond. A photo of the Test Facility is shown in Figure 1. The tankhouse, tank farm, and solvent extraction plant were pre-existing to the AART project. In order to operate the Test Facility in AART mode, several unit operations were added: 1618 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Demonstration of the Ferrous/Ferric Anode Reaction for Copper Electrowinning_ - A sulfur dioxide absorption tower was installed. The tower contained two absorption columns, one 12 inches internal diameter and one 16 inches internal diameter. Packed height of each was 31 feet. The tower was equipped with a sulfur dioxide vaporizer for converting liquid sulfur dioxide to vapor and also gas mixing equipment to add nitrogen, oxygen, and NOx to the vapor in order to simulate a typical sulfur burner gas. - Fixed-bed activated carbon modules were installed. The modules were polyethylene lined steel vessels. The activated carbon utilized was 20 Ч 50 bituminous coal activated carbon. - An acid recovery unit was installed. - A metal building was erected to store liquid sulfur dioxide to feed the plant. The economics of AART are dependent on power cost (AART decreases cell voltage and generates power through sulfur burning), acid credit to the project (AART produces sulfuric acid), sulfur cost (from which sulfur dioxide is generated to feed the process) and capital costs of incremental AART equipment. Active surface area of each cathode was 3.5 by 3.1 feet. Current was 3570 amps

, which corresponded to a copper production rate of just over 31 lbs/hr at 84 % current efficiency. Current density was 27 amps/ft<sup>2</sup> of plating surface. Electrolyte flow was 19 gpm per cell, which corresponded to a specific flow rate of 0.14 gpm/ft<sup>2</sup> of plating surface. An electrolyte distribution manifold was utilized in the bottom of each cell. Lean electrolyte (i.e. electrowinning cell discharge) chemistry parameters maintained during operation were 38 g/L Cu, 27 g/L Fe, 3.5 g/L Fe<sup>3+</sup> , 180 g/L sulfuric acid, and approx. 52 °C electrolyte temperature. 

Demonstration of voltage savings through continuous operation of AART using projected operating conditions was one of the goals of this study. Table 1 displays the average cell voltage measured during continuous operation with the anode types shown. Each anode design in Table 1 was a flow-though anode that allowed electrolyte to move through the screens. This was shown to be beneficial for AART voltage reduction [2]. The stainless steel anodes were not superior in voltage performance to the titanium anodes but the cost differential made the stainless steel anodes attractive in order to decrease capital cost. Still, the lower voltage achieved with the coated titanium anodes may make them attractive for a particular project depending on power costs. More importantly, addition of the second screen helped protect the anode from corrosion. Benchscale tests showed that at 45 ASF (i.e. the current density during cathode harvesting when portions of the cell cathodes are removed), a single screen stainless steel anode experienced some corrosion at the corners, indicating that the current distribution was higher at the corners. This effect was eliminated with double-screens. The mechanism of corrosion of stainless steel anodes in AART is related to diffusion of ferrous ions to the anode. If current density exceeds diffusion rate of ferrous ions to the anode surface, voltage will increase and the stainless steel will begin to corrode. Doubling the screen decreases screen current density, thus lowering the limiting diffusion rate

of ferrous ions. In order to protect the stainless steel anode from electrochemical attack, cell voltage was controlled to a maximum of 1.3 volts at the rectifier. The 1.07 volts measured with the two-screen stainless steel anodes represents a 46 % reduction in cell voltage versus conventional electrowinning with Pb-Ca-Sn anodes (which typically operate at 2.0 volts). 

After the AART demonstration was complete, samples of the stainless steel anode screen were analyzed by SEM. The screens showed very little indication of corrosion, as demonstrated in Figure 4. 

Copper cathode produced during the AART demonstration measured less than 10 ppm sulfur and less than 3 ppm iron, which met FCX standards for “AA” cathode. No lead was present in the circuit because of the anodes used. 

Current efficiency of the AART process averaged 84 %. Total iron concentration in electrolyte entering the cell averaged 29.9 g/L. Cell inlet ferric concentration averaged 1.1 g/L. Cell overflow ferric concentration averaged 3.4 g/L.

###### 3.2 Absorption of Sulfur Dioxide 

One goal of the AART demonstration was to continuously absorb sulfur dioxide into copper electrolyte. In order to establish solubility targets, sulfur dioxide solubility was determined in bench-scale measurements using synthetic copper electrolyte containing 38 g/L copper, 160 g/L sulfuric acid, and 30 g/L iron. Results are displayed in Figure 5. The results show that required amounts of sulfur dioxide can be absorbed into copper electrolyte with increasing sulfur dioxide partial pressure and decreasing electrolyte temperature. Based on these results a model was developed that treated type of absorption tower packing, pressure of sulfur dioxide and absorption tower liquid loading. A plot of the model is shown in Figure 6. Tower input conditions were 2-inch Pall rings, 75 ppm SO2 exit gas, 25 feet of packing height, and approx. 52 °C temperature. The model predicted percent sulfur dioxide required at the absorption tower inlet (for AART) that would simultaneoulsy yield a 75 ppm sulfur dioxide exit gas from the tower. 

The Technology Center evaluated operating conditions over a range of feasible pressures and inlet sulfur dioxide concentrations (6 to 12 psi and 12 to 16 % SO2). It was concluded that a design with lower operating pressure was more economical even though sulfur dioxide solubility would be less. To compensate for the lower sulfur dioxide solubility the absorption tower design incorporated a high flowrate of electrolyte (up to 48 gpm per square foot of absorption tower cross-section). Almost 100 % of the AART electrolyte recirculation flow would be used to absorb the sulfur dioxide.

###### 3.5 Solvent Extraction 

The solvent extraction process for AART would have been the same as conventional SX-EW circuits except for the requirement to provide both copper and iron make-up to off-set losses in the byproduct acid stream. Conventional SX-EW circuits typically bleed electrolyte from the circuit to 

1628

_Demonstration of the Ferrous/Ferric Anode Reaction for Copper Electrowinning_ 



control iron build-up over time. The AART process does not require this bleed because of the iron already present in the electrolyte, but the by-product acid stream more than equals a conventional bleed stream. 

Copper make-up to the AART circuit can be achieved by balancing the SX-EW process accordingly. The “re-circulating load” of copper (about 10 % of production) that passes through solvent extraction, by-product acid recovery, leaching and back to solvent extraction becomes an inefficiency in the process (although partially off-set versus conventional SX-EW by no longer requiring a tankhouse bleed stream). The needed iron make-up required by AART can also be addressed through solvent extraction if the extractant utilized extracts iron in sufficient quantities from the pregnant leach solution (PLS). With this approach the Cu/Fe selectivity in AART solvent extraction needs to be low, in the 15 to 20 range. This is a reversal of direction in terms of modern extractant development which has sought to maximize Cu/Fe selectivity, achieving well over 1000 in conventional SX-EW plants. Of course other approaches are possible to make up iron in the AART circuit. A smaller-scale SX circuit could be implemented to extract only iron from the PLS on a dedicated basis; or iron as iron sulfate could be added directly to the circuit if economically feasible.

### Development and Commercialization of an Alternative Anode for Copper Electrowinning 

S. Sandoval, C. Clayton, S. Dominguez, C. Unger, T. Robinson 

Freeport-McMoRan Mining Company 4521 U.S. Highway 191 Morenci, USA 

**Keywords:** Electrowinning, energy, anode, cathode quality 

#### Abstract 

In 2006, the Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc. (FCX) Technology Center in Safford, Arizona undertook research to develop an alternative anode for copper electrowinning. The objectives of the development included a 15 % voltage reduction versus conventional Pb-Ca-Sn anodes and the removal of lead and associated lead contamination from the copper electrowinning circuit. An anode development lab was established that included bench-scale electrowinning cells as well as accelerated life testing cells. 

This paper describes the development of the FCX alternative anode including its structure and associated anode coating. In 2008, the Chino electrowinning plant was fully converted to the new FCX anode becoming the first copper electrowinning plant in the world to exclusively utilize non-lead anodes. A 15 % electrowinning voltage reduction was achieved. Cleaning of electrowinning cells for lead sludge and addition of cobalt to the circuit for stabilizing lead anodes were discontinued. Lead content of copper cathodes measured less than 0.3 ppm. 

#### 1 Introduction 

In 2006, Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc. Technology Center established an anode development lab at its SX-EW Test Facility located in Morenci, Arizona. The purpose of the lab was to explore opportunities for replacing conventional Pb-Ca-Sn anodes in copper electrowinning with an alternative anode that would decrease energy consumption and remove lead contamination from the copper electrowinning circuit. A 15 % voltage reduction target was established. The lab operated on a 7-day, 24-hr basis as part of the Technology Center’s SX-EW Test Facility. 

Figures 1, 2, and 3 display the anode development lab and associated testing cells. A dual approach was implemented for the development. Accelerated life testing cells were utilized to compare life-

time of anode coatings as a function of coating composition. The test coatings were applied to expanded titanium metal coupons. In addition, voltage testing cells were utilized to compare voltage performance of candidate anode coatings in copper electrolyte during copper electrowinning. Using this approach, coating life was maximized while coating voltage was minimized. 



Figure 1: Technology Center anode development lab. 

The anode development lab incorporated ten accelerated life testers (on the right in Figure 1) containing eight coupon cells each (Figure 2) for a total lab capacity of 80 coupon cells that could be operated simultaneously. Each coupon cell contained a 1-in

ch by 3-inch anode coupon made of titanium expanded metal with one square inch of coating applied to the bottom of the coupon. The cathode utilized in the accelerated life cells was an uncoated coupon of titanium expanded metal. In the accelerated life cells the coupons were subjected to a 180 g/L sulfuric acid solution at room temperature. Current was 3.5 amps per square inch of 40 % open expanded titanium. This calculates to a current density of 840 amps/ft<sup>2</sup> of titanium metal. 

The anode development lab also incorporated ten voltage testing cells (on the left in Figure 1). In these cells a 3-inch by 6-inch coupon of 40 % open expanded titanium with the candidate anode coating was tested (Figure 3). The voltage testing cells were fitted with 316L stainless steel cathodes

Current density was controlled at 30 amps/ft<sup>2</sup> on the cathode which equated to 50 amps/ft<sup>2</sup> of titanium metal on the anode. 

Various coatings were evaluated for lifetime in the accelerated life cells and for voltage performance in the voltage testing cells. The anode coating development work focused primarily on mixtures of iridium oxide and tantalum oxide and the associated coating preparation and processing parameters. Coatings that met the 15 % voltage reduction criteria and exceeded 3000 hours in the accelerated life testing cells were carried forward to pilot testing in Test Facility cells, which contained full-scale commercial electrodes.

The conductor rods were made by cold-rolling 5/8-inch titanium tube onto an aluminium core and sealing the end with titanium. The aluminum cores at the top of the rods were press-fitted into the copper hanger bar, and the titanium tubes were seated into the copper hanger bar to seal the rod/hanger bar connection from the tankhouse environment. Aluminum was chosen for the conductor rod core material (over copper), although copper could be used, depending on the price of aluminum. The screens were composed of expanded titanium metal that was 40 % open and 0.022 inches thick. The anode structure was designed so that the screens could be removed when the anode coating lifetime was spent, and the anode could be re-screened with a screen having a fresh coating. Thus the anode screen with coating became the consumable portion of the anode. A 2 % increase in current efficiency was noted versus operation with Pb-Ca-Sn anodes. This was probably due to the increased care taken by Chino operators to control short circuits. The FCX alternative anodes are more easily damaged by short circuits than conventional Pb-Ca-Sn anodes. This is because the titanium screen becomes very hot locally during a short circuit and a hole is produced in the screen. Holes that become too large require repair, which is accomplished by spot welding a patch of screen over the hole. Control of short circuits decreases alternative anode repair rate. The keys to controlling short circuits in the Chino tankhouse were: - Maintain straight cathode starter sheets in the electrowinning cells. The straightness of the cathode was the main factor affecting formation of short circuits. Chino inspected starter sheets for straightness during insertion into the cells and pulled the cathodes after two days of plating to press the cathodes flat. - Remove “edge hair” or other inhomogeneities from the cathode starter sheet before insertion in the cell. This prevents formation of a dendrite that could lead to a short circuit. - Maintain anode-cathode alignment in cells. The steps noted above supported uniform current distribution in the electrowinning cell and minimized potential for short circuits. In addition, Chino had installed an FCX double-double contact system to distribute current to anodes and cathodes in each cell. The double-double contact system consisted of a main distribution b

ar with “sawtooth” contacts and equalizer bars on each side to aid

###### 2.3.3 Cathode Quality 

Two melts were conducted with 100 % Chino cathode (produced with alternative anodes) at FCX rod mills. The first melt was 163,529 lbs and was conducted at the El Paso (TX) rod mill. Lead content was analyzed using a Thermo Jerrell Ash Atom Comp 2000 DC Arc unit and measured below the detection level of the instrument (< 0.3 ppm). The second melt was 100,524 lbs and was conduced at the Miami (AZ) rod mill. Lead content was analyzed using an Applied Research Laboratories 4460 Metal Analyzer Quantometer Arc Spark unit. Lead content measured below the detection level of the instrument (< 1.0 ppm). Cathode sulfur content was 2 to 4 ppm in the two melts. ###### 2.3.4 Lessons Learned from the First Alternative Anode Installation 

Targets for alternative anode voltage and coating life performance were met in the Chino conversion. A 15 % voltage reduction was achieved and coating life projections were in agreement with estimations developed through anode development lab testing. With introduction of alternative anodes at Chino, cobalt addition to electrolyte ceased and cell cleaning for removal o

f lead sludge was discontinued. These were the key benefits that were projected, and they became reality. Lead content of cathode decreased below detection limits. 

Lessons learned from the Chino installation were several, and are noted below. 

- Chino used copper starter sheets for cathodes. During copper starter sheet plating, the cell electrolyte solution level was varied in order to plate copper up onto the loops that connect the starter sheet to the cathode hanger bar. This strengthened the loops. 

When the Chino cell electrolyte level was set to its lowest level, one inch of anode screen protruded above solution level (and thus extended into the heat retention balls (HRB) floating on top of the cell). If a short circuit occurred and continued under these conditions, the anode screen above solution level became very hot and ignited the HRB, producing a low-level cell fire. 

It was found that the screen height could be decreased by 1 inch and still plate copper up onto the starter sheet loops. This would maintain the top of the alternative anode screens below solution level and prevent an HRB fire. 

- Chino tankhouse operators reported that trading labor required for cleaning of cells (to remove lead sludge) for labor to more diligently prevent short circuits in the tankhouse was a good trade. Elimination of lead anodes and associated lead sludge also eliminated employee exposure to lead. 

1645 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Sandoval, Clayton, Dominguez, Unger, Robinson_ 



- Spot welding was used to connect the anode screens to the anode conductor rods. In the initial anode production, the welds were not quite strong enough and some of the welds began to fail in operation. The welds were strengthened, and it was determined that the screens could still be removed for re-screening purposes when the anode coating life was spent. 

- Around the perimeter of the alternative anode the screens were initially manufactured open, meaning that the screen on each side of the conductor rods did not connect, and there was a gap between the screens equal to the diameter of the conductor rods. During operation it was found that edges of the screens could become flared out towards the cathode, resulting in a potential short circuit. The anode design was improved by spot welding the screens together around the perimeter of the anode. This added strength and straightness to the anode, and also helped to feather the copper cathode deposit around the edges.

Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc. (FCX) Technology Center developed an alternative anode for use in copper electrowinning at its SX-EW Test Facility located in Morenci, Arizona. The anode was implemented at FCX’s Chino electrowinning plant in 2008 and has met targets for voltage reduction (15 %) and coating lifetime projections (minimum 6 years). 

Cleaning of electrowinning cells for lead sludge and addition of cobalt to the circuit for stabilizing lead anodes were discontinued

with the alternative anodes. Lead content of copper cathodes decreased to less than 0.3 ppm.

### Measuring and Modelling Copper Electrowinning Current Efficiency in Chloride Media 

Prashant K. Sarswat, Michael L. Free 

Department of Metallurgical Engineering University of Utah-84112 

Salt Lake City, USA 

**Keywords:** Electrowinning, current efficiency, model, chloride media, copper 

#### Abstract 

Leaching of chalcopyrite ore from chloride media has potential to reduce energy consumption in copper production by reducing comminution, and eliminating mineral concentration and smelting. Leaching in chloride media can be coupled with electrowinning to reduce reagent consumption. Oxidant needed for leaching can b

e generated at the anode during electrowinning. This process requires careful control of Fe<sup>3+</sup> /Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Cu<sup>2+</sup> /Cu<sup>+</sup> ratios as well as acid in order to optimize both leaching and electrowinning. In order to explore the effects of individual components like acid concentration, concentration of ferric and ferrous ion, concentration of cupric and cuprous ion, twolevel factorial design sets of electrowinning experiments were conducted. To simulate actual tank house electrowinning, experiments were conducted with inert lead anodes in a parallel plate configuration. The ratio of cupric to cuprous ions, ferric to ferrous ions and HCl concentration were chosen as factors and current efficiency as the response variable. By careful analysis of experiments, it can be concluded that ratios of Cu<sup>2+</sup> /Cu<sup>+</sup> and Fe<sup>3+</sup> /Fe<sup>2+</sup> have a direct correlation with current efficiency, which is directly related to energy consumption. Thus a mathematical model has been used for current efficiency simulation, where Cu<sup>2+</sup> /Cu<sup>+</sup> and Fe<sup>3+</sup> /Fe<sup>2+</sup> ratios are defined as independent variables and current efficiency as the dependent variable. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Electrochemical processing of copper in aqueous media is common in copper production. This process of removing metal from solution electrolytically is termed as electrowinning. Chalcopyrite leaching and copper electrowinning in chloride media can be a possible alternative to traditional processing, not only due to faster leaching kinetics than sulfate processing but also due to reduced energy consumption during electrowinning from the cuprous ion rather than from the cupric ion. Conventional sulfate based chalcopyrite leaching is very slow due to passivation [7]. However, it is

found that chalcopyrite leaching in chloride media is faster and can be coupled with electrowinning. Here consumption of electron/ion is half of that needed for sulfate based electrowinning. In this case copper electrodeposition occurs due to reduction of cuprous ions which consume one electron per copper atom in contrast to reduction from cupric ions which require 2 electrons per atom. Cupric chloride and ferric chloride solutions are very efficient oxidizing agents for sulfide mineral leaching [9-10]. Leaching of chalcopyrite in chloride media is represented by [4, 6]. 





These reactions suggest that chloride based leaching of chalcopyrite using cupric chloride and ferric chloride as leachant, produces cuprous as well as ferrous ions. The reaction systems contains ferric ion and cupric ion as well. Direct electrowinning of copper from such solutions containing Cu<sup>+</sup> , Cu<sup>2+</sup> , Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Fe<sup>3+</sup> ions can be accomplished. A study shown by Hirato _et al_ that discusses leaching of chalcopyrite indicates there is a dependency on the

concentration of FeCl3, CuCl2 and CuCl [1-2]. The leach liquor contains substantial iron in ferric form. The presence of iron in ferric form in electrolyte solution causes a loss in current efficiency. The quality of electrodeposited copper is also very poor in ferric environment electrowinning [11]. The cumulative effects of these ionic species (Cu<sup>+</sup> , Cu<sup>2+</sup> , Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Fe<sup>3+</sup> ) on current efficiency is measured and modeled in further sections of this study.

It has been already reported that electrolysis of cupric chloride causes excessive corrosion of copper cathode and causes precipitation of CuCl [8]. Reduction in current efficiency in the presence of cupric ion in cuprous chloride solution is already reported. A possible explanation for such reduction of current efficiency is dissolution of copper cathode in presence of cupric ion [8]. Current efficiency drops with increasing concentration of ferric ions as is evident from factorial design experiments as well as simulation. Power consumption also increases with increase in concentration of ferric ions. The rate of ferric ion reduction is limited by diffusion of ferric ions to the electrode surface. The standard reduction potential for Fe<sup>3+</sup> /Fe<sup>2+</sup> is 0.77 V and that for Cu<sup>2+</sup> /Cu is 0.34V. Thus, when ferric ion is present during electrowinning, reduction of ferric takes place first which consumes much of the current. These ions reduce rapidly as they diffuse to the surface. High dissolution of cathode due to chloride ion presence has also been reported [8]. Hydrochloric acid is a source of chloride ions, and it therefore has an adverse effect on electrowinning current efficiency.

#### 4 Summary 

Simulation and measurement of copper electrowinning current efficiency in chloride media were conducted in an effort to find out the best experimental regime for maximum current efficiency. Direct Cu electrowinning (without SX) of leaching solution (6 gram of copper/liter) was performed. Low cupric ion to cuprous ion ratio, high pH, and low ferric ion concentrations are the best studied conditi

ons for optimal current efficiency when electrowinning is carried out in chloride media. Simulation of electrowinning current efficiency, matched reasonably well with experimental data. Potentiodynamic scan results of actual experiments and simulations also matched well over a wide range of current density.

### Process Change for the Treatment of Spent Electrolyte at Aurubis Hamburg 

Peter Stantke, Dr. Guenther Leuprecht 

Aurubis AG HovestraЯe 50 Hamburg, Germany 

**Keywords:** Copper electrorefining, electrolyte treatment, nickel, evaporation, impurities 

#### Abstract 

The purpose of a copper tankhouse is firstly to produce reliable high-grade cathodes and secondly to concentrate as much as possible of the by-elements in the anodes in order that their extraction becomes economically interesting and can provide additional value added. 

To achieve these aims, Aurubis Hamburg modified the process of electrolyte treatment at the end of 2006 and thus doubled the processing capacity for nickel. 

This paper discusses the changes in the process and presents the differences in operating parameters in comparisons of before and after the changeover. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The real purpose of the tankhouse is to produce high-purity copper. As in every refining process, however, the “impurities” in the anode must inevitably be controlled. 

These are on the one hand the insoluble or slightly soluble elements, such as lead and in particular the precious metals Au, Ag, Pt and Pd, which are enriched in the anode slimes, and are profitably sold or processed further. 

On the other hand there are also the fully or partly soluble elements, such as As, Bi, Sb, Zn and above all Ni. Nickel must be especially mentioned in this group since it is in Hamburg by far the most valuable element in the group and in addition is found in the anode in the highest concentration. Aurubis therefore had the aim of doubling the Ni processing capacity from about 500 tonnes p.a. to 1000 tonnes p.a. in 2006 so as to increase the flexibility in the concentrate processing and generate additional value added. Since the maximum Ni concentration should remain unchanged at 

1663 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Stantke, Leuprecht_ 



20 g/l in the copper electrolyte, it was necessary to increase the processing capacity for spent electrolyte. 

Topic of this paper is therefore the conversion of the process for treating electrolyte and nickel extraction. 

#### 2 Old process 

In the old process, the electrolyte was initially partly decopperised in the refining tankhouse in regulating cells that are filled with Pb anodes. Since the copper is deposited on stainless steel sheets (ISA process), it was necessary to produce a strippable deposit of saleable quality. This in turn requires a sufficient el

ectrolyte circulation. To ensure this, the volume flow had to be increased to about 100 l/min, which had the consequence that the copper content could be only reduced by 10 g/l. In order to deposit sufficient copper in the refining tankhouse and to relieve the decopperisation tankhouse, the electrolyte was therefore channelled through a second cell in series with the result that it could be discharged with a copper concentration of about 25 g/l. 

The decopperising at Aurubis Hamburg took place in 24 cells that decopperised the electrolyte to about 0.8 g/l in 3 stages. The first stage consists of 12 parallel cells that are circulated via a collector tank. The second and third stages each consist of 6 cells. The electrolyte also circulates here via a collector tank and flows through the parallel arranged cells. Part of the outflow of the third stage with 0.8-1 g/l Cu is continuously released for nickel crystallisation. 

The collector tanks are connected and communicate with one another via pipelines. The liquid level is therefore always the same in all the tanks. Depending on how much electrolyte is discharged to the Ni crystallisation it is therefore only necessary to add the corresponding amount of electrolyte into the first decopperisation circuit. 

The copper concentration is continuously monitored and controlled in the third stage only. 

The copper concentrations in the two first stages adjust by means of the communicating system. When the Cu concentration in the inflowing electrolyte is increasing, the outflow quantity of decopperised electrolyte is automatically decreasing. This results in a rise in the collector tanks liquid level. This has to be manually balanced by increasing the amperage of the rectifier. 

The decopperised electrolyte is evaporated to about 1000 g/l H2SO4 in the next step, which causes nickel sulphate to crystallise. Ten evaporators are available for the evaporation process, which are usually operated as 5 parallel pairs. The nickel sulphate is filtered via a vacuum belt filter and filled into big-bags for selling.

A dissolving tank is available for the production of copper sulphate solution and is positioned on weighing cells so as to ensure a constant and defined copper concentration.

The condensate used must be heated previously to 60° so as to dissolve quickly and to avoid that it crystallises in storage tanks or the piping. 

###### 4.1.5 Cooling 

Cooling is required for the vapour condenser and the heat exchanger of the cooling crystalliser. This is provided by a cooling tower with a capacity of 5 MW and is operated with treated Elbe river water. 

###### 4.1.6 Vacuum production 

Two water ring pumps are available for the vacuum production, of which one is in operation. The second is kept on standby. Vapour condensate is used as propulsion water. If necessary freshwater can be fed in the event of a water deficit.

###### 4.2 Plant operation 

The plant was designed for an evaporation rate of 4.6 m³ of water per hour. The actual evaporation rate is significantly higher since the heat exchanger was designed very generously due to the expected formation of accretions from electrolyte constituents which have build up much less than expected. Therefore continuous evaporation of 120 m³/d is possible. The maximum figure is even above 6 m³/h. 

The maximum quantity of electrolyte that can be processed is dependent on the acid concentration of the bleed electrolyte and the evaporation degree. 

The tankhouse’s bleed electrolyte generally has a sulphuric acid content of about 180 g/l. The aim is to achieve an acid concentration of at least 360 g/l sulphuric acid, which represents an evaporation degree of 50 % or the evaporation of 0.5 m³ of water per m³ spent electrolyte. 

An acid concentration of 420 g/l has proved most sensible. When concentrations are higher, copper sulphate accretions on the reactor walls and the agitator are increasing. High evaporation ratios also lead to problems in the

cooling circuit. The copper sulphate is then inclined to form accretions in the chiller. A final acid concentration of 400 g/l results in an evaporation degree of 55 % respectively with a throughput of 8.3 m³/h (=200 m³/d) spent electrolyte an evaporation rate of 4.5 m³/h water. Likewise costs for the operation of the electrowinning cells (lead anodes, additives) and the monitoring of same are eliminated, electricity consumption has decreased (elimination of oxygen overvoltage) and higher wear of the stainless steel blanks during winning electrolysis is avoided. - The negative effect is that the increased copper losses through the increased amount the rejected electrolyte must be compensated by the addition of copper sulphate. A basic level of about 0.8 % Ni in the copper sulphate cannot however be undercut without recrystallisation. By separating the evaporator and crystalliser, there is the possibility to reach the desired final copper and acid concentration at different working points. High evapora

Lower evaporation rates make a higher copper yield in the winning tankhouse necessary with higher costs. At the same time, however, less circuit nickel in the copper sulphate must be passed on to the smelter. 

- The nickel crystallisation is in any case massively helped, since a large part of the water to be evaporated is already evaporated during the copper crystallisation. Despite the significantly higher volume flow from 3 to 4.1 m³/h under nominal conditions, considerably less water must be evaporated on account of the higher feed acid concentration.

Adding the copper sulphate crystallisation plant to the electrolyte treatment process has been a success for Aurubis in every respect. The maximum bleed electrolyte quantity in the tankhouse could be increased from 110 to 220 m³/d. The nickel limit values in the anodes could be substantially increased. Anodes with average nickel contents of up to 3500 g/t are processed nowadays, without causing the electrolyte nickel content to increase to over 20 g/l. 

In summary this lead to a nearly doubled nickel capacity of about 1000 t/a. Apart from that, a series of other impurities can be tolerated in higher concentrations since these are discharged in the spent electrolyte.

### Copper Electrorefining at High Current Densities 

Michael Stelter, Hartmut Bombach 

TU Bergakademie Freiberg Institut fьr Nichteisenmetallurgie und Reinststoffe Leipziger StraЯe 34 09596 Freiberg, Germany 

**Keywords:** Copper, electrorefining, high current density, electrolyte temperature, PCR, flow conditions 

#### Abstract 

Today approx. 75 % of the world copper production is produced by means of electrorefining. In recent years, many copper producers have increased the current density up to 300-350 A/m<sup>2</sup> . The target of our studies was a further increase of the current density up to 1000 A/m<sup>2</sup> in conventional electrolysis cells. To assess the maximum possible current density under conventional industrial electrolysis conditions, the current density was increased in steps of 150 A/m² starting from 400 A/m². The tests were conducted trouble-free without short circuits up to a current density of 700 A/m². However, the shape of the cathode deposits deteriorated considerably with higher current densities. From 850 A/m², the hazard of short circuits and anode passivation increased strongly. In the current density range from 300 to 500 A/m<sup>2</sup> all cathodes meet the demands concerning chemical purity of grade A copper. At higher current densities the concentrations of some impurities in the

cathodes increase strongly. 

During the application of the PCR technique no anode passivation occurred at current densities up to 1000 A/m². The formation of dendrites at the cathode was reduced and therefore the number of short circuits. The concentration of cathode contaminations could not be reduced by PCR. 

The temperature of the electrolyte was increased stepwise from 65 to 80 °C. At higher temperatures the formation of nodules was considerably reduced. Strong edge overgrowths and formation of dendrites resulted in short circuits. This could even not be avoided by optimization of the glue and thiourea addition. Elevated electrolyte temperatures led to an increase of the silver concentration in the cathodes and thus to silver losses. However, the concentrations of most of the other contaminations decreased.

#### 1 Problem 

With an annual worldwide production of 17 Mio t copper is one of the major metals together with steel and aluminium. At present, approx. 12 Mio t of copper are produced all over the world by electrorefining in sulfuric acid electrolytes. 

A major focus of research and development in copper electrorefining is increasing the current density. On the basis of investigations in the early 20<sup>th</sup> century, the current density was increased from 100 to 200 A/m² between 1900 and 1930. Any further increase required extensive research for a better understanding of the electrolysis processes and a further optimization of the electrolysis parameters. Therefore the next step in current efficiency increase up to 300-380 A/m² occurred only from 1980 until now. This progress was partly enabled by using stainless steel sheets as cathodes and by improved control of the effective inhibitor concentrations in the electrolyte. 

At present many companies and research teams work on a further increase of current density in copper electrorefining. Recent research on copper electrowinning has shown that a current density of 1000 A/m<sup>2</sup> enables principally the deposition of high-purity cathode-copper, but only in special electrolysis cells with an intensive electrolyte convection [1]. This process, however, is not applicable for copper electrorefining. Copper electrorefining at high current densities was already performed in laboratory scale using so called flow cells with high flow velocities [2]. The investment costs and economic expenditure for this technique is much higher in comparison to conventional copper electrorefining cells. Therefore flow cells have not been utilized in industrial scale for copper electrorefining until today. 

Formerly we already reported on investigations concerning the increase of current density in copper electrorefining using conventional electrolysis cells [3]. The investigations have shown that copper electrorefining in conventional cells is possible in principle up to current densities of approx. 1000 A/m<sup>2</sup> ; however, the

deposition quality and chemical purity of the cathode deposits deteriorated considerably with increasing current density. Cathodes deposited at 400 and 550 A/m<sup>2</sup> generally met the demands for grade A copper. At current densities of 700 and 850 A/m<sup>2</sup> the sulfur concentrations exceeded the threshold for grade A copper. Simultaneously the Ni and As concentrations of the cathodes increased due to the inclusion of electrolyte in the rough and nodular cathodes. Moreover the bad cathode surface led to the inclusion of anode slime and the concentration of Se, Pb, Sn and Sb in some cathodes exceeded the demands for grade A copper. At high current densities the formation of dendrites and therefore the frequency of short circuits increased. During some experiments current densities above 800 A/m<sup>2</sup> caused passivation of the anodes. 

The target of further investigations was the optimization of the electrolysis conditions for the deposition of high quality copper in the current density range of 500 to 800 A/m<sup>2</sup> in common electrolysis cells.
