#### 3 Results 

###### 3.1 Periodical Current Reverse Technique (PCR) 

The PCR technique is applied in some copper refineries to prevent anodic passivation at current densities from 300 A/m² upwards and unfavorable anode compositions. The change of the current direction causes a decrease of the Cu<sup>2+</sup> concentration within the anode slime layer. Simultaneously copper, predominantly from dendrites and nodules, dissolves from the cathode. Therefore the frequency of short circuits should be reduced and the quality of the cathodic copper deposition improves. Literature statements concerning the influence of the PCR technique on the cathode purity are inconsistent. Mostly an improvement of the chemical purity could not be attained [4]. 

Jaskula [4] gives an overview of the operation parameters of several copper refineries using the PCR technique at current densities between 300 and 400 A/m². The duration of the forward current (20 to 200 s) differs considerably from the duration of the reverse current (1 to 10 s). One major disadvantage of the PCR technique, in addition to higher costs for the rectifier, is significantly reduced the space-time efficiency and current efficiency with the duration and intensity of the reverse current. The specific energy consumption increases correspondingly. Thus in our experiments the reverse current was applied only shortly with very low current density. 

Forward current: 40 s with 100 % nominal current density 

Reverse current: 1 s with 5 % nominal current density 

The results are as follows: 

1. The PCR technique prevented passivation of the anodes even at 1000 A/m<sup>2</sup> and 65 °C electrolyte temperature. The anodes dissolved uniformly, and the anode surfaces did not show any signs of beginning passivation. 

2. At 700 and 850 A/m² the deposition quali

ty was clearly better than in the tests without PCR. However, the strong edge overgrowths were strongly nodulated in the tests with PCR as well. Thus the PCR technique did not lead to significant improvements in this respect. In some testes larger dendrites were formed at the edges resulting in short circuits. 

3. Despite the improved cathodic deposition the PCR technique did not effectuate a decrease of cathode contaminations. 

4. In tests without short circuits the cathodic current efficiency ranged between 98.3 and 99.4 %. This is only slightly lower than in tests without PCR. However, the space-time efficiency yielded only 94 % of the space-time efficiency without PCR. The specific energy consumption changed only slightly. 

The advantage of preventing anode passivation is opposed to the increased technical expenditure and the decreased space-time efficiency. Therefore no further tests applying the PCR technique were performed.

###### 3.2 Influence of the electrolyte temperature 

According to theoretical considerations, high electrolyte temperatures should favorably influence the electrolysis at higher current densities. E.g. a higher electrolyte temperature increases the cathodic limiting current density, the solubility of Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions in the electrolyte and the electrical conductivity of the electrolyte. The hazard of anodic passivation is reduced. Disadvantages are an increase in electrolyte evaporation and the faster decomposition of inhibitors. 

The electrolysis tests were carried out with two different kinds of anodes (Table 1) and were conducted for one anode life consisting of three cathode periods at 500, 650 and 800 A/m<sup>2</sup> and temperatures of 65, 70, 75 and 80 °C. Although at higher temperatures the glue decomposes more rapidly the amount of glue was not increased and remained at 100 g per ton of deposited copper. Also the amount of thiourea remained at 60 g/t. 

The investigations show that increasing of the electrolyte temperature has both a positive and a negative effect on the quality of cathodic deposition. On the one hand, the cathode surface becomes substantially smoother with increasing temperature. Thus, very smooth and almost nodule-free cathodes were produced at 500 and 650 A/m² and 75 and 80 °C. On the other hand, higher temperatures led to substantially stronger edge overgrowth. In the edge area, large nodules and dendrites formed increasingly. This caused short circuits particularly at 80°C and 650 and 800 A/m². 

The tests showed that increasing electrolyte temperature leads to a significant increase of the Ag concentration, whereas an increase in current density causes a slight reduction of this value (Figure 2). The relatively strong temperature influence caused a slight exceed of the concentration limit of 15 µg/g at 80 °C and 500 A/m². These results are by trend in agreement with our earlier investigations at current densities betw

The following parameters were examined: - Application of the Periodical Current Reverse Technique (PCR) - Optimization of the electrolyte temperature - Optimization of the addition of glue and thiourea at elevated temperatures - Improvement of the oncoming flow of the electrolyte towards the cathode The investigations have shown that cathodes deposited at current densities up to 500 A/m² and at optimized electrolysis conditions met the demands for grade A copper. The electrolysis generally runs trouble-free up to 700 A/m² even though the impurity concentration increases, which affects the copper quality. #### 1 Problem 

Up to now copper electrorefining has been performed exclusively in strong sulfuric acid electrolytes. The application of the additives glue and thiourea enables compact and smooth depositions on the cathodes. 

In silver electrorefining solely silver nitrate electrolyte containing 0.5 to 3 g/l free nitric acid is used. The silver is deposited on the cathodes strongly dendritic. To avoid short circuits the crystal pins are stripped periodically and accumulated at the cell ground. It is not yet definitely clear whether strongly dendritic silver deposition is caused only by the metal properties or by the nitric electrolyte too. Only few investigations concerning the effect of additives on the silver deposition from nitric electrolytes have been performed. 

In the fields of ultrapure copper production and hydrometallurgical separation of copper and silver the use of nitric electrolytes is of special interest. Various investigations on copper deposition on stationary electrodes using nitric electrolytes showed generally strongly dendritic depositions and NOx emissions. Therefore the aim of this work was the deposition of smooth copper cathodes from nitric electrolytes and the prevention of NOx emissions. Moreover it should be checked whether the copper deposition from nitric electrolytes can be improved by addition of additives which are normally used in sulphuric copper electrorefining. 

#### 2 Copper deposition from nitric electrolytes

Subsequently the cathodes were vacuum melted in a graphite crucible and purified by means of zone melting. The quality of the deposited cathodes depended considerably on the pH of the electrolyte. Comparable to the sulfuric copper electrolysis an overdose of glue caused a streaky deposition. With glue concentrations above 20 mg/l the cathodes became mechanically unstable and containing high Cu2O concentrations (Figure 8). 

The effect of thiourea on the nature of copper deposition could not definitely be clarified during the experiments. The current-density potential curves show that thiourea acts polarising at current densities below 100 A/m² and depolarizing at values above 100 A/m². Thus thiourea seems to be electrochemically ineffective below 100 A/m². 

During the sulphuric copper electrolysis thiourea causes sulphur contaminations of the cathodes to some extent. In spite of this the addition of thiourea is essential to produce smooth cathodes. In contrast the addition of thiourea is not necessary to produce smooth cathodes from nitric electrolytes. This offers the chance to produce cathodes with very low sulphur concentrations. 

###### 4.2.5 Current efficiency 

The cathodic current efficiency is defined as the mass of the effectively deposited copper divided by the theoretically deposited mass, as predicted by Faraday's law. The theoretically deposited mass was calculated considering the reduction of Cu<sup>2+</sup> to metallic copper (Reaction 1). The effectively deposited copper mass consists of metallic copper and the copper portion of Cu2O and was determined from the weight of the cathodes less the oxygen fraction.

The cathodic current efficiency is mainly influenced by the emitted amount of NOx, the Cu2O content of the cathodes and the occurrence of short circuits. Short circuits result in a decreasing current efficiency. The same applies to increasing NOx emissions due to the higher power demand for the nitrate reduction. On the other hand the current efficiency increases with an increasing Cu2O content of the cathodes because Cu<sup>2+</sup> becomes just reduced to the oxidation state +1. 

The lowest current efficiency can be observed at low copper concentrations and low pH values (e. g. 85 % at pH = 1 and 50 g/l Cu<sup>2+</sup> in the electrolyte). An increase of the pH leads to an increase of the current efficiency of 13 % because of decreasing NOx emissions and a higher Cu2O content of the cathode, but also results in a significant worsening of the cathode quality. 

#### 5 Summary 

The investigations have shown that the deposition of smooth and comp

act copper cathodes in nitric electrolytes requires a well adjusted pH range because a compromise between NOx formation and Cu2O deposition must be found. The formation of dendrites can be reduced by the addition of glue. The NOx emission can be minimized at 25 °C electrolyte temperature. This results in an optimum current density of approximately 100 A/m<sup>2</sup> .

### The Oxidation of Manganese Ions on Lead Alloys During the Electrowinning of Copper 

Venny Tjandrawan, Michael J. Nicol 

Murdoch University, Parker Centre South Street, Murdoch 6150 Perth, Western Australia 

**Keywords:** Electrowinning, anodes, lead, manganese 

#### Abstract 

Manganese ions are often encountered as impurities in the electrolyte used in the electrowinning of copper. The effects of manganese ions in the electrolyte on the anodic behaviour of lead-calcium-tin anodes used in the electrowinning of copper have not previously been definitively established. Potentiostatic oxidation of rotating disc electrodes of Pb-Ca-Sn anodes has been used to investigate the anodic behaviour of these anodes and the oxidation reactions of manganese ions in sulphuric acid solutions. The electrochemical measurements were complemented by chemical analyses of the oxidized manganese species formed during the anodisation process. 

The oxidation of manganese on these anodes was found to occur at potentials above about 1.7 V and is also accompanied by oxidation of the lead and evolution of oxygen at potentials above about 2.0 V. The amount of manganese oxidized increases with increasing oxidation potential. 

The presence of manganese in the electrolyte decreases the rate of formation of lead dioxide and reduces the fraction of the charge associated with oxygen evolution. Higher concentrations of manganese(II) and lower oxidation potentials favour the production of manganese(III) which can form a MnOOH intermedi

ate layer, while permanganate is produced at low concentrations of manganese(II). MnO2 powder produced by chemical precipitation reactions involving manganese(III) and permanganate(VII) ions, was also formed in the bulk electrolyte and on the walls of the cell. 

Mechanisms for the various reactions are presented together with recommendations for minimization of permanganate formation in copper tankhouse electrolytes. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Lead calcium tin (Pb-Ca-Sn) anodes are the typical materials used in the copper electrowinning process. Industrial copper electrolytes generally contain between 1 and 250 mg/L manganese that

During electrolysis, Mn<sup>2+</sup> ions are oxidized at the anode surface producing either soluble species such as permanganate and manganic ions or insoluble MnO2 and possibly MnOOH layers. These layers are believed to be beneficial in that they retard anode degradation and corrosion [2, 3]. However excessive amounts of MnO2 scale have a tendency to break away from the anode causing increased corrosion of the underlying lead anode [3]. The formation of permanganate and manganic ions has been shown to be responsible for oxidation of the organic reagents in plants which have an integrated solvent extraction circuit. An understanding of the reactions of manganese occurring both on the lead anodes and in the electrolytes and of the level of manganese that is most beneficial in terms of anode corrosion and slime formation could assist in the optimisation of the electrowinning process. 

Several studies have been carried out to determine the possible manganese reactions occurring on the inert electrodes used in the field of lead-acid batteries, but little detail is available for these reactions during the electrowinning of metals such as copper and zinc. #### 2 Experimental 

The electrochemical studies were performed using a conventional three-electrode system. A modified Metrohm glass cell covered with a detachable lid was used as a reaction vessel. The working electrode was a rotating disc (5 mm diameter) fabricated from commercial rolled Pb0.080 % Ca-1.23 % Sn alloy. The reference electrode was an Hg|Hg2SO4 (saturated K2SO4) electrode (SSE, E = +0.645 V versus SHE) which was joined to the main cell by a Lugging capillary passing through a screw fitting in the base of the cell. The tip of the Lugging capillary was placed ~0.5 cm below the surface of the working electrode. The counter electrode was a platinum wire housed in a glass tube which was separated from the bulk solution by a glass frit. All potentials are reported with respect to the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE). 

The rotating disc electrode (RDE) was rotated using a drive consisting of an optically controlled unit coupled to a dc motor. Voltammetric experiments were carried out using a Princeton Applied Research Model 173 Potentiostat/Galvanostat and Model 376 Logarithmic Current Converter together with an EG&G PARC Model 175 Universal Programmer. Analogue data from the potentiostat were collected using a National Instrument data acquisition board controlled by Labview software. The temperature of the electrolyte was maintained at 40 ± 0.1 ºC by using a water thermoregulator (Rowe Scientific Pty Ltd). 

Prior to all tests, the exposed surface of the working electrode was wet-polished using 800 followed by 1200 silicon carbide papers and rinsed with deionised water. After immersion in the electrolyte the anode was potentiostatically anodised for a specific time (30 minutes to 24 hours) at various potentials, at a rotation speed of 500 rpm. This was followed by a potential sweep in a negative direction at a rate of 1 mV/sec. 

Sulphuric acid (150 g/L) and manganese(II) solutions of various concentrations (0.1 and 1 g/L) were prepared using AR grade 98 % sulphuric acid, manganese sulphate and Milli-Q distilled water. Each test was conducted in 200 mL of

electrolyte. 

Visible spectroscopy was used to identify the high-oxidation state manganese species in solution, namely manganic and permanganate. The visible spectrum of the manganic ion has a broad absorbance maximum at 482 nm, while permanganate ion has maxima at 488, 506, 524, 544 and 565 nm [10]. Samples of spent electrolyte were transferred to a Unicam 1.0 cm Optical Path Length Quartz Glass cell for immediate spectral analysis. An Agilent 8453 UV-Visible Spectrophotometer was used to scan from 900 to 350 nm at a rate of 600 nm//min.

The amount of manganese oxidized increases with increasing potential. The presence of manganese in the electrolyte decreases the rate of formation of PbO2. In addition, the presence of manganese also reduces the charge fraction for oxygen evolution. It appears that higher concentrations of manganese ions and lower oxidation potentials favour the formation of manganese(III) species, while permanganate is produced under the opposite conditions. After oxidation for 2 hours in a solution containing 1 g/L manganese ions at 2.0 V, MnO2 powder was also formed in the bulk electrolyte and on the walls of the cell as a result of chemical precipitation reactions involving disproportionation of manganese(III) ions. Anecdotal evidence from the industry has suggested that high (greater than about 50 mg/L) concentrations of manganese in the el

ectrolyte can result in excessive lead contamination of the copper cathodes. This could be due to increased rates of spalling of the oxide layer from the anodes due to the accumulation of both lead and manganese oxidation products. On the basis of the present results this is a likely mechanism. While it appears from this study that permanganate is not the primary product of oxidation of manganese ions at the anode, the experimental technique used could not confirm this because permanganate is unstable in the presence of manganese(II) ions (Reactions 4 or 8+9). The kinetics of this reduction of permanganate by manganese(II) ions is second-order [13] with respect to manganese(II) and therefore is a very sensitive function of the manganese(II) ion concentration. Thus, one will only observe permanganate in the electrolyte at low concentrations of manganese ions under which conditions it is metastable.

#### Abstract 

The METTOP-BRX-Technology is a new electrolysis technology that can be applied in existing and new tankhouses. It uses a parallel electrolyte flow to achieve high current efficiencies, even at high current densities. In the last years, the METTOP-BRX-Technology has been tested in different types of tankhouses, and also half of the new tankhouse at Montanwerke Brixlegg AG, Austria, was equipped with this new technology in 2007. The newest development for the installation of the METTOP-BRX-Technology in existing tankhouses is the so-called Internal Loop (IL). The IL is a new piping solution that minimizes the installation costs of the METTOP-BRX-Technology in an existing tankhouse. With the IL, the existing piping can be used and shut downs during installation can be avoided. The latest big success of the METTOP-BRX-Technology was the decision of Xiangguang Copper, China, in 2009 to install the METTOP-BRX-Technology in all 720 cells of the new tankhouse – the designed current density is 410 A/m² and the tankhouse has being specially designed for the new technology. 

#### 1 General – METTOP-BRX-Technology 

The METTOP-BRX-Technology is a new electrolysis technology to improve tankhouse operations: Using a parallel electrolyte flow, the current efficiency, and density can be increased. The system can be installed in new and existing tankhouses, both in electrorefining and electrowinning. 

To increase the productivity of a copper tankhouse the current efficiency and/or current density needs to be increased. According to physical and chemical laws, the only way to increase the current density in a way that ensures that the electrodeposition is still pure and the copper sheets are smooth

and of a high quality, is to minimize the diffusion boundary layer, for example by increasing the electrolyte velocity. 

Higher velocities can be realized by using a parallel electrolyte flow between the electrodes. For that, the METTOP-BRX-Technology uses the Parallel Flow Device (PFD, Figure 1), which se

rves to increase current efficiency and current density in copper electrolysis by creating a parallel electrolyte flow inside the electrolysis cells (Figure 2). Special designed nozzles govern the fresh electrolyte in an upwards natural electrolyte flow in front of the cathode. Instead of a frontal and centralized electrolyte inlet the electrolyte is introduced into each individual electrode spacing - that means that the electrolyte enters the cell through separate inlet nozzles. Therefore, other than with conventional cell design (Figure 3), the fresh electrolyte and also the additives enter directly at the cathode, where they are needed, and the bypass-flow is minimized. Additionally, the parallel electrolyte flow results in a more homogeneous distribution of concentrations and temperature in the cell. The flow design and pressure drop analysis of the Parallel Flow Device for the METTOPBRX-Technology are calculated with the help of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulation (Figure 4).

#### 2 Latest Projects 

In the last years, tests were carried out in different types of tankhouses all over the world, and the METTOP-BRX-Technology was optimized for industrial application. In 2007 half of the new tankhouse at Montanwerke Brixlegg AG, Austria, was equipped with this new technology. In 2009 it was decided to equip the whole new tankhouse at Xiangguang Copper, Yanggu, China, with the METTOP-BRX-Technology. To minimize costs when installing the METTOP-BRX-Technology in existing tankhouses a special piping solution, the Internal Loop (IL) was developed. 

###### 2.1 Internal Loops 

The Internal Loop was developed as a cost minimization solution when installing the METTOPBRX-Technology in an existing tankhouse. As the METTOP-BRX-Technology uses higher electrolyte flow rates than in conventional cells, the pumps and piping have to be adjusted correspondingly. If the existing pipes and pumps were all replaced by larger dimensions, this exchange would not only result in costs for the new parts but also a certain standstill of operations during the replacement. The IL (Figure 6 and Figure 7) uses the existing inlet piping (green lines in Figure 6) and an additional piping, collecting tank, and pump, and the standstill during implementation of the METTOP-BRX-Technology can be reduced to zero.

#### 3 Implementation Costs 

General calculations on the economics of the METTOP-BRX-Tech

nology were made; however, detailed customer-specific calculations for the implementation of the METTOP-BRX-Technology have to be done for the actual individual situation. Basically, there are three different cases, namely building a new tankhouse with METTOP-BRX-Technology or installing the METTOP-BRXTechnology in an existing tankhouse to increase the current density and therefore the production or to increase the current efficiency at the same current density as before. 

Different calculations together with the customer have shown that the ROI is between < 1 to < 3 years depending on the actual situation. 

Based on the results during the last years an increase in current efficiency of around 3 % can be achieved compared a standard technology with the METTOP BRX Technology. 

Due to the higher electrolyte flow the pumping has to be adjusted accordingly when the METTOPBRX-System is installed. The costs for the pumps for the installation of the METTOP-BRX-

#### 4 Summary 

The METTOP-BRX-Technology is an effective and economic way to increase productivity and production in existing and new tankhouses. The implementation costs in existing tankhouses can be minimized by using Internal Loops. In the last years numerous tests in different types of tankhouses worldwide have been carried out, and the METTOP-BRX-Technology was installed in half of the new tankhouse at Montanwerke Brixlegg AG in 2007. The first new tankhouse totally equipped with METTOP-BRX-Technology at Xiangguang Copper, China, will start operation in June 2011 using a current density of 410 A/m².
